questions.explanation: Soft thresholding: $|S_{xy}| - \lambda/2 = 18 - 15 = 3 > 0$, so $b = \operatorname{sign}(S_{xy}) \cdot 3/40 = -0.075$. The slope is zero only when $\lambda \ge 2|S_{xy}| = 36$. $-0.45$ is least squares and $-0.257 = -18/70$ is ridge with the same $\lambda$.

questions.stem: Which method can set some regression coefficients exactly to zero, and so selects variables?
choices: Ridge regression with $\lambda$ chosen by cross-validation
questions.explanation: The absolute-value penalty has a kink at 0, so the minimum can sit exactly at 0 (soft thresholding); geometrically, the diamond constraint has corners on the axes. Ridge divides by $S_{xx} + \lambda$ (or adds $\lambda\mathbf I$), which shrinks coefficients toward 0 but leaves them nonzero for any finite $\lambda$.

questions.stem: Why are predictors usually standardized before fitting ridge or lasso?
choices: Standardizing makes the errors normally distributed
Without it the matrix $\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X + \lambda\mathbf I$ may not be invertible
Cross-validation only works with standardized predictors
The penalty treats all coefficients alike, so a coefficient's size must not depend on the units of its predictor
questions.explanation: A coefficient's size depends on its predictor's units: switching from metres to millimetres divides the coefficient by 1000 and nearly removes its penalty. Standardizing puts every predictor on the same scale so the penalty is fair. $\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X + \lambda\mathbf I$ is invertible for any $\lambda > 0$ either way, and standardizing does nothing to the error distribution.

questions.stem: For a single centered predictor with true slope $\beta = 2$ and error variance $\sigma^2 = 9$, which ridge penalty $\lambda$ minimizes the MSE of the slope estimate?
questions.explanation: $\operatorname{MSE}(\lambda) = (\sigma^2S_{xx} + \lambda^2\beta^2)/(S_{xx} + \lambda)^2$ has derivative $2S_{xx}(\lambda\beta^2 - \sigma^2)/(S_{xx} + \lambda)^3$, which is zero at $\lambda^* = \sigma^2/\beta^2 = 9/4 = 2.25$, whatever $S_{xx}$ is. 0.444 inverts the ratio, 4.5 uses $\sigma^2/\beta$, and 1.5 uses $\sigma/\beta$.

questions.stem: With $N(0, \sigma^2)$ errors, the ridge estimate with penalty $\lambda$ is the posterior mean of $\boldsymbol\beta$ under which prior?
choices: Independent Laplace (double exponential) priors on the $\beta_j$
questions.explanation: The log posterior is $-\text{RSS}/(2\sigma^2) - \sum\beta_j^2/(2\tau^2)$ plus a constant; multiplying by $-2\sigma^2$ gives RSS $+ (\sigma^2/\tau^2)\sum\beta_j^2$, so $\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2$, that is $\tau^2 = \sigma^2/\lambda$. The posterior is normal, so its mean and mode agree. Larger $\lambda$ means a tighter prior, not a wider one. A flat prior gives least squares; Laplace priors give the lasso as the posterior mode.

questions.stem: Why can't $\lambda$ be chosen by minimizing the residual sum of squares on the data used to fit the model?
choices: The residual sum of squares does not depend on $\lambda$
The residual sum of squares is always smallest at the largest $\lambda$
It would choose the $\lambda$ that maximizes the bias
Least squares minimizes that sum, so the training error is always smallest at $\lambda = 0$
questions.explanation: Least squares is by definition the minimizer of the training RSS, so any penalty can only raise it. Training error measures fit to this sample, noise included; the error on new data is what matters, and cross-validation or a held-out test set estimates it.

questions.stem: Cross-validation errors for four values of $\lambda$ are $\lambda = 0.1$: 3.20; $\lambda = 1$: 2.95; $\lambda = 10$: 3.05; $\lambda = 100$: 3.60. The standard error at the minimum is 0.15. Which $\lambda$ does the one-standard-error rule choose?
questions.explanation: The minimum is 2.95 at $\lambda = 1$, so the threshold is $2.95 + 0.15 = 3.10$. The rule takes the largest $\lambda$ (the most heavily penalized, simplest model) with CV error at most 3.10: $\lambda = 10$ (3.05). $\lambda = 100$ (3.60) is above the threshold, and $\lambda = 1$ is the plain minimum rule.

questions.stem: One centered predictor has $S_{xx} = 20$ and $S_{xy} = 12$. With $\lambda = 8$ the lasso estimate of the slope (criterion RSS $+ \lambda|b|$) is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $|S_{xy}| - \lambda/2 = 12 - 4 = 8 > 0$, so $b = 8/20 = 0.4$. (Least squares gives $12/20 = 0.6$; ridge with $\lambda = 8$ would give $12/28 \approx 0.429$.)

questions.stem: One centered predictor has $S_{xx} = 25$ and $S_{xy} = -15$. The lasso slope (criterion RSS $+ \lambda|b|$) is exactly zero for every $\lambda$ at or above ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Soft thresholding gives zero when $|S_{xy}| - \lambda/2 \le 0$, that is $\lambda \ge 2|S_{xy}| = 30$. The sign of $S_{xy}$ does not matter, and $S_{xx}$ only scales the nonzero answers.

questions.stem: Put the steps of choosing $\lambda$ by $K$-fold cross-validation in order.
choices: Split the data at random into $K$ folds
Fit the model for each $\lambda$ on all folds but one
Compute the squared prediction errors on the held-out fold
Average the errors over all $K$ folds for each $\lambda$
Choose the $\lambda$ with the smallest average error
Refit on all the data with the chosen $\lambda$
questions.explanation: The folds must exist before anything is held out; each fit is evaluated only on the fold it did not see; the CV error for a $\lambda$ is the average over all $K$ folds; and only after $\lambda$ is chosen is the final model fitted to the full data set.

questions.stem: Which statements about ridge regression are true? Select all that apply.
choices: For every $\lambda > 0$, $\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X + \lambda\mathbf I$ is invertible, even when $p > n$
With a moderate $\lambda$ it sets the weakest coefficients exactly to zero
At $\lambda = 0$ it is ordinary least squares
Increasing $\lambda$ lowers the variance of the coefficient estimates
The intercept is normally penalized along with the slopes
questions.explanation: $\mathbf v^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X + \lambda\mathbf I)\mathbf v = \|\mathbf X\mathbf v\|^2 + \lambda\|\mathbf v\|^2 > 0$ for $\mathbf v \ne \mathbf 0$, so the matrix is positive definite and invertible. $\lambda = 0$ removes the penalty. More penalty means less variance (and more bias). Ridge never gives exact zeros (that is the lasso), and the intercept is left unpenalized; with centered data it is $\bar y$.

questions.stem: Match each term to its description.
choices: Sum of squared coefficients times λ
Sum of absolute coefficients times λ
Estimates prediction error on held-out data
Moves an estimate toward 0 by a fixed amount and stops at 0
Average squared residual on the data used for fitting
questions.explanation: Ridge adds $\lambda\sum\beta_j^2$ and the lasso adds $\lambda\sum|\beta_j|$. Cross-validation holds out part of the data to estimate error on new data; the training error (the distractor) is what it replaces. Soft thresholding, $\operatorname{sign}(z)(|z| - c)_+$, is the lasso's one-predictor solution.

questions.stem: Both panels show the same contours of the residual sum of squares and a constraint region: a diamond on the left, a disk on the right. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Two panels with axes b1 and b2. In each, nested ellipses surround a point in the upper right. Left: a shaded diamond centered at the origin, with a dot where the outer ellipse touches its top corner on the b2 axis. Right: a shaded disk centered at the origin, with a dot where the outer ellipse touches it at a point off both axes.

choices: Contour of the residual sum of squares
questions.explanation: The ellipses are contours of the residual sum of squares, centered at the least squares estimate. The penalized solution is where the smallest contour touches the constraint region. The diamond $|b_1| + |b_2| \le t$ is the lasso region, and its contact point is a corner on the $b_2$ axis, so $b_1 = 0$. The disk $b_1^2 + b_2^2 \le t^2$ is the ridge region; its contact point has both coefficients nonzero. Marker 5 is inside the disk, so it is the ridge region, not the lasso region.

questions.stem: Ten independent tests are run at $\alpha = 0.05$, and every null hypothesis is true. What is the probability of at least one false rejection?
questions.explanation: $P(\text{no false rejection}) = 0.95^{10} = 0.599$, so $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - 0.599 = 0.401$. $0.5 = m\alpha$ is the expected number of false rejections (and a Bonferroni upper bound), not a probability; 0.599 is the complement.

questions.stem: With $V$ false rejections and $R$ total rejections ($V/R$ taken as 0 when $R = 0$), the false discovery rate is
questions.explanation: The false discovery proportion is $V/R$ and the FDR is its expectation. $P(V \ge 1)$ is the familywise error rate. $E(V)/m$ is the per-comparison error rate, which divides by the number of tests, not the number of discoveries.

questions.stem: Five sorted p-values are 0.002, 0.009, 0.012, 0.030, 0.20. How many hypotheses does Holm's procedure reject at $\alpha = 0.05$?
Six sorted p-values are 0.003, 0.014, 0.016, 0.035, 0.041, 0.30. How many hypotheses does Benjamini–Hochberg reject at $q = 0.05$?
questions.explanation: The BH lines $kq/m$ are 0.0083, 0.0167, 0.025, 0.0333, 0.0417, 0.05. $p_{(4)} = 0.035$ is above its line, but $p_{(5)} = 0.041 \le 0.0417$, and $p_{(6)} = 0.30 > 0.05$. The largest $k$ under the line is 5, so BH rejects the five smallest, including $p_{(4)}$. Answering 3 stops at the first failure, which is how a step-down method works, not the step-up BH.

questions.stem: For a test with a continuous test statistic, what is the distribution of the p-value when the null hypothesis is true?
questions.explanation: For an upper-tailed test the p-value is $1 - F_0(T)$, and $F_0(T) \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)$ under $H_0$ by the probability integral transform; so is one minus it. Hence $P(p \le u) = u$. Concentration near 0 is what happens under the alternative.

questions.stem: If every one of the $m$ null hypotheses is true, how do FDR and FWER compare for any procedure?
questions.explanation: With every null true, every rejection is false, so $V = R$ and $V/R = 1$ whenever $R \ge 1$. Then $\text{FDR} = E(V/R) = P(R \ge 1) = P(V \ge 1) = \text{FWER}$. This is why BH still controls FWER in the "nothing is going on" case. When some nulls are false, $\text{FDR} \le \text{FWER}$.

questions.stem: A screen runs 2,000 tests at $\alpha = 0.01$ each. 1,800 nulls are true; the 200 real effects are each detected with power 0.6. About what fraction of the discoveries are false?
questions.explanation: Expected false discoveries $1800(0.01) = 18$; expected true discoveries $200(0.6) = 120$. Of about 138 discoveries, $18/138 \approx 0.13$ are false. 0.15 divides by the true discoveries only, 0.09 divides by the 200 real effects, and 0.01 is the per-test level, which is not the fraction of discoveries that are false.

questions.stem: With $m = 10$, the sorted p-values are 0.001, 0.005, 0.012, 0.014, 0.03, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9. What is the BH-adjusted p-value of the third smallest, 0.012?
questions.explanation: $\tilde p_{(3)} = \min_{j \ge 3} \tfrac{m}{j}p_{(j)}$. The candidates are $10(0.012)/3 = 0.04$, $10(0.014)/4 = 0.035$, $10(0.03)/5 = 0.06$, and larger ones after that. The minimum is 0.035: if BH rejects the fourth hypothesis it rejects the third too. 0.04 forgets the minimum; 0.12 is the Bonferroni adjustment $10 \times 0.012$.

questions.stem: Holm's procedure is run on $m = 10$ p-values at $\alpha = 0.05$. If it gets that far, the third smallest p-value is compared with the threshold ___. Give the number.
questions.explanation: The $k$-th smallest p-value is compared with $\alpha/(m - k + 1)$. For $k = 3$: $0.05/(10 - 3 + 1) = 0.05/8 = 0.00625$. (A fraction such as 1/160 is accepted as the same number.)

questions.stem: Five sorted p-values are 0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.09, 0.4. At $q = 0.10$, Benjamini–Hochberg rejects ___ hypotheses. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The lines $kq/m = 0.02k$ are 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10. $0.4 > 0.10$ and $0.09 > 0.08$, but $0.05 \le 0.06$, so the largest $k$ under the line is 3 and the three smallest are rejected.

questions.stem: With $m = 10$ tests and $\alpha = q = 0.05$, put the thresholds that the second smallest p-value is compared with in order, from strictest (smallest) to most lenient.
questions.explanation: The numbers are $0.05/10 = 0.005$, $0.05/9 = 0.00556$, $2(0.05)/10 = 0.01$ and $0.05$. Holm is a little more lenient than Bonferroni at every step after the first; BH's line rises linearly in $k$ and is more lenient still, because it controls the weaker FDR.

questions.stem: Which procedures control the familywise error rate at level $\alpha$ whatever the dependence among the tests? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Bonferroni and Holm both rest on the union bound, which needs no independence. BH and Benjamini–Yekutieli control the false discovery rate, which is weaker than FWER when some nulls are false. Running every test at $\alpha$ controls nothing across the family: with $m$ independent true nulls, $P(V \ge 1) = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^m$.

questions.stem: Match each term to its description.
choices: Probability of at least one false rejection
Expected fraction of rejections that are false
Starts at the smallest p-value and stops at the first failure
Finds the largest index under its threshold and rejects all smaller p-values
Fraction of all hypotheses that are true nulls
questions.explanation: FWER $= P(V \ge 1)$ and FDR $= E(V/R)$. Holm is step-down; Benjamini–Hochberg is step-up. The distractor describes $m_0/m$, which appears in the BH theorem ($\text{FDR} = m_0q/m$) but is not an error rate.

questions.stem: Eight sorted p-values are plotted against their rank $k$, with $m = 8$ and $\alpha = q = 0.05$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Sorted p-values against rank 1 to 8. A rising straight line through the origin region up to 0.05 at rank 8; a nearly flat dashed line at about 0.006; a dotted curve of square points starting at 0.006 and bending up to 0.05 at rank 8. Five filled dots lie on or below the straight line, a sixth open dot lies above it, and two more are off the top of the chart.

questions.explanation: The straight line through rank $k$ at height $0.05k/8$ is the BH line. The flat dashed line is Bonferroni's $0.05/8 = 0.00625$. The bending curve is Holm's $0.05/(9 - k)$: equal to Bonferroni at $k = 1$ and rising to 0.05 at $k = 8$. The fifth p-value (0.031) is the last on or below the BH line, so BH rejects ranks 1 to 5; the sixth (0.044) is above its line, 0.0375, and is not rejected.

questions.stem: Why can the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm sample from a posterior whose normalizing constant $Z$ is unknown?
choices: It estimates $Z$ by numerical integration before the chain starts
It approximates the posterior by a normal distribution
The acceptance probability uses only the ratio $f(y)/f(x)$, in which $Z$ cancels
It samples from the prior, which needs no normalizing constant
questions.explanation: The target is $\pi(x) = f(x)/Z$, and the algorithm only ever uses $\pi(y)/\pi(x) = f(y)/f(x)$ (times a proposal ratio), so $Z$ is never needed. That is exactly what makes MCMC useful for posteriors, which are known only up to a constant.

questions.stem: A random-walk Metropolis sampler targets $N(0, 1)$, so $f(x) = e^{-x^2/2}$. The current state is $x = 1$ and the proposal is $y = 2$. What is the acceptance probability?
questions.explanation: The proposal is symmetric, so $\alpha = \min(1, f(2)/f(1)) = \min(1, e^{-(4 - 1)/2}) = e^{-1.5} = 0.223$. 0.5 compares the states themselves, 0.777 is $1 - \alpha$, and 1 would be right only for a move to higher density.

questions.stem: A transition matrix $P$ satisfies $\pi(x)P(x, y) = \pi(y)P(y, x)$ for all states $x, y$. What follows?
choices: $\pi$ is a stationary distribution of the chain
questions.explanation: This is detailed balance. Summing over $x$: $\sum_x \pi(x)P(x, y) = \pi(y)\sum_x P(y, x) = \pi(y)$, so $\pi P = \pi$. It does not make $P$ symmetric (that needs $\pi$ uniform), and it says nothing about irreducibility, which is a separate condition for convergence.

questions.stem: Three states in a cycle have weights $f = (3, 1, 2)$. From each state a Metropolis sampler proposes each of the other two states with probability 1/2. What is $P(1, 1)$, the probability of staying at state 1?
questions.explanation: From state 1 ($f = 3$): propose 2 with probability 1/2, accepted with probability $\min(1, 1/3) = 1/3$, so $P(1, 2) = 1/6$; propose 3 with probability 1/2, accepted with probability $2/3$, so $P(1, 3) = 1/3$. The rest is rejections: $P(1, 1) = 1 - 1/6 - 1/3 = 1/2$. The answer 0 forgets that rejected proposals leave the chain where it is.

questions.stem: With an asymmetric proposal, $f(x) = 2$, $f(y) = 3$, $q(y \mid x) = 0.5$ and $q(x \mid y) = 0.2$. What is the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability for moving from $x$ to $y$?
questions.explanation: $\alpha = \min\left(1, \dfrac{f(y)q(x \mid y)}{f(x)q(y \mid x)}\right) = \min\left(1, \dfrac{3(0.2)}{2(0.5)}\right) = 0.6$. Ignoring the Hastings correction gives $\min(1, 3/2) = 1$; 0.667 inverts the target ratio; 0.3 leaves out $q(y \mid x)$.

questions.stem: An MCMC run of $N = 5000$ draws has autocorrelations close to $\rho^k$ with $\rho = 0.8$. About how many independent draws is it worth?
questions.explanation: $\text{ESS} \approx N(1 - \rho)/(1 + \rho) = 5000(0.2)/1.8 \approx 556$. 1000 forgets the $1 + \rho$, 2778 forgets the $1 - \rho$, and 4000 multiplies by $\rho$.

questions.stem: A random-walk Metropolis sampler uses a very small step size. What happens?
choices: Almost every proposal is rejected, so the chain rarely moves
The chain converges in fewer iterations
Almost every proposal is accepted, but the chain moves slowly and its draws are highly correlated
questions.explanation: A tiny step barely changes the density, so the ratio is near 1 and nearly every move is accepted, but each move is tiny, so exploring the posterior takes very long and the effective sample size is small. Very large steps cause the opposite problem, mostly rejections. The stationary distribution is $\pi$ for any step size; only the speed changes.

questions.stem: When a Metropolis–Hastings proposal is rejected, what is recorded as the next draw?
choices: Nothing; only accepted values are kept
A fresh draw from the proposal distribution
questions.explanation: The chain stays put, and the current state is recorded again. Repeats are part of the correct sample: they give extra weight to high-density states, where proposals tend to be rejected. Dropping them would bias the draws toward low-density regions.

questions.stem: A random-walk Metropolis sampler targets $f(x) = e^{-x^2/2}$. From $x = 0$ it proposes $y = 1$. The acceptance probability, to 3 decimal places, is ___.
questions.explanation: $\alpha = \min(1, f(1)/f(0)) = e^{-1/2} \approx 0.607$. A move away from the mode is accepted with probability equal to the density ratio.

questions.stem: The early iterations of an MCMC run, discarded because they still reflect the starting value rather than the target distribution, are called the ___.
questions.explanation: They are the burn-in (some software says warm-up). Discarding them removes the influence of the starting point; it does not fix a chain that mixes slowly.

questions.stem: Put the parts of one Metropolis–Hastings iteration in order, starting from the current state $x$.
choices: Record the next state: $y$ if accepted, $x$ again if not
questions.explanation: $\alpha$ depends on $y$, so the proposal comes first; the uniform draw is compared with $\alpha$, so $\alpha$ must be known; and the recorded state depends on that comparison.

questions.stem: Which statements about MCMC output are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Consecutive draws are usually positively correlated
Under the conditions of the ergodic theorem, chain averages converge to expectations under the target
The target's normalizing constant must be computed before sampling
Draws from early in the run may need to be discarded
An acceptance rate of 100% means the sampler is working perfectly
questions.explanation: Each state is built from the previous one, so draws are correlated; the ergodic theorem is a law of large numbers for the chain; and burn-in draws reflect the start, not the target. The constant cancels in the acceptance ratio. An acceptance rate near 100% usually means tiny steps and slow exploration (Gibbs sampling, which accepts every update by design, is the exception).

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning.
choices: The next state depends on the past only through the current state
If the chain is in it at one step it stays in it at the next
Equilibrium flow from x to y equals the flow from y to x
Number of independent draws with the same precision
Probability that every proposal is accepted
questions.explanation: These are the definitions from the lesson: the Markov property, $\pi P = \pi$, $\pi(x)P(x, y) = \pi(y)P(y, x)$, and ESS $\approx N(1 - \rho)/(1 + \rho)$ for AR(1)-type autocorrelation.

questions.stem: This trace plot shows 200 Metropolis iterations for a Poisson rate $\lambda$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A trace plot of lambda against iteration from 0 to 200. A dot marks the first value at 9. The line drops through a shaded band covering the first 25 iterations, then moves up and down between about 1 and 4, with some short flat stretches.

questions.explanation: The chain starts at 9, far from where the posterior has its mass, and the shaded early stretch is burn-in, discarded. A flat segment means the same value was recorded several times: proposals were rejected and the chain stayed put. After burn-in the chain moves back and forth over the posterior (mostly between 1 and 4; the posterior mean is about 2.28).

questions.stem: Events $A$, $B$, $C$ each have probability 0.4, each pair has intersection probability 0.15, and $P(A \cap B \cap C) = 0.05$. Then $P(A \cup B \cup C) =$ ___. Give a decimal or fraction.
questions.explanation: Inclusion–exclusion: add the singles, subtract the pairs, add the triple: $3(0.4) - 3(0.15) + 0.05 = 1.2 - 0.45 + 0.05 = 0.8$. Stopping after the pairs gives 0.75, which leaves out the triple region.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the proof of the complement rule $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$ in order.
choices: $A$ and $A^c$ are disjoint, and $A \cup A^c = S$
questions.explanation: Additivity may only be used once we know the two events are disjoint, so that fact comes first. Additivity turns $P(A \cup A^c)$ into a sum; since the union is $S$, axiom 2 says the sum is 1; and subtracting $P(A)$ gives the rule.

questions.stem: Match each description to the event it describes.
left: At least one of $A$ and $B$ occurs
questions.explanation: "At least one" is the union $A \cup B$. "Neither" is its complement, which De Morgan's law writes as $A^c \cap B^c$. "Not both" is the complement of $A \cap B$, which is $A^c \cup B^c$. "$A$ but not $B$" is the difference $A \cap B^c$.

questions.stem: Which statements are true for every pair of events $A$ and $B$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $A \cap B \subseteq A$, so monotonicity gives the first. The union bound is the second, and the Bonferroni inequality (from $P(A \cup B) \le 1$) is the last. The plain sum $P(A) + P(B)$ equals $P(A \cup B)$ only for disjoint events, and the product rule holds only for independent events.

questions.stem: Name each numbered region of the Venn diagram of events $A$, $B$ and $C$.

image.alt: Three overlapping circles A (top left), B (top right) and C (bottom) inside a rectangle S. Marker 1 is in the center, inside all three circles. Marker 2 is where only A and B overlap, at the top. Marker 3 is where only A and C overlap, at the lower left. Marker 4 is in the part of C outside A and B. Marker 5 is in the rectangle outside all three circles.

questions.explanation: For each region, ask which circles contain it: an event appears plain if the region is inside its circle and with a complement if it is outside. Region 1 is inside all three; region 2 is inside $A$ and $B$ but not $C$; region 3 is inside $A$ and $C$ but not $B$; region 4 is only in $C$; region 5 is outside every circle, so it is $(A \cup B \cup C)^c = A^c \cap B^c \cap C^c$.

questions.stem: From 9 runners, 4 are chosen and assigned to the four legs of a relay (first, second, third, anchor). This can be done in ___ ways. If instead 4 runners are simply chosen as a group, with no legs assigned, there are ___ possible groups.
questions.explanation: Assigning legs makes order matter: $9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 = 3024$. An unordered group is $\binom94 = \dfrac{3024}{4!} = 126$, because each group of 4 can be put in order in $4! = 24$ ways.

questions.stem: Match each situation to its count.
left: A 5-letter code from 26 letters, repeats allowed
Gold, silver and bronze winners among 26 runners
Distinct arrangements of the letters of BANANA
questions.explanation: Order matters with repeats allowed: $26^5$. Ordered without repeats (distinct medals): $26 \cdot 25 \cdot 24$. Unordered: $\binom{26}{3}$. BANANA has 6 letters with 3 A's and 2 N's, so $6!/(3!\,2!) = 60$; dividing only by $3!$ forgets the identical N's.

questions.stem: In which situations does the order of the selected items matter? Select all that apply.
choices: Electing a president, treasurer and secretary from a club
Recording the first three finishers of a race in order
questions.explanation: Order matters when positions or roles differ: distinct offices, the digits of a PIN (1234 and 4321 are different PINs), and finishing places. A card hand and a set of lottery numbers are the same no matter the order in which they were drawn.

questions.stem: Put these counts in order from smallest to largest.
questions.explanation: $\binom83 = 56$, $8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 = 336$ (which is $3! \times 56$), $8^3 = 512$ (repeats allowed adds more), and $3^8 = 6561$.

questions.stem: Three letters are put at random into their three addressed envelopes, one per envelope. The probability that no letter is in its own envelope is ___. Give an exact fraction.
questions.explanation: Of the $3! = 6$ equally likely assignments, only 2 move every letter (the two cyclic shifts), so the probability is $2/6 = 1/3$. The matching formula agrees: $P(\text{some match}) = 1 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac23$, and $1 - \tfrac23 = \tfrac13$.

questions.stem: Of a supplier's parts, 2% are defective. An inspection flags 90% of defective parts and 10% of good parts. Then $P(\text{flagged}) =$ ___ and $P(\text{defective and flagged}) =$ ___. Give decimals.
questions.explanation: The path for defective and flagged is $0.02 \times 0.90 = 0.018$. The path for good and flagged is $0.98 \times 0.10 = 0.098$. Total probability: $P(\text{flagged}) = 0.018 + 0.098 = 0.116$. (So $P(\text{defective} \mid \text{flagged}) = 0.018/0.116 \approx 0.155$.)

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding a posterior probability $P(B_j \mid A)$ in order.
choices: Draw the tree, with the priors on the first branches and the likelihoods on the second
Add the paths that end in $A$ to get $P(A)$
questions.explanation: Each step uses the one before it: the path products need the branch probabilities, the total $P(A)$ is the sum of the path products, and Bayes' theorem divides one path by that total.

questions.stem: Scenario $B$ and its complement form a partition, and $A$ is the evidence. Match each quantity to its notation.
left: Probability of the tree path through $B$ that ends in $A$
questions.explanation: The prior is how likely $B$ was before the evidence, $P(B)$. The likelihood is how likely the evidence is if $B$ holds, $P(A \mid B)$. The posterior is the updated probability of $B$, $P(B \mid A)$. A path's probability is the product $P(B)P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)$.

questions.stem: For events with positive probabilities, which expressions always equal $P(A \cap B)$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The first two are the multiplication rule, written both ways. The last holds because $B$ splits into the disjoint parts $A \cap B$ and $A^c \cap B$. $P(A)P(B)$ is correct only for independent events, and the product of the two conditional probabilities has no meaning as a rule (with $P(A) = P(B) = 0.5$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.25$, it gives $0.25$, but with $P(A \cap B) = 0.4$ it gives $0.64$).

questions.stem: Name each numbered part of this probability tree for a scenario $B$ and evidence $A$.

image.alt: A probability tree with no probabilities written. From a starting point, an upper branch leads to node B and a lower branch to a second node. From each of those, branches lead to leaves A (upper) and A complement (lower). Marker 1 is on the branch from the start to B. Marker 2 is on the branch from B to its A leaf. Marker 3 is beside the A leaf reached through B. Marker 4 is beside the A leaf reached through the lower node. Marker 5 is on the lower node itself.

questions.explanation: First-stage branches carry the priors, so marker 1 is $P(B)$. A second-stage branch carries the probability of the evidence given the branch it leaves, so marker 2 is $P(A \mid B)$. Each leaf gets the product of its path: marker 3 is $P(B)P(A \mid B) = P(B \cap A)$ and marker 4 is $P(B^c \cap A)$. The lower node is $B^c$. The posterior $P(B \mid A)$ is not on the tree; it is marker 3 divided by the sum of markers 3 and 4.

questions.stem: Five sensors each detect a leak with probability 0.6, independently. The probability that at least one detects it is ___. Give the exact decimal.
questions.explanation: All five miss with probability $0.4^5 = 0.01024$, so at least one detects it with probability $1 - 0.01024 = 0.98976$. Adding $5 \times 0.6 = 3$ is an expected count, not a probability.

questions.stem: Each component works with probability 0.9, independently of the others. Match each system to its reliability.
questions.explanation: Series: every component must work, $0.9^2 = 0.81$ and $0.9^3 = 0.729$. Parallel: the system fails only if all fail, $1 - 0.1^2 = 0.99$ and $1 - 0.1^3 = 0.999$. (0.19 is the chance that at least one of two components fails.)

questions.stem: $A$ and $B$ are independent, with $P(A) = 0.5$ and $P(B) = 0.4$. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Independence gives $P(A \cap B) = 0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.2$, so $P(A \cup B) = 0.5 + 0.4 - 0.2 = 0.7$. Complements of independent events are independent. They are not mutually exclusive, because their intersection has probability 0.2, not 0. And $P(A \mid B) = P(A) = 0.5$, not 0.4.

questions.stem: In the unit square, $A$ is the strip of width $P(A) = 0.4$ on the left and $B$ is the strip of height $P(B) = 0.3$ at the bottom, for independent events $A$ and $B$. Name each numbered piece and its probability.

image.alt: A unit square split by a vertical line, with P(A) = 0.4 marked on the left part and P(A complement) = 0.6 on the right, and by a horizontal line, with P(B) = 0.3 marked on the bottom part and P(B complement) = 0.7 on the top. Markers: 1 bottom left, 2 top left, 3 bottom right, 4 top right.

questions.explanation: Each piece is a rectangle, so its probability is width times height: $0.4 \times 0.3 = 0.12$ (bottom left), $0.4 \times 0.7 = 0.28$ (top left), $0.6 \times 0.3 = 0.18$ (bottom right) and $0.6 \times 0.7 = 0.42$ (top right). The four add to 1. Adding the widths and heights (0.7, or $1 - 0.7$) is not how the areas work.

questions.stem: Each component works with probability 0.8, independently. Put these systems in order from least reliable to most reliable.
questions.explanation: Reliabilities: $0.8^3 = 0.512$, $0.8^2 = 0.64$, $0.8$, and $1 - 0.2^2 = 0.96$. Each extra component in series lowers reliability; a parallel backup raises it.

questions.stem: Ann and Ben take turns tossing a fair coin, Ann first. The first person to toss heads wins. What is the probability that Ann wins?
questions.explanation: First-step analysis on a round: Ann wins at once with probability $\tfrac12$, and both miss with probability $\tfrac14$, which restarts the game. So $a = \tfrac12 + \tfrac14 a$, giving $a = \tfrac23$. Going first is worth a lot: Ben wins only $\tfrac13$ of the time.

questions.stem: Ann and Ben take turns, Ann first. On each of her turns Ann succeeds with probability $\tfrac14$; on each of his, Ben succeeds with probability $\tfrac13$. The first to succeed wins. The probability that Ann wins is ___.
questions.explanation: Condition on a full round: $a = \tfrac14 + \tfrac34 \cdot \tfrac23\, a = \tfrac14 + \tfrac12 a$, so $a = \tfrac12$. Or use $a = p/(p + r - pr) = \tfrac14 / \bigl(\tfrac14 + \tfrac13 - \tfrac1{12}\bigr) = \tfrac14/\tfrac12$. Going first exactly makes up for Ann's lower success rate.

questions.stem: In craps, the point is 6. What is the probability that the shooter rolls a 6 before a 7?
questions.explanation: Only the race between 6 and 7 matters: $P(6) = \tfrac5{36}$ and $P(7) = \tfrac6{36}$, so $w_6 = \dfrac{5}{5 + 6} = \tfrac5{11}$. $\tfrac5{36}$ is the chance of a 6 on a single roll, and $\tfrac6{11}$ is the chance that the 7 comes first.

questions.stem: Once a point $k$ is set in craps, why can the rolls that are neither $k$ nor 7 be ignored?
choices: They are less likely than $k$ and 7 combined
They count as half a win each
After such a roll the situation is exactly as before, so they do not change the chance of winning
The rules say they are rerolled with a different pair of dice
questions.explanation: First-step analysis: after a roll that is neither $k$ nor 7, the game is in the same state as before, so $w_k = P(k) + (1 - P(k) - P(7))w_k$. Solving gives $w_k = P(k)/(P(k) + P(7))$, the conditional probability of $k$ given that the roll is $k$ or 7. (Other sums are in fact more likely than $k$ and 7 combined, so the first choice is false as well as irrelevant.)

questions.stem: A gambler with \$30 makes fair \$1 bets until she has \$50 or nothing. What is the probability that she goes broke?
questions.explanation: In a fair game $P_i = i/N$, so she reaches \$50 with probability $30/50 = 0.6$ and goes broke with probability $1 - 0.6 = 0.4$. Choosing 0.6 answers the wrong question, and 0.5 ignores where she starts.

questions.stem: In a fair game of \$1 bets, a gambler starts with \$3 and stops at \$10 or \$0. The probability that she reaches \$10 is ___.
questions.explanation: Fair game: $P_i = i/N = 3/10 = 0.3$.

questions.stem: A gambler wins each \$1 bet with probability 0.4. She starts with \$2 and stops at \$4 or \$0. What is the probability that she reaches \$4?
questions.explanation: $\rho = q/p = 0.6/0.4 = 1.5$, so $P_2 = \dfrac{1 - 1.5^2}{1 - 1.5^4} = \dfrac{-1.25}{-4.0625} = \dfrac{4}{13} \approx 0.308$. Check by first-step analysis: $P_2 = 0.4P_3 + 0.6P_1$, $P_1 = 0.4P_2$, $P_3 = 0.4 + 0.6P_2$, so $P_2 = 0.16 + 0.48P_2$ and $P_2 = 0.16/0.52 = 4/13$. $\tfrac12$ is the fair-game answer and $\tfrac4{25} = 0.4^2$ counts only winning the next two bets.

questions.stem: Which statements about the gambler's ruin with target $N$ are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The recursion $P_i = pP_{i+1} + qP_{i-1}$ alone determines $P_i$
If $p < \tfrac12$ and the opponent has unlimited money, ruin is certain
In the roulette example (\$20, goal \$40), \$1 bets give a better chance of reaching the goal than one bold bet
questions.explanation: The fair-game formula, the absorbing ends and certain ruin against an unlimited opponent when $p \le \tfrac12$ are all results of the lesson. The recursion needs the boundary conditions $P_0 = 0$, $P_N = 1$ to pick one solution. In the roulette example, timid play reaches \$40 with probability about 0.108 and bold play about 0.474.

questions.stem: Put the steps for solving the gambler's ruin in order.
choices: Condition on the first bet: $P_i = pP_{i+1} + qP_{i-1}$
Rewrite it as $p(P_{i+1} - P_i) = q(P_i - P_{i-1})$
Conclude that the steps grow geometrically: $d_i = \rho^{i-1} d_1$
questions.explanation: The recursion comes from the first bet; splitting $P_i$ as $pP_i + qP_i$ turns it into a statement about consecutive differences, which therefore form a geometric sequence. Adding the differences from $P_0 = 0$ gives $P_i$ in terms of $d_1$, and the other boundary condition $P_N = 1$ fixes $d_1$.

questions.stem: This picture shows the gambler's ruin with target $N = 6$ as a random walk. Name each numbered part.

image.alt: Seven circles in a row for the states 0 to 6, with right arrows on top and left arrows below between neighbors. The two end circles are double circles. Marker 1 is on the left end circle, marker 2 on the right end circle, marker 3 on a right-pointing arrow, marker 4 on a left-pointing arrow, and marker 5 on the highlighted circle for state 2.

questions.explanation: The walk moves right (up one dollar) with probability $p$ and left with probability $q = 1 - p$. It stops for good at 0 (ruin) and at $N = 6$ (the target), which is why those are drawn as double circles with no arrows leaving them. The highlighted state is where the gambler starts.

questions.stem: A gambler wins each \$1 bet with probability 0.6 and plays against an opponent with unlimited money. Starting with \$3, what is the probability that she is never ruined?
questions.explanation: With $p > \tfrac12$, $P(\text{never ruined}) = 1 - (q/p)^i = 1 - (0.4/0.6)^3 = 1 - \tfrac{8}{27} = \tfrac{19}{27} \approx 0.704$. $\tfrac{8}{27}$ is the probability that she is eventually ruined.

questions.stem: A match between equally skilled players is interrupted when A needs 1 more win and B needs 3. What fraction of the stake should A get?
questions.explanation: B wins the match only by winning the next 3 rounds in a row, with probability $(\tfrac12)^3 = \tfrac18$. So A's share is $1 - \tfrac18 = \tfrac78$. Fermat's method agrees: A needs at least 1 win in $1 + 3 - 1 = 3$ rounds.

questions.stem: Player A wins each round with probability 0.6. The first to win 2 more rounds takes the stake, and each player needs 2. What is the probability that A wins the match?
questions.explanation: The match is decided within $2 + 2 - 1 = 3$ rounds. A wins if she wins at least 2 of 3: $3(0.6)^2(0.4) + 0.6^3 = 0.432 + 0.216 = 0.648$. 0.36 counts only winning the next two rounds, and 0.5 ignores A's edge.

questions.stem: Match each problem to its first-step equation ($q = 1 - p$).
left: Alternating race, success $p$ for the first player and $r$ for the second
Craps once the point $k$ is set
Problem of points, A needs $a$ and B needs $b$
questions.explanation: Each equation conditions on the next step. In the race, a full round with two misses restarts the game. In the ruin problem a win (probability $p$) moves the fortune up to $i + 1$; the distractor has the moves backwards. In craps a roll that is neither $k$ nor 7 leaves things unchanged. In the problem of points, a round won by A lowers the number A needs.

questions.stem: A roulette player (red wins with probability $18/38$) has \$20 and wants \$40. Which strategy gives the better chance, and roughly what are the chances?
choices: \$1 bets: about 0.47, against about 0.11 for one \$20 bet
One \$20 bet: about 0.47, against about 0.11 for \$1 bets
They are equal, since every bet has the same odds
\$1 bets, because small bets average out the losses
questions.explanation: One bold bet wins with probability $18/38 \approx 0.474$. Timid play has $\rho = 10/9$ and $P_{20} = \dfrac{1 - (10/9)^{20}}{1 - (10/9)^{40}} \approx 0.108$. In an unfavorable game, many small bets give the house edge many chances to act.

questions.stem: For a fair game, which sequences satisfy the recursion $P_i = \tfrac12 P_{i+1} + \tfrac12 P_{i-1}$ for $1 \le i \le N - 1$?
choices: Every sequence of the form $P_i = c_1 + c_2 i$
questions.explanation: The recursion says each value is the average of its neighbors, which holds exactly for sequences that change by the same amount at each step: $P_i = c_1 + c_2 i$. That is why the boundary conditions $P_0 = 0$ and $P_N = 1$ are needed; they force $c_1 = 0$ and $c_2 = 1/N$. ($2^i$ fails: $\tfrac12(2^{i+1} + 2^{i-1}) = 1.25 \cdot 2^i$.)

questions.stem: A treatment works in 18 of 20 mild cases and 30 of 80 severe cases. Its overall success rate is ___%. Give the percent.
questions.explanation: Combine the counts: $(18 + 30)/(20 + 80) = 48/100 = 48\%$. Averaging the two rates, $(90\% + 37.5\%)/2 \approx 63.8\%$, is wrong because the groups have different sizes; the overall rate weights each group by its share of the cases.

questions.stem: Drug P cures 60 of 80 men and 10 of 20 women. Drug Q cures 16 of 20 men and 48 of 80 women. Which statement is correct?
choices: Q has the higher cure rate among men and among women, but P has the higher overall rate
P has the higher cure rate among men, among women and overall
Q has the higher cure rate among men, among women and overall
The two drugs have the same overall cure rate
questions.explanation: Men: P $75\%$, Q $80\%$. Women: P $50\%$, Q $60\%$. Overall: P $70/100 = 70\%$, Q $64/100 = 64\%$. Q wins in each group and loses overall: Simpson's paradox.

questions.stem: In the previous drug example (P: 60 of 80 men, 10 of 20 women cured; Q: 16 of 20 men, 48 of 80 women cured), what explains the reversal?
choices: Drug Q has side effects that the table does not show
The samples are too small for percentages to mean anything
Drug P works better on average for each patient
Most of P's patients were men, who were cured more often with either drug
questions.explanation: Each overall rate is a weighted average of the group rates. P's weights are $0.8$ on men and $0.2$ on women; Q's are the reverse. Men are cured more often with either drug, so P's overall rate is pulled up by its mix of patients, not by being the better drug in either group.

questions.stem: Which statements about Simpson's paradox are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Each overall rate is a weighted average of its group rates
It cannot happen if both treatments have the same mix of groups
It shows that the law of total probability can fail
The combined table is always the right one to use
Assigning treatments at random makes a reversal unlikely
questions.explanation: The law of total probability makes each overall rate a weighted average, and it is exactly this law that explains the paradox, so it does not fail. With equal mixes the weights match, and no reversal is possible; randomization makes the mixes alike on average. Whether to use the combined or the split table depends on how the groups arose.

questions.stem: The chart shows success rates for two repair methods: Method A fixed 90% of small faults, 50% of large faults and 60% of all faults; Method B fixed 80%, 40% and 70%. The legend and values have been removed. Name each numbered bar.

image.alt: A bar chart with a percent axis from 0% to 100% and three groups of two bars, labeled small faults, large faults and all faults. Marker 1 is on the left bar of the small faults group, about 90% tall. Marker 2 is on the right bar of the large faults group, about 40% tall. Marker 3 is on the left bar of the all faults group, about 60% tall. Marker 4 is on the right bar of the all faults group, about 70% tall.

questions.explanation: Read the heights against the axis: bar 1 reaches 90% (A on small faults), bar 2 reaches 40% (B on large faults), bar 3 reaches 60% (A overall) and bar 4 reaches 70% (B overall). The left bar of each group is A: A is taller in both fault groups, but B is taller overall.

questions.stem: A prize goes to every applicant with a high score ($H$) or a strong essay ($E$). Among all applicants $P(H) = 0.4$, $P(E) = 0.25$, independently. What is $P(H \mid \text{winner})$?
questions.explanation: $P(\text{winner}) = P(H \cup E) = 0.4 + 0.25 - 0.1 = 0.55$. Every high scorer wins, so $P(H \mid \text{winner}) = 0.4/0.55 = 8/11 \approx 0.727$. 0.4 is the rate among all applicants, and 0.55 is $P(\text{winner})$ itself.

questions.stem: In the same prize example ($P(H) = 0.4$, $P(E) = 0.25$, independent, winners are $H \cup E$), what is $P(H \mid \text{winner with a strong essay})$?
questions.explanation: Every strong essay wins, so "winner with a strong essay" is just $E$, and $P(H \mid E) = P(H) = 0.4$ by independence. Among winners, a strong essay lowers the chance of a high score from $8/11$ to $0.4$ (and among winners with a weak essay it is 1): selection has created a negative association.

questions.stem: Two diseases are independent in the general population, but among hospital patients, people with one disease are less likely to have the other. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: One disease protects against the other
Either disease can put a person in the hospital, so looking only at patients selects on a common effect
Independence in a population always reverses in a subgroup
questions.explanation: This is Berkson's original example. Patients are selected because they have one disease or the other (or something else), and conditioning on a common effect of two independent causes makes them negatively associated, as in the scholarship example. No biological link is needed.

questions.stem: A parent of two children answers yes to "Do you have at least one daughter?" Assuming each child is independently a girl or a boy with probability $\tfrac12$, what is the probability that both children are girls?
questions.explanation: The condition leaves $GG$, $GB$, $BG$, equally likely, and only one of them is $GG$: $\tfrac{1/4}{3/4} = \tfrac13$. The answer $\tfrac12$ would be right if we had learned that one particular child (say the older) is a girl.

questions.stem: A family has two children, each independently a girl or a boy with probability $\tfrac12$. You learn that the older child is a girl. The probability that both are girls is ___.
questions.explanation: The condition leaves $GG$ and $GB$ (older first), equally likely, so the answer is $\tfrac12$: the younger child's sex is independent of the older child's.

questions.stem: Three cards: one red on both sides, one white on both sides, one red on one side and white on the other. A card is picked at random and laid down with a random side up. The side showing is red. What is the probability that the other side is red?
questions.explanation: This is Bertrand's box in another form. Likelihood of showing red: 1 for the red–red card, $\tfrac12$ for the mixed card, 0 for the white card. So $P(\text{red–red} \mid \text{red showing}) = \dfrac{\tfrac13}{\tfrac13 + \tfrac16} = \tfrac23$. Counting sides: three red sides are equally likely to be showing, and two of them are on the red–red card.

questions.stem: Match each situation to the idea it illustrates.
left: A comparison that holds in every group reverses when the groups are combined
Traits that are independent in the population look related among those selected
A gold coin is drawn, which makes the gold–gold box more likely than the mixed box
A variable affects both which treatment is chosen and the outcome
questions.explanation: Simpson's paradox is the reversal on combining groups; Berkson's paradox is association created by selection on a common effect; Bertrand's box shows that scenarios must be weighted by how likely they were to produce the evidence; a confounder influences both the treatment and the outcome.

questions.stem: Put these conditional probabilities from the lesson in order from smallest to largest (two children, each a boy or girl with probability $\tfrac12$).
choices: $P(BB \mid \text{at least one boy born on a Tuesday})$
$P(\text{other coin is gold} \mid \text{gold drawn})$ in Bertrand's box
questions.explanation: The values are $\tfrac13 \approx 0.333$, $\tfrac{13}{27} \approx 0.481$, $\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac23$. The Tuesday detail nearly singles out one child, so its answer lies between the "at least one" answer and the "particular child" answer.

questions.stem: Each child is independently a boy or a girl with probability $\tfrac12$ and born on any of the 7 weekdays with probability $\tfrac17$. A family has two children, and at least one is a boy born on a Tuesday. What is the probability that both are boys?
questions.explanation: Use 14 equally likely types per child, so $196$ ordered pairs. Pairs with no Tuesday boy: $13^2 = 169$, so $27$ pairs have at least one. Both are boys in $7^2 - 6^2 = 13$ of them (boy–boy pairs minus those with no Tuesday boy). The answer is $\tfrac{13}{27} \approx 0.48$.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts conditioning on a common cause with conditioning on a common effect?
choices: Conditioning on a common effect can remove a dependence; conditioning on a common cause can create one
Conditioning on a common cause can remove a dependence; conditioning on a common effect can create one
questions.explanation: In lesson 4 the two tosses were dependent because of the unknown coin (a common cause); given the coin, they were independent. In Berkson's paradox, independent traits share a common effect (winning); given the effect, they become dependent.

questions.stem: This is the cdf of a discrete random variable with values 0, 1, 2 and 3. Name the numbered features.

image.alt: A step-function cdf with jumps at 0, 1, 2 and 3 and five numbered markers

choices: Value F(2) at the jump (filled dot)
Limit from the left at 2 (open dot)
questions.explanation: A discrete cdf is a step function. It is flat between possible values (2), jumps at each value by $p(x)$ (1 marks the jump at $x = 1$, from 0.4 to 0.7, so $P(X = 1) = 0.3$), and is right-continuous: at a jump the filled dot (3) is the value $F(2) = 0.9$, and the open dot (4) is the limit from the left, $F(2^-) = 0.7$. After the largest value, $F$ stays at 1 (5).

questions.stem: An integer-valued random variable has cdf values $F(4) = 0.62$ and $F(5) = 0.81$. Then $P(X = 5) =$ ___ and $P(X \ge 5) =$ ___. Give only the numbers.
questions.explanation: The jump at 5 is $P(X = 5) = F(5) - F(4) = 0.81 - 0.62 = 0.19$. For an integer variable, $P(X \ge 5) = 1 - P(X \le 4) = 1 - F(4) = 0.38$. (Using $1 - F(5) = 0.19$ would give $P(X \ge 6)$ instead.)

questions.stem: $E(X) = 4$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 5$. Let $Y = 3X + 2$. Match each quantity to its value.
questions.explanation: $E(Y) = 3(4) + 2 = 14$. The shift does not change spread and the scale is squared: $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = 9(5) = 45$, so $\operatorname{SD}(Y) = \sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt5 \approx 6.71$. From the computing formula, $E(X^2) = \operatorname{Var}(X) + [E(X)]^2 = 5 + 16 = 21$. 17 is the mistake $3 \cdot 5 + 2$ for the variance, and 15 is $3 \cdot 5$.

questions.stem: Which statements are true for every discrete random variable $X$ whose mean and variance exist? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A cdf never decreases; a shift does not change spread; and $E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2$ is the variance, which is never negative. LOTUS warns that $E[g(X)] \ne g(E(X))$ for nonlinear $g$: for $X$ equally likely to be 1 or 2, $E(1/X) = 0.75$ but $1/E(X) = \tfrac23$. And the cdf is $P(X \le x)$, with "$\le$"; for a discrete variable $P(X < x)$ differs at every possible value.

questions.stem: $X$ takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1. Put these quantities in order from smallest to largest.
In this tree for three trials, up branches are successes S (probability $p$) and down branches are failures F (probability $q$). Name the outcome in each numbered box.

image.alt: A probability tree for three trials with eight empty outcome boxes, four of them numbered

questions.explanation: Follow each box back to the start, reading up as S and down as F. Box 1: up, down, up = SFS. Box 2: up, down, down = SFF. Box 3: down, up, up = FSS. Box 4: down, down, up = FFS. Boxes 1 and 3 have two successes, probability $p^2q$ each; together with SSF they make up the $\binom32 = 3$ paths counted in $P(X = 2) = 3p^2q$.

questions.stem: $X \sim \text{Bin}(10, 0.3)$. Then $E(X) =$ ___ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) =$ ___. Give only the numbers.
questions.explanation: $E(X) = np = 10(0.3) = 3$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) = np(1 - p) = 10(0.3)(0.7) = 2.1$. (The standard deviation is $\sqrt{2.1} \approx 1.45$.)

questions.stem: Match each count to the distribution that models it exactly.
left: Whether one particular shipment arrives late
Heads in 20 tosses of a fair coin
Defective parts in 5 drawn without replacement from a box of 12 with 3 defective
questions.explanation: One yes/no outcome is Bernoulli. A fixed number of independent tosses with the same $p$ gives a binomial count. Drawing without replacement from a small box changes the chance of a defective after each draw, so the count is hypergeometric with $N = 12$, $K = 3$, $n = 5$. Geometric counts trials until a success, and Poisson counts events with no fixed number of trials; neither fits these situations.

questions.stem: A box of 50 bearings has 6 defective. $X$ is the number of defectives in 5 drawn without replacement, and $Y \sim \text{Bin}(5, 0.12)$. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The five draws that make up $X$ are independent.
With the sample size fixed at 5 and 12% defective, the distribution of $X$ gets closer to that of $Y$ as the box gets larger.
questions.explanation: Both means are $5 \times 0.12 = 0.6$. The hypergeometric variance carries the factor $\tfrac{N - n}{N - 1} = \tfrac{45}{49} < 1$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) \approx 0.485 < 0.528$. As $N$ grows with $n$ fixed, that factor tends to 1 and the hypergeometric approaches the binomial. But the draws are dependent: each draw changes what is left in the box.

questions.stem: What is the most likely value (mode) of $X \sim \text{Bin}(9, 0.4)$?
questions.explanation: $(n + 1)p = 10(0.4) = 4$ is a whole number, so the two values $4 - 1 = 3$ and $4$ tie: $P(X = 3) = \binom93 0.4^3 0.6^6 \approx 0.2508$ and $P(X = 4) = \binom94 0.4^4 0.6^5 \approx 0.2508$ (exactly equal). 3.6 is the mean $np$, which is not even a possible value.

questions.stem: A technician runs trials until the third success (S). Name the numbered parts of the record.

image.alt: Nine trial boxes F F S F S F F F S with braces under them and five numbered markers

questions.explanation: The successes are at trials 3, 5 and 9. Marker 1 is on trial 3 (first success), marker 2 on trial 5 (second success) and marker 3 on trial 7, a failure. The braces split the record into geometric waits: trials 1–3 (3 trials), 4–5 (2 trials, marker 4) and 6–9 (4 trials, marker 5). The negative binomial count is their sum, $X = 3 + 2 + 4 = 9$.

questions.stem: Each trial succeeds with probability 0.2, independently, and $X$ is the number of trials up to and including the first success. Then $E(X) =$ ___ and $P(X > 5) =$ ___ (exact decimal). Give only the numbers.
questions.explanation: $E(X) = 1/p = 1/0.2 = 5$. More than 5 trials are needed exactly when the first 5 all fail, so $P(X > 5) = 0.8^5 = 0.32768$. (The common slip $0.8^4 = 0.4096$ is $P(X > 4)$.)

questions.stem: $X \sim \text{Geometric}(p)$ counts trials to the first success, with $q = 1 - p$. Match each quantity to its formula.
questions.explanation: The pmf is $q^{k-1}p$ (fail $k - 1$ times, then succeed). More than $k$ trials means the first $k$ fail, probability $q^k$. The mean is $1/p$ and the variance $q/p^2$. $q/p$ is the mean of the other convention (failures before the first success).

questions.stem: $X \sim \text{Geometric}(0.25)$ (trials). Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: After four failures, the next trial succeeds with probability 0.25.
questions.explanation: Memorylessness: $P(X > 7 \mid X > 4) = 0.75^7/0.75^4 = 0.75^3 = P(X > 3)$. The mean is $1/0.25 = 4$. Independent trials do not remember past failures, so the next trial still succeeds with probability 0.25. But $P(X > 3) = 0.75^3 \approx 0.42$, not $0.75^2$: three failures are needed.

questions.stem: Boxes each hold one of 4 toys, equally likely and independently. On average, how many boxes must you open to collect all 4?
questions.explanation: After collecting $j$ toys, each box is new with probability $(4 - j)/4$, so the wait for the next new toy is geometric with mean $4/(4 - j)$. Adding: $\tfrac44 + \tfrac43 + \tfrac42 + \tfrac41 = 4\left(1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 + \tfrac14\right) = \tfrac{25}{3} \approx 8.33$. 6.25 forgets the factor 4 in front; 4 assumes no repeats.

questions.stem: Events of a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ per unit time are marked as dots. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A time line from 0 to 10 with event dots, two shaded intervals and a bracket, and four numbered markers

choices: Count is Poisson with mean λ
questions.explanation: Marker 1 sits on an event. The shaded interval at marker 2 runs from 1 to 3 (length 2), so its count is Poisson$(2\lambda)$; the one at marker 3 runs from 5.5 to 8.5 (length 3), so its count is Poisson$(3\lambda)$. The two intervals do not overlap, so their counts are independent. Marker 4 is the gap between two consecutive events (Module 3 shows these gaps are exponential).

questions.stem: Calls arrive as a Poisson process at 4 per hour. In a 45-minute period the mean number of calls is ___, and the probability of no calls is ___ (4 decimal places).
questions.explanation: Rescale the rate: 45 minutes is 0.75 hour, so the mean is $4 \times 0.75 = 3$. Then $P(N = 0) = e^{-3} \approx 0.0498$. Using $e^{-4} \approx 0.0183$ forgets to rescale.

questions.stem: Which counts are reasonably modeled by a Poisson distribution? Select all that apply.
choices: Radioactive decays detected in one second from a large sample
Typing errors on one page of a long manuscript
Heads in 10 tosses of a fair coin
Rainy days in one week, in a city where it rains on about half the days
questions.explanation: Decays and typos are many tiny chances of a rare event with no fixed number of trials, the Poisson setting. Ten tosses is a fixed, small number of trials with $p = 0.5$: binomial. Rainy days in a week are capped at 7 and are common, not rare (and wet days tend to cluster), so the Poisson does not fit.

questions.stem: Calls arrive as a Poisson process at 3.2 per hour. Match each time period to the Poisson mean of its count.
questions.explanation: The mean is the rate times the length of the period: $3.2 \times 0.5 = 1.6$, $3.2 \times 0.25 = 0.8$, $3.2 \times 2.5 = 8$ and $3.2 \times 24 = 76.8$.

questions.stem: $X \sim \text{Poisson}(2.5)$. Put these probabilities in order from smallest to largest.
questions.explanation: Use $p(k) = \tfrac{2.5}{k}\,p(k - 1)$ with $p(0) = e^{-2.5} \approx 0.0821$: $p(1) \approx 0.2052$, $p(2) \approx 0.2565$, $p(3) \approx 0.2138$, $p(4) \approx 0.1336$, $p(5) \approx 0.0668$. The pmf rises while $k < 2.5$ and falls after, so the mode is 2, and the far tail $p(5)$ is smallest.

questions.stem: $X$ has MGF $M(t) = (0.6 + 0.4e^t)^{15}$. Then $E(X) =$ ___ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) =$ ___. Give only the numbers.
questions.explanation: This is the binomial form $(q + pe^t)^n$ with $n = 15$ and $p = 0.4$, so by uniqueness $X \sim \text{Bin}(15, 0.4)$: $E(X) = 15(0.4) = 6$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 15(0.4)(0.6) = 3.6$. (Differentiating gives the same: $M'(0) = 15(0.4) = 6$.)

questions.stem: Match each MGF to its distribution.
questions.explanation: Poisson$(\lambda)$: $e^{\lambda(e^t - 1)}$. Binomial: $(q + pe^t)^n$. Geometric (trials): $pe^t/(1 - qe^t)$, so the coefficient in front of $e^t$ on top is $p = 0.2$. Bernoulli: $q + pe^t$, and $p$ multiplies $e^t$, so $p = 0.3$, not 0.7.

questions.stem: Which statements about moment generating functions are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Two random variables with the same mean and variance have the same MGF.
questions.explanation: $M_X(0) = E(e^0) = 1$. Independence turns the MGF of a sum into a product. For $aX + b$, $M(t) = e^{bt}M_X(at)$, here $e^{t}M_X(2t)$. But $M''(0) = E(X^2)$, so the variance is $M''(0) - M'(0)^2$. And matching two moments does not make MGFs equal: Bernoulli(0.5) and a normal with mean 0.5 and variance 0.25 share both but are different distributions.

questions.stem: $X$ and $Y$ are independent. Put the steps of the MGF method for finding the distribution of $X + Y$ in order.
choices: Simplify and compare with the table of known MGFs
Conclude by the uniqueness theorem that $X + Y$ has the matching distribution
questions.explanation: You need the two MGFs before you can multiply them, the product before you can recognize it, and a recognized form before uniqueness tells you the distribution.

questions.stem: $X \sim \text{Poisson}(2)$ and $Y \sim \text{Poisson}(3)$ are independent. Find $P(X + Y = 2)$.

questions.explanation:
$G'(s) = 0.3 + 1.2s$, so $E(X) = G'(1) = 1.5$. Check: $0(0.1) + 1(0.3) + 2(0.6) = 1.5$. The value
0.3 is $G'(0) = P(X = 1)$, the mistake of differentiating at 0.

questions.stem: For the PGF $G(s) = 0.1 + 0.3s + 0.6s^2$ (so $E(X) = 1.5$), find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.
questions.explanation:
$G''(s) = 1.2$, so $E[X(X - 1)] = 1.2$ and
$\operatorname{Var}(X) = G''(1) + G'(1) - G'(1)^2 = 1.2 + 1.5 - 2.25 = 0.45$. 1.2 stops at the factorial moment, 2.7 forgets to subtract $\mu^2$, and 1.05 is $|1.2 - 2.25|$ without adding $\mu$.

questions.stem: $X$ has PGF $G(s) = (0.4 + 0.6s)^3$. Then $P(X = 0) =$ ___ and $P(X = 3) =$ ___. Give exact decimals.
questions.explanation: $P(X = 0) = G(0) = 0.4^3 = 0.064$. The coefficient of $s^3$ in the expansion is $0.6^3 = 0.216$. (This is the Bin(3, 0.6) PGF.)

questions.stem: $X$ has PGF $G(s) = \tfrac14 s(1 + s)^2$. What is $P(X = 2)$?
questions.explanation: Expand: $\tfrac14 s(1 + 2s + s^2) = \tfrac14 s + \tfrac12 s^2 + \tfrac14 s^3$. The coefficient of $s^2$ is $P(X = 2) = \tfrac12$. ($X$ is 1 plus a Bin(2, 0.5) count.)

questions.stem: Customers enter a shop as Poisson(5) per hour, and each buys something with probability 0.4, independently. What is the probability that exactly one purchase is made in an hour?
questions.explanation: The PGF of the number of purchases is $G_N(0.6 + 0.4s) = e^{5(0.4s - 0.4)} = e^{2(s - 1)}$, so it is Poisson(2) (thinning). $P(S = 1) = 2e^{-2} \approx 0.2707$. 0.0337 uses Poisson(5), and 0.1353 is $P(S = 0)$.

questions.stem: $N$ is a count with PGF $G_N$, and $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ are independent with PGF $G_X$, independent of $N$. What is the PGF of $S = X_1 + \cdots + X_N$?
questions.explanation: Given $N = n$, $E(s^S) = G_X(s)^n$. Averaging over $N$: $\sum P(N = n)G_X(s)^n = G_N(G_X(s))$, the count's PGF evaluated at $G_X(s)$. The product $G_NG_X$ is the PGF of $N + X$ for independent $N$ and $X$, a different quantity.

questions.stem: Each individual has 0, 1, 2 or 3 children with probabilities 0.2, 0.3, 0.3, 0.2. Which describes this branching process?
questions.explanation: $m = 0(0.2) + 1(0.3) + 2(0.3) + 3(0.2) = 1.5 > 1$, so the process is supercritical and survives forever with positive probability. Neither 0.75 nor 2 is the probability-weighted sum $\sum k\,p_k$.

questions.stem: Offspring are 0, 1 or 2 with probabilities 0.3, 0.2, 0.5. Starting from one individual, what is the extinction probability?
In a branching process every individual has a Poisson(0.8) number of children. What is the probability that the line eventually dies out?
questions.explanation: The mean offspring number is $m = 0.8 \le 1$, so the process is subcritical and extinction is certain: $q = 1$. $e^{-0.8}$ is only the chance that the first individual has no children, $P(Z_1 = 0)$.

questions.stem: A branching process has mean offspring number $m = 1$ and $p_1 < 1$. Which statement is true?
choices: Each generation has exactly one individual.
Extinction is certain even though $E(Z_n) = 1$ for every $n$.
questions.explanation: $E(Z_n) = m^n = 1$ for all $n$, yet the extinction theorem gives $q = 1$ when $m \le 1$ (and $p_1 < 1$). The mean stays at 1 because the rare surviving lines become very large. Exactly one child each time would need $p_1 = 1$, and $p_0$ is only the chance of dying out in the first generation.

questions.stem: Offspring are 0, 1 or 2 with probabilities 1/4, 1/4, 1/2, starting from one individual. $P(Z_2 = 0) =$ ___ (exact).
Offspring are 0, 1 or 2 with probabilities 1/4, 1/4, 1/2, starting from one individual. Put these in order from smallest to largest.
questions.explanation: $P(Z_1 = 0) = 0.25$, $P(Z_3 = 0) \approx 0.395$, and these increase toward $q = 0.5$. Then $m = 1.25$ and $E(Z_2) = m^2 = 1.5625$.

questions.stem: Match each offspring law to what happens to the population, starting from one individual.
questions.explanation: The extinction theorem: $q = 1$ when $m \le 1$ (unless $p_1 = 1$) and $q < 1$ when $m > 1$. If every individual has exactly one child, $Z_n = 1$ for all $n$, the excluded trivial case.

questions.stem: The graph shows an offspring PGF $f$ (solid) and a dashed line on $0 \le s \le 1$, for offspring 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 1/4, 1/4, 1/2. Name the numbered features.

image.alt: A convex curve starting at height 0.25 and a dashed diagonal line, crossing at s = 0.5 and meeting at s = 1, with five numbered markers

choices: f(0), the chance of no children
questions.explanation: The curve starts at $f(0) = p_0 = \tfrac14$ (3). It crosses the dashed line $y = s$ (5) first at $s = \tfrac12$, the smallest fixed point and so the extinction probability (1), and meets it again at $s = 1$ (2), which is a fixed point of every PGF. The mean $m$ is the slope of the curve at $s = 1$, not a point on the graph.

questions.stem: $X$ takes values in $\{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$ and has PGF $G$. Which statements are always true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $G(1) = \sum p(k) = 1$ and $G(0) = p(0)$. The series has coefficients that add to 1, so it converges for $|s| \le 1$. But $G'(0) = p(1)$; the mean is $G'(1)$.

questions.stem: $X$ takes the values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.5, 0.3, 0.2, and $Y$ takes them with probabilities 0.4, 0.4, 0.2. Find $d_{TV}(X, Y)$.
$X \sim \text{Bin}(200, 0.01)$ is approximated by Poisson(2). What bound does Le Cam's inequality give on the total variation distance?
questions.explanation:
With every $p_i = 0.01$, $\sum p_i^2 = 200(0.01)^2 = 0.02$. Equivalently $\lambda p = 2(0.01)$.
0.0002 is a single $p^2$, and 0.01 is $p$ itself.

questions.stem: Three independent events have probabilities 0.1, 0.05 and 0.05, and $S$ counts how many occur. For the Poisson approximation, $\lambda =$ ___, and Le Cam's bound on the total variation error is ___. Give only the numbers.
A computation shows $d_{TV}(S, \text{Poisson}(\lambda)) \le 0.01$. What does this guarantee?
choices: Every probability about $S$ is within 1% of its Poisson approximation, in relative terms.
Every probability about $S$ is within 0.01 of its Poisson approximation.
The means of $S$ and the Poisson differ by at most 0.01.
questions.explanation:
Total variation is the largest absolute disagreement over all events, so every probability (single values, tails, intervals) is within 0.01. It says nothing about relative error: a tail of
0.008 approximated by 0.010 is within 0.01 but 25% off. In Le Cam's setting the means are equal anyway ($\lambda = \sum p_i$).

questions.stem: Why is Poisson(3) a poor approximation to $\text{Bin}(12, 0.25)$?
choices: Because the binomial mean is not 3.
Because each success probability, 0.25, is not small.
questions.explanation: Le Cam's bound is $\sum p_i^2 = 12(0.25)^2 = 0.75$, and the actual distance is about 0.07: the error is driven by the size of each $p_i$, not by $n$. The mean is $12(0.25) = 3$, matching, and the trials are independent. A small $n$ alone is not the problem; $\text{Bin}(12, 0.005)$ is very close to Poisson(0.06).

questions.stem: $S$ and $T$ are defined on the same sample space. Which inequality is the key step in the coupling proof of Le Cam's inequality?
questions.explanation:
For any $A$, $P(S \in A) - P(T \in A) = P(S \in A, T 
otin A) - P(T \in A, S 
otin A) \le P(S 
e T)$. Building $S$ and the Poisson $T$ so that they rarely differ then bounds the distance. The reverse inequality fails in general: two independent copies of a fair coin flip have the same distribution ($d_{TV} = 0$) but differ half the time.

questions.stem: Ten letters go into their ten envelopes at random, and $X$ is the number in the right envelope. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$?
questions.explanation: With $A_i$ = "letter $i$ correct", $\lambda = 10 \cdot \tfrac{1}{10} = 1$ and $E[X(X-1)] = \sum_{i \ne j} P(A_i \cap A_j) = 90 \cdot \tfrac{1}{90} = 1$. So $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 1 + 1 - 1^2 = 1$, the Poisson(1) value. 0.9 is the binomial variance $10(0.1)(0.9)$, which wrongly treats the events as independent.

questions.stem: Use the Poisson paradigm to approximate the probability that at least two of 30 people share a birthday (365 equally likely days).
questions.explanation: There are $\binom{30}{2} = 435$ pairs, each sharing with probability $\tfrac{1}{365}$, so $\lambda = 435/365 \approx 1.192$ and $P(\text{at least one}) \approx 1 - e^{-1.192} \approx 0.696$ (the exact value is 0.706). 0.304 is $P(\text{none})$, and 0.079 uses 30 people instead of 435 pairs.

questions.stem: For which counts is a Poisson model reasonable by the Poisson paradigm? Select all that apply.
choices: Accidents in one day among 1,000 drivers who each have a small chance of an accident
Pairs sharing a birthday among 25 people
Houses on one street damaged by the same tornado
Heads in 50 tosses of a fair coin
questions.explanation: Drivers' accidents are many rare, roughly independent events, and birthday pairs are rare and only weakly dependent. Tornado damage clusters (one house damaged makes its neighbors likely to be damaged too), so the count is overdispersed. Coin heads have $p = 0.5$, not rare.

questions.stem: 200 independent events each have probability 0.01, and $X$ counts how many occur. $E[X(X - 1)] =$ ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $E[X(X - 1)] = \sum_{i \ne j} P(A_i)P(A_j) = 200 \cdot 199 \cdot 0.01^2 = 3.98$, close to $\lambda^2 = 4$, as the Poisson paradigm expects. (Counting each unordered pair once gives 1.99.)

questions.stem: Match each idea to its meaning.
choices: Largest disagreement about the probability of any event
Error at most the sum of the squared success probabilities
Building two variables on one sample space
Many rare, weakly dependent events give a nearly Poisson count
questions.explanation: These are the four ideas of the lesson: the error measure, the bound for independent indicators, the proof technique, and the rule of thumb for dependent events.

questions.stem: Each binomial below has mean 2. Order them from farthest from Poisson(2) to closest, in total variation distance.
questions.explanation: The Le Cam bound $\lambda p = 2p$ shrinks as $p$ does: 0.4, 0.2, 0.04, 0.004. The actual distances follow the same order: about 0.052, 0.024, 0.0046 and 0.00045.

questions.stem: In Bortkiewicz's horse-kick data, the 200 corps-years had a mean of 0.61 deaths. About how many corps-years does a Poisson(0.61) model expect to have no deaths?
questions.explanation: $200\,e^{-0.61} \approx 200(0.5434) \approx 108.7$, very close to the 109 observed. 122 is the total number of deaths, and about 66 is the expected number of corps-years with exactly one death.

questions.stem: A count of events has $\lambda = E(X) = 2$ and $E[X(X - 1)] = 6$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, and what does it suggest?
choices: 4: larger than the mean, so the events cluster
2: equal to the mean, as for a Poisson count
8: smaller than expected, so the events repel
questions.explanation: $\operatorname{Var}(X) = E[X(X - 1)] + \lambda - \lambda^2 = 6 + 2 - 4 = 4$. A Poisson count would have $E[X(X - 1)] = \lambda^2 = 4$ and variance 2; the excess means the events tend to occur together (overdispersion).

questions.stem: The picture shows the density of a continuous random variable $X$. The dashed line splits the area under the curve into two equal halves. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A right-skewed density curve over the x-axis with points a, b and c marked. Five parts are numbered: the curve itself, a shaded area between a and b, a shaded tail to the right of c, a solid vertical segment from the axis up to the curve, and a dashed vertical line.

choices: The height f(x₀), a density value
questions.explanation: Probabilities are areas under a density curve: the shaded region between $a$ and $b$ is $P(a \le X \le b)$ and the shaded region beyond $c$ is $P(X > c)$. The solid segment is the height of the curve at $x_0$, which is a density (probability per unit length), not a probability; $P(X = x_0)$ is 0 for a continuous variable. The dashed line has half the area on each side, so it is the median. The cdf would be a different, increasing curve.

questions.stem: The pdf of $X$ is $f(x) = c\,x^3$ for $0 \le x \le 2$ and 0 elsewhere. Then $c =$ ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The total area must be 1: $\int_0^2 c\,x^3\,dx = c \cdot \dfrac{2^4}{4} = 4c = 1$, so $c = \tfrac14$.

questions.stem: $X$ has pdf $f(x) = x^2/9$ on $[0, 3]$ (Example 1 of the lesson). Put these values in increasing order.
questions.explanation: The cdf is $F(x) = x^3/27$. The 25th percentile solves $x^3/27 = 0.25$: $x = 3(0.25)^{1/3} \approx 1.890$. The mean is 2.25 and the median $3 \cdot 2^{-1/3} \approx 2.381$. The density $x^2/9$ increases all the way to the right end, so the mode is 3. The long left tail pulls the mean below the median.

questions.stem: Which of these functions (each 0 outside the interval shown) are valid probability density functions? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A pdf must be nonnegative and have total area 1. $2 \times 0.5 = 1$, so the first is valid even though its height exceeds 1. $\int_0^1 x\,dx = \tfrac12$, not 1. $\int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,dx = 1$. $x - 0.5$ has area $2 - 1 = 1$ on $[0, 2]$ but is negative on $[0, 0.5)$, so it fails. $\int_0^1 1.5(1 - x^2)\,dx = 1.5 \cdot \tfrac23 = 1$, and it is nonnegative.

questions.stem: Match each quantity for a continuous random variable $X$ with pdf $f$ and cdf $F$ to how it is computed.
choices: The integral of f from a to b
The derivative of F at x
The integral of P(X > x) from 0 to infinity
E(X²) minus the square of the mean
The integral of x² f(x) with nothing subtracted
questions.explanation: Probabilities of intervals are areas, $\int_a^b f$, which also equal $F(b) - F(a)$ (a difference, not a sum). The pdf is the derivative of the cdf. For a nonnegative variable the tail formula gives $E(X) = \int_0^\infty P(X > x)\,dx$. The variance is $E(X^2) - \mu^2$; $\int x^2 f$ alone is $E(X^2)$.

questions.stem: The picture shows events of a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ on a time line. Name the numbered parts by their role or distribution. (The shaded window has length 3.)

image.alt: A time line starting at 0 with six events marked as dots. Four parts are numbered: one of the dots, a bracket below the line between two neighboring events, a bracket above the line from 0 to the third event, and a shaded window containing two events.

questions.explanation: Counts are Poisson and gaps are exponential: the gap between neighboring events is Exponential($\lambda$), and the number of events in a window of length 3 is Poisson with mean $3\lambda$. The time of the 3rd event is the sum of three independent exponential gaps, which is Gamma$(3, 1/\lambda)$ (lesson 13), not exponential.

questions.stem: $X \sim \text{U}(2, 8)$. Then $E(X) =$ ___ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) =$ ___. Give numbers only.
questions.explanation: The mean is the midpoint, $(2 + 8)/2 = 5$. The variance is $(b - a)^2/12 = 36/12 = 3$.

questions.stem: $X$ is exponential with rate $\lambda$. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: $P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)$ for all $s, t \ge 0$
The hazard rate is the constant $\lambda$
The median $\ln 2/\lambda$ is below the mean
questions.explanation: The first two are the memoryless property and its hazard-rate form. The median $\ln 2/\lambda \approx 0.693/\lambda$ is below the mean $1/\lambda$ because of the long right tail. The variance is $1/\lambda^2$, not $1/\lambda$, and $1 - e^{-\lambda x}$ is the cdf; the survival function is $e^{-\lambda x}$.

questions.stem: Customers arrive as a Poisson process. Match each quantity to its usual model.
left: Rounding error of a length recorded to the nearest 0.1 mm
Time from now until the next arrival
Number of arrivals in the next hour
Time from now until the third arrival
questions.explanation: Rounding error is equally likely anywhere within half a unit, so it is uniform. In a Poisson process the waiting time to the next event is exponential, the count in a fixed interval is Poisson, and the waiting time to the $k$-th event is a sum of $k$ exponential gaps, a gamma variable.

questions.stem: A waiting time is exponential with rate 0.2 per minute. Put these values in increasing order.
questions.explanation: Percentiles solve $1 - e^{-0.2t} = p$, so $t = -\ln(1 - p)/0.2$: the 25th is about 1.44, the median about 3.47, the 90th about 11.51 and the 99th about 23.03 minutes. The mean is $1/0.2 = 5$, which lies between the median and the 90th percentile.

questions.stem: The picture shows a $\text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ density. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A bell-shaped curve with tick marks from mu minus 3 sigma to mu plus 3 sigma, a dashed center line, a dot on each side of the curve, a shaded center region, a small shaded upper tail and three brackets below the axis. Five parts are numbered: the top of the center line, the dot on the right side, the shortest bracket, the middle bracket, and the shaded upper tail.

choices: The peak, at the mean μ
questions.explanation: The normal curve peaks at its mean and changes from bending down to bending up at $\mu \pm \sigma$, the inflection points. About 68% of the area lies within one standard deviation and 95% within two. Only the upper tail beyond $\mu + 2\sigma$ is shaded: $1 - \Phi(2) \approx 0.023$. The 5% figure is both tails together. The 99.7% bracket is the longest one, which is not numbered.

questions.stem: Bolt lengths are $\text{N}(50, 0.4^2)$ mm. A bolt of length 50.8 mm has z-score ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $z = \dfrac{50.8 - 50}{0.4} = \dfrac{0.8}{0.4} = 2$. Divide by the standard deviation 0.4, not the variance 0.16.

questions.stem: IQ-type scores are $\text{N}(100, 15^2)$. Put these values in increasing order.
questions.explanation: Each percentile is $100 + 15z_p$: the 5th is $100 - 1.645(15) \approx 75.3$, the first quartile $100 - 0.674(15) \approx 89.9$, the median 100 (the mean, by symmetry), $\mu + \sigma = 115$ (about the 84th percentile), and the 99th $100 + 2.326(15) \approx 134.9$.

questions.stem: $X \sim \text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ and $Y \sim \text{N}(\nu, \tau^2)$ are independent. Which of these are normally distributed? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Linear functions of a normal variable are normal: $3X - 2 \sim \text{N}(3\mu - 2, 9\sigma^2)$, and the z-score is $\text{N}(0, 1)$. Independent normals add to a normal, $\text{N}(\mu + \nu, \sigma^2 + \tau^2)$. But $X^2$ is never negative (for $\mu = 0$ it is $\sigma^2$ times a chi-square), and $e^X$ is lognormal (lesson 14); neither is normal.

questions.stem: $X$ is binomial and $Y$ is the approximating normal variable. Match each binomial probability to the normal region used with the continuity correction.
questions.explanation: Picture each value $k$ as a bar from $k - 0.5$ to $k + 0.5$. $X \le 25$ includes the bar at 25, so stop at 25.5. $X < 25$ means $X \le 24$, so stop at 24.5. $X \ge 25$ includes the bar at 25, so start at 24.5. $X > 25$ means $X \ge 26$, so start at 25.5.
