u}$ if $T \sim t_
u$; $1/F \sim F_{
u_2,
u_1}$ if $F \sim F_{
u_1,
u_2}$.
$E[S^2] = \sigma^2$, $\operatorname{Var}(S^2) = \dfrac{2\sigma^4}{n - 1}$.
$\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta) = E[\hat\theta] - \theta$; unbiased if 0 for every $\theta$.
$\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta) = \operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) + \operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta)^2$.
$E[\hat\sigma^2] = \tfrac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2$, bias $-\sigma^2/n$; $S^2$ (divide by $n - 1$) is unbiased.
No: $E[S] < \sigma$, because $\operatorname{Var}(S) = \sigma^2 - (E[S])^2 > 0$.
$\hat\theta_n \xrightarrow{P} \theta$. Sufficient: bias $\to 0$ and variance $\to 0$ (MSE $\to 0$).
For unbiased estimators: $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_2)/\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_1)$.
Variances $\theta^2/(3n)$ and $\theta^2/(n(n+2))$; relative efficiency $(n+2)/3$.
$I(\theta) = E[(\partial_\theta\ln f)^2] = -E[\partial_\theta^2\ln f]$. Bernoulli $1/(p(1-p))$; Poisson $1/\lambda$; normal mean $1/\sigma^2$.
Unbiased $\hat\theta$, regular family: $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) \ge \dfrac{1}{nI(\theta)}$. Attained ⟹ efficient.
Solve $E[X^k] = \tfrac1n\sum x_i^k$ for $k = 1, \dots, p$.
Exponential $1/\bar x$; Uniform$(0, \theta)$: $2\bar x$; normal: $\bar x$ and $\tfrac1n\sum(x_i - \bar x)^2$.
$L(\theta) = \prod f(x_i; \theta)$, $\ell(\theta) = \sum\ln f(x_i; \theta)$; maximize over $\theta$ with the data fixed.
$\hat p = \bar x$; $\hat\lambda = \bar x$; exponential rate $\hat\lambda = 1/\bar x$.
$\hat\mu = \bar x$, $\hat\sigma^2 = \tfrac1n\sum(x_i - \bar x)^2$ (divide by $n$).
$\hat\theta = \max x_i$, at the boundary where $L$ jumps; $L'(\theta) = 0$ has no solution.
The MLE of $g(\theta)$ is $g(\hat\theta)$ (but unbiasedness is not preserved).
If $\hat\theta \approx N(\theta, v)$, then $g(\hat\theta) \approx N\big(g(\theta), [g'(\theta)]^2v\big)$ for differentiable $g$ with $g'(\theta) \ne 0$.
$T = u(\mathbf X)$ is sufficient for $\theta$ iff $f(\mathbf x; \theta) = \phi(u(\mathbf x); \theta)\,h(\mathbf x)$ with $h$ free of $\theta$. Example: $\sum X_i$ for Poisson data.
$\hat\theta \approx N\big(\theta, 1/(nI(\theta))\big)$; SE $\approx 1/\sqrt{nI(\hat\theta)}$.
A function of data and $\theta$ with a fully known distribution; invert $P(a \le Q \le b) = 1 - \alpha$.
$\bar x \pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma/\sqrt n$.
$\bar x \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,s/\sqrt n$.
$\left[\dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_U},\ \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_L}\right]$ with $\chi^2_L, \chi^2_U$ the $\alpha/2$ and $1 - \alpha/2$ quantiles of $\chi^2_{n-1}$.
$\hat p \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)/n}$; needs $n\hat p, n(1 - \hat p) \ge 10$.
$n = \left(\dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}\sigma}{E}\right)^2$, rounded up.

cards.front: Exact CI for an exponential rate
cards.back: $2\lambda\sum X_i \sim \chi^2_{2n}$, so $\lambda \in \left[\dfrac{\chi^2_L}{2\sum x_i},\ \dfrac{\chi^2_U}{2\sum x_i}\right]$.
The procedure covers the fixed parameter in 95% of repeated samples; a given interval either does or does not.
Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior: $\pi(\theta \mid x) \propto f(x \mid \theta)\pi(\theta)$.
Beta$(a, b)$ prior, $x$ successes in $n$: posterior Beta$(a + x, b + n - x)$.
$\dfrac{a + x}{a + b + n}$: weights $\dfrac{a + b}{a + b + n}$ on the prior mean and $\dfrac{n}{a + b + n}$ on $x/n$.
$\dfrac{1}{\tau_n^2} = \dfrac{1}{\tau_0^2} + \dfrac{n}{\sigma^2}$, $\mu_n = \tau_n^2\left(\dfrac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2} + \dfrac{n\bar x}{\sigma^2}\right)$.
Gamma$(\alpha, \beta)$ prior (shape $\alpha$, rate $\beta$), Poisson counts: posterior Gamma$(\alpha + \sum x_i,\ \beta + n)$.
$\dfrac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha + \beta - 2}$ for $\alpha, \beta > 1$.
Credible: $P(\theta \in I \mid \text{data}) = 0.95$. Confidence: the procedure covers fixed $\theta$ 95% of the time.

cards.front: Type I and Type II errors
cards.back: Type I: reject $H_0$ when it is true (probability at most $\alpha$). Type II: fail to reject $H_0$ when $H_1$ is true (probability $\beta(\theta) = 1 - \pi(\theta)$).
$\pi(\theta) = P_\theta(\text{reject } H_0)$ for every $\theta$. On $\Omega_0$ it gives Type I error probabilities; on $\Omega_1$ it gives the power.

cards.front: Size of a test with a composite null
cards.back: $\alpha = \sup_{\theta \in \Omega_0}\pi(\theta)$, the worst-case Type I error probability. For monotone power functions it is attained at the boundary $\theta_0$.
The probability, computed under $H_0$, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. Reject at level $\alpha$ exactly when $p \le \alpha$.
Uniform(0, 1), for a continuous test statistic and simple $H_0$, by the probability integral transform. So $P(p \le \alpha) = \alpha$.
It is not $P(H_0 \text{ true} \mid \text{data})$, and $1 - p$ is not the probability that $H_1$ is true.

cards.front: Power of the upper-tailed $z$ test at $\mu$
cards.back: $\pi(\mu) = 1 - \Phi\!\left(z_\alpha - \dfrac{\mu - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\right)$

cards.front: Sample size for a one-sided $z$ test with power $1 - \beta$ at $\mu_0 + \delta$
cards.back: $n \ge \left(\dfrac{(z_\alpha + z_\beta)\sigma}{\delta}\right)^2$, rounded up. For a two-sided test use $z_{\alpha/2}$.
Larger $n$, larger $\alpha$, a true parameter farther from $H_0$, smaller $\sigma$ (less noise, pairing), and a correctly chosen one-sided alternative.

cards.front: Duality of tests and confidence intervals
cards.back: A two-sided level-$\alpha$ test rejects $\theta = \theta_0$ exactly when $\theta_0$ is outside the $1 - \alpha$ confidence interval (for the usual $z$ and $t$ procedures).
For $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$ and $H_1: p > p_0$, the p-value is $P_{p_0}(X \ge x)$. With discrete data, choose the largest achievable size not above $\alpha$.
$T = \dfrac{\bar X - \mu_0}{S/\sqrt n} \sim t_{n-1}$ under $H_0$ for a normal sample.
$T = Z/\sqrt{V/(n-1)}$ with $Z = (\bar X - \mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n) \sim N(0,1)$, $V = (n-1)S^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}$, and $\bar X$ independent of $S^2$.
$T = \dfrac{\bar X - \bar Y - \Delta_0}{S_p\sqrt{1/m + 1/n}} \sim t_{m+n-2}$, with $S_p^2 = \dfrac{(m-1)S_1^2 + (n-1)S_2^2}{m+n-2}$. Assumes $\sigma_1 = \sigma_2$.
$T = \dfrac{\bar X - \bar Y}{\sqrt{S_1^2/m + S_2^2/n}}$, approximately $t_\nu$ with $\nu = \dfrac{(S_1^2/m + S_2^2/n)^2}{\frac{(S_1^2/m)^2}{m-1} + \frac{(S_2^2/n)^2}{n-1}}$.
Take differences $D_i = X_i - Y_i$ and run a one-sample $t$ test: $T = \bar D/(S_D/\sqrt n)$ on $n - 1$ df.
$\operatorname{Var}(X - Y) = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$: positive correlation within pairs removes unit-to-unit variation.
$\chi^2 = (n-1)S^2/\sigma_0^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}$ under $H_0: \sigma^2 = \sigma_0^2$. Two-sided critical values are not symmetric.
$F = S_1^2/S_2^2 \sim F_{m-1,\,n-1}$ under $H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$. Lower critical value: $F_{1-\alpha/2,\,m-1,\,n-1} = 1/F_{\alpha/2,\,n-1,\,m-1}$.
$t$ tests for means are fairly robust to non-normality (CLT). Chi-square and $F$ tests for variances are not, even in large samples.
For simple $H_0: \theta_0$ vs simple $H_1: \theta_1$, rejecting when $L(\theta_0)/L(\theta_1) \le k$ (with size $\alpha$) is most powerful among tests of size at most $\alpha$.
One test that is most powerful against every alternative in $H_1$. Exists for one-sided alternatives under a monotone likelihood ratio; usually not for two-sided alternatives.

cards.front: MP test for a normal mean, $\mu_1 > \mu_0$, $\sigma$ known
cards.back: The likelihood ratio is decreasing in $\sum x_i$, so reject when $\bar x \ge \mu_0 + z_\alpha\sigma/\sqrt n$; the region does not depend on $\mu_1$, so it is UMP.

cards.front: MP test for an exponential rate, $H_1: \lambda_1 < \lambda_0$
cards.back: Reject when $\sum x_i \ge c$, using $2\lambda_0\sum X_i \sim \chi^2_{2n}$ under $H_0$: $c = \chi^2_{\alpha,2n}/(2\lambda_0)$.
$\Lambda = \dfrac{\sup_{\Omega_0}L(\theta)}{\sup_{\Omega}L(\theta)} = \dfrac{L(\hat\theta_0)}{L(\hat\theta)} \in (0, 1]$; reject $H_0$ when $\Lambda$ is small.
Under $H_0$ and regularity conditions, $-2\ln\Lambda \approx \chi^2_r$ for large $n$, with $r = \dim\Omega - \dim\Omega_0$.

cards.front: LRT for a normal mean with $\sigma$ unknown
cards.back: $\Lambda = (1 + t^2/(n-1))^{-n/2}$, a decreasing function of $\lvert t\rvert$: the LRT is the two-sided $t$ test.
$2n\left[\bar x\ln(\bar x/\lambda_0) - (\bar x - \lambda_0)\right]$, compared with $\chi^2_1$.
$2\left[x\ln\dfrac{x}{np_0} + (n - x)\ln\dfrac{n - x}{n(1 - p_0)}\right]$, compared with $\chi^2_1$.
$Z = \dfrac{\hat p - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}}$; the standard error uses $p_0$ because it is computed under $H_0$. Needs $np_0, n(1-p_0) \ge 10$.
$Z = \dfrac{\hat p_1 - \hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)(1/n_1 + 1/n_2)}}$ with pooled $\hat p = (X_1 + X_2)/(n_1 + n_2)$.
$X^2 = \sum\dfrac{(O - E)^2}{E}$ over all cells; reject $H_0$ for large values.
$P(o_1, \dots, o_k) = \dfrac{n!}{o_1!\cdots o_k!}p_1^{o_1}\cdots p_k^{o_k}$; $E(O_i) = np_i$, $\operatorname{Var}(O_i) = np_i(1 - p_i)$, $\operatorname{Cov}(O_i, O_j) = -np_ip_j$.
$k - 1 - m$, for $k$ categories and $m$ parameters estimated from the data.

cards.front: Expected counts in a two-way table
cards.back: $E_{ij} = R_iC_j/n$ (row total times column total over grand total).
$(r - 1)(c - 1)$ = $(rc - 1) - [(r - 1) + (c - 1)]$, the free parameters of the full model minus those under independence.
With two categories $X^2 = Z^2$. In general $X^2 \approx G^2 = -2\ln\Lambda$, so Wilks gives $\chi^2$ with df = number of free probabilities fixed by $H_0$.

cards.front: Rule of thumb for chi-square tests
cards.back: Every expected count at least about 5. Otherwise combine categories or use an exact test.
Independence: one sample classified two ways. Homogeneity: separate samples (fixed row totals), testing whether they share one column distribution. Same $X^2$, same df.
$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + \varepsilon_i$, $x_i$ fixed, $\varepsilon_i$ i.i.d. $N(0, \sigma^2)$.
$b_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$, $b_0 = \bar y - b_1\bar x$. Also the MLEs under normal errors.
$\sum(y_i - b_0 - b_1x_i) = 0$ and $\sum x_i(y_i - b_0 - b_1x_i) = 0$, i.e. $\sum e_i = 0$, $\sum x_ie_i = 0$.
$b_1 \sim N(\beta_1, \sigma^2/S_{xx})$, since $b_1 = \sum c_iY_i$ with $c_i = (x_i - \bar x)/S_{xx}$.
$\operatorname{Var}(b_0) = \sigma^2\left(\dfrac1n + \dfrac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\right)$
$s^2 = \text{SSE}/(n-2)$, unbiased; $\text{SSE}/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-2}$. Shortcut: $\text{SSE} = S_{yy} - b_1S_{xy}$.
$T = \dfrac{b_1 - \beta_1}{s/\sqrt{S_{xx}}} \sim t_{n-2}$. Interval: $b_1 \pm t_{\alpha/2,n-2}\,s/\sqrt{S_{xx}}$.

cards.front: Confidence interval for the mean response at $x_0$
cards.back: $\hat y_0 \pm t_{\alpha/2,n-2}\,s\sqrt{\dfrac1n + \dfrac{(x_0 - \bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}}$

cards.front: Prediction interval for a new $Y$ at $x_0$
cards.back: $\hat y_0 \pm t_{\alpha/2,n-2}\,s\sqrt{1 + \dfrac1n + \dfrac{(x_0 - \bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}}$. The extra 1 is the new error; it never shrinks to zero.
$\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}$; $r^2 = \text{SSR}/\text{SST} = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}$; $F = \text{SSR}/s^2 = t^2$.
Curve: mean not linear. Funnel: variance not constant. Isolated far point: outlier. Want a patternless horizontal band.
$Y_{ij} = \mu_i + \varepsilon_{ij}$, $\varepsilon_{ij}$ i.i.d. $N(0, \sigma^2)$. $H_0$: all $\mu_i$ equal; $H_1$: not all equal.
$\text{SSTr} = \sum n_i(\bar y_{i\cdot} - \bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2$ ($k - 1$ df); $\text{SSE} = \sum(n_i - 1)s_i^2$ ($N - k$ df); $\text{SST} = \text{SSTr} + \text{SSE}$ ($N - 1$ df).
$F = \dfrac{\text{SSTr}/(k-1)}{\text{SSE}/(N-k)} \sim F_{k-1,\,N-k}$ under $H_0$; reject for large $F$ (upper tail only).
$E(\text{MSE}) = \sigma^2$; $E(\text{MSTr}) = \sigma^2 + \dfrac{\sum n_i(\mu_i - \bar\mu)^2}{k-1}$.
$F = t^2$ for the pooled two-sample $t$ statistic; the tests are equivalent.
Independent observations, normal populations (fairly robust), equal variances (rule of thumb: largest $s_i \le 2\times$ smallest).

cards.front: Familywise error rate with $m$ independent tests
cards.back: $1 - (1 - \alpha)^m$; for 10 tests at 0.05 about 0.40.
Run each of $m$ comparisons at $\alpha/m$; the union bound keeps the familywise error rate at most $\alpha$.
$\bar y_i - \bar y_j \pm t_{\alpha/(2m),\,N-k}\sqrt{\text{MSE}(1/n_i + 1/n_j)}$
Count positive differences (drop zeros): $B \sim \text{Bin}(n, 1/2)$ under $H_0$: median $= 0$. Assumes only independence and continuity.
Rank $\lvert D_i\rvert$; $W^+$ = sum of ranks of positive $D_i$. $E(W^+) = n(n+1)/4$, $\operatorname{Var}(W^+) = n(n+1)(2n+1)/24$. Assumes symmetry.
Rank all $N = m + n$ values; $W$ = sum of the first sample's ranks. $E(W) = m(N+1)/2$, $\operatorname{Var}(W) = mn(N+1)/12$.
$U = W - m(m+1)/2$ = number of pairs with $X_i > Y_j$; ranges from 0 to $mn$; $U/(mn)$ estimates $P(X > Y)$.
Under $H_0$ all relabelings of the data are equally likely; the p-value is the fraction of relabelings whose statistic is at least as extreme as observed.

cards.front: Parametric test and its rank-based alternative
cards.back: Paired / one sample $t$: sign or signed-rank test. Two-sample $t$: rank-sum (Mann–Whitney). One-way ANOVA: Kruskal–Wallis.
Wilcoxon vs $t$ under normality: $3/\pi \approx 0.955$ (never below 0.864). Sign test vs $t$: $2/\pi \approx 0.64$. Heavy tails can favor rank tests.

$f_{U,V}(u, v) = f_{X,Y}(x(u, v), y(u, v))\,\lvert J\rvert$, where $J = \det\dfrac{\partial(x, y)}{\partial(u, v)}$ comes from the *inverse* map. For a linear map with determinant $D$, $\lvert J\rvert = 1/\lvert D\rvert$.
Unbiased for $\tau(\theta)$, with variance no larger than any other unbiased estimator for every $\theta$. It need not attain the Cramér–Rao bound.
$W$ unbiased, $T$ sufficient: $\phi(T) = E[W \mid T]$ is unbiased and $\operatorname{Var}(\phi(T)) \le \operatorname{Var}(W)$ (law of total variance). Sufficiency makes $\phi$ free of $\theta$.
$E_\theta[g(T)] = 0$ for all $\theta$ implies $g(T) = 0$ with probability 1. Then at most one function of $T$ is unbiased for a given $\tau(\theta)$.
An unbiased function of a complete sufficient statistic is the unique MVUE. Recipe: find complete sufficient $T$, then any unbiased $\phi(T)$.
$f(x; \theta) = h(x)c(\theta)e^{w(\theta)t(x)}$: $\sum t(X_i)$ is complete sufficient if $w(\theta)$ fills an interval. Bernoulli, Poisson, exponential, normal with known $\sigma^2$.
$(1 - 1/n)^T$ with $T = \sum X_i$, from $X_1 \mid T \sim \text{Bin}(T, 1/n)$. The MLE $e^{-\bar X}$ is biased.
$N(\mu, \sigma^2)$: $\bar X$ for $\mu$, $S^2$ for $\sigma^2$, $\bar X^2 - S^2/n$ for $\mu^2$. Uniform$(0, \theta)$: $\tfrac{n+1}{n}X_{(n)}$. Exponential rate: $(n-1)/\sum X_i$.
$n$ draws *with replacement* from the observed data (the empirical distribution). A given point is left out with probability $(1 - 1/n)^n \approx 0.368$.
SE: the SD of the $B$ replicates $\hat\theta^*_b$. Bias estimate: $\bar\theta^* - \hat\theta$. Larger $B$ cuts Monte Carlo noise, not the SE.

cards.front: Ideal bootstrap SE of a mean
cards.back: $\hat\sigma/\sqrt n$ with $\hat\sigma^2 = \tfrac1n\sum(x_i - \bar x)^2$, which is $\sqrt{(n-1)/n}\;s/\sqrt n$.
$100(1-\alpha)\%$: the $\alpha/2$ and $1 - \alpha/2$ quantiles of the replicates (for $B = 2000$ and 95%, about the 50th and 1950th smallest).

cards.front: When the bootstrap fails or needs care
cards.back: Extremes such as the maximum (the resample keeps $X_{(n)}$ with probability $\approx 0.632$), very small $n$, and dependent data; resample the way the data were sampled (pairs, groups).
Bootstrap: resample *with* replacement to mimic sampling variability (SEs, intervals). Permutation: reshuffle labels *without* replacement under $H_0$ (p-values).

cards.front: Total risk of $\mathbf X$ for $p$ independent $N(\theta_i, \sigma^2)$ means
cards.back: $E\sum(X_i - \theta_i)^2 = p\sigma^2$, the same for every $\boldsymbol\theta$
$c^* = \|\boldsymbol\theta\|^2/(\|\boldsymbol\theta\|^2 + p\sigma^2)$, risk $p\sigma^2\|\boldsymbol\theta\|^2/(\|\boldsymbol\theta\|^2 + p\sigma^2)$
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} = \big(1 - (p - 2)\sigma^2/\|\mathbf X\|^2\big)\mathbf X$, for $p \ge 3$
$p\sigma^2 - (p - 2)^2\sigma^4E[1/\|\mathbf X\|^2] < p\sigma^2$ for every $\boldsymbol\theta$; equals $2\sigma^2$ at $\boldsymbol\theta = \mathbf 0$
For $W \sim \chi^2_p$, $E(1/W) = 1/(p - 2)$, so $(p - 2)\sigma^2/\|\mathbf X\|^2$ is unbiased for the Bayes shrinkage $\sigma^2/(\sigma^2 + \tau^2)$ when $\theta_i \sim N(0, \tau^2)$
$Z \sim N(\theta, \sigma^2)$: $E[(Z - \theta)g(Z)] = \sigma^2E[g'(Z)]$ (integration by parts)
$\hat\theta_i = \bar X + \big(1 - (p - 3)\sigma^2/\sum(X_j - \bar X)^2\big)(X_i - \bar X)$; beats $\mathbf X$ for $p \ge 4$
Use $\max(0, \text{factor})$; never flips signs, and its risk is no larger than James–Stein for every $\boldsymbol\theta$
Total squared error over all coordinates; a single unusual $\theta_i$ can be estimated worse

cards.front: When is $\mathbf X$ admissible for normal means?
cards.back: For $p = 1$ and $p = 2$; inadmissible for $p \ge 3$ (Stein, 1956)
Minimize RSS $+ \lambda\sum\beta_j^2$; $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X + \lambda\mathbf I)^{-1}\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y$ (centered, standardized predictors)

cards.front: Ridge slope for one centered predictor
cards.back: $b = S_{xy}/(S_{xx} + \lambda)$
Minimize RSS $+ \lambda\sum|\beta_j|$; can set coefficients exactly to 0

cards.front: Lasso slope for one centered predictor
cards.back: $b = \operatorname{sign}(S_{xy})\max(|S_{xy}| - \lambda/2, 0)/S_{xx}$ (soft thresholding); zero when $\lambda \ge 2|S_{xy}|$

cards.front: MSE of a one-predictor ridge slope
cards.back: $\big(\sigma^2S_{xx} + \lambda^2\beta^2\big)/(S_{xx} + \lambda)^2$; minimized at $\lambda^* = \sigma^2/\beta^2$
Posterior mean (and mode) with independent $N(0, \sigma^2/\lambda)$ priors on the coefficients
The diamond $\sum|\beta_j| \le t$ has corners on the axes, where the RSS contours usually touch it first; the ridge disk has no corners
K-fold cross-validation (often K = 5 or 10), then refit on all the data; never by training error, which always prefers $\lambda = 0$
Take the largest $\lambda$ whose CV error is within one SE of the minimum CV error
Standardize the predictors and leave the intercept unpenalized (center $y$)

cards.front: FWER for $m$ independent true-null tests at level $\alpha$
cards.back: $1 - (1 - \alpha)^m$; expected false rejections $m\alpha$
Uniform(0, 1) for a continuous test statistic: $P(p \le u) = u$
FWER $= P(V \ge 1)$; FDR $= E(V/R)$ with $V/R = 0$ when $R = 0$; FDR $\le$ FWER, with equality when all nulls are true
Sort p-values; reject while $p_{(k)} \le \alpha/(m - k + 1)$, stop at the first failure; controls FWER under any dependence
Largest $k$ with $p_{(k)} \le kq/m$; reject the $k$ smallest p-values
Independent tests: FDR $= m_0q/m \le q$; arbitrary dependence: use $q/(1 + \tfrac12 + \dots + \tfrac1m)$ (Benjamini–Yekutieli)
Step-down (Holm) starts at the smallest p-value and stops at the first failure; step-up (BH) finds the largest index under its line and rejects everything below it
$\tilde p_{(k)} = \min_{j \ge k}\min(1, mp_{(j)}/j)$; compare with $q$

cards.front: When to control FWER vs FDR
cards.back: FWER for a few confirmatory claims where one false claim is costly; FDR for large-scale screening with follow-up

cards.front: Expected share of false discoveries in a screen
cards.back: About $m_0\alpha/(m_0\alpha + m_1 \cdot \text{power})$
To draw from a distribution known only up to a constant ($\pi = f/Z$, $Z$ unknown), such as a non-conjugate posterior
$\pi P = \pi$: if $X_t \sim \pi$ then $X_{t+1} \sim \pi$
$\pi(x)P(x, y) = \pi(y)P(y, x)$ for all $x, y$; summing over $x$ shows $\pi P = \pi$
$\alpha = \min\big(1, f(y)q(x \mid y)/(f(x)q(y \mid x))\big)$; with a symmetric proposal, $\min(1, f(y)/f(x))$
Stay at $x$ and record $x$ again
$\pi(x)q(y \mid x)\alpha(x, y) = \min\big(f(x)q(y \mid x), f(y)q(x \mid y)\big)/Z$ is symmetric in $x, y$, so detailed balance holds
$\text{ESS} \approx N(1 - \rho)/(1 + \rho)$; Monte Carlo SE $\approx s/\sqrt{\text{ESS}}$
Too small: high acceptance, slow crawl. Too large: frequent rejections. Rough targets: acceptance near 0.44 in one dimension, 0.23 in many
Discard burn-in, look at trace plots, run several chains from different starts (Gelman–Rubin R-hat), and use the ESS for standard errors
Update each parameter in turn from its full conditional distribution; every update is accepted

Condition on the first step; if the process afterward is a copy of the original problem, the unknown probability appears on both sides of the law of total probability. Solve the equation, using the boundary conditions.

cards.front: Alternating race: first player succeeds with $p$ per turn, second with $r$
cards.back: $a = p + (1-p)(1-r)\,a$, so $a = \dfrac{p}{p + r - pr}$. A fair die, first six wins: $6/11$.

cards.front: Why the alternating race ends with probability 1
cards.back: "Never ends" is contained in "no success in the first $2n$ turns," whose probability $[(1-p)(1-r)]^n \to 0$; by monotonicity $P(\text{never ends}) = 0$.
Only the race between $k$ and 7 matters: $w_k = \dfrac{P(k)}{P(k) + P(7)}$. Points 4/10: $1/3$; 5/9: $2/5$; 6/8: $5/11$.

cards.front: Probability of winning at craps (pass line)
Gambler's ruin: recursion and boundary conditions
cards.back: $P_i = p\,P_{i+1} + q\,P_{i-1}$ for $1 \le i \le N-1$, with $P_0 = 0$ and $P_N = 1$.
Fair ($p = \tfrac12$): $P_i = i/N$. Otherwise, with $\rho = q/p$: $P_i = \dfrac{1 - \rho^i}{1 - \rho^N}$.

cards.front: Gambler's ruin against an unlimited opponent
cards.back: If $p \le \tfrac12$, ruin is certain. If $p > \tfrac12$, $P(\text{never ruined}) = 1 - (q/p)^i$.

cards.front: Bold versus timid play in an unfavorable game
cards.back: Bold play reaches a fixed goal more often. Roulette, \$20 to \$40: one bet $\approx 0.474$, \$1 bets $\approx 0.108$.
If A needs $a$ wins and B needs $b$, A's fair share is $P(\text{at least } a \text{ wins in } a + b - 1 \text{ rounds})$. Recursion: $W(a,b) = pW(a-1,b) + qW(a,b-1)$.
A comparison that holds in every group reverses when the groups are combined, because each overall rate is a weighted average of group rates with different weights.

cards.front: Overall rate as a weighted average
cards.back: $P(S \mid A) = \sum_g P(g \mid A)\,P(S \mid A, g)$, by the law of total probability within $A$.
When both treatments have the same mix of groups (same weights). Randomization makes the mixes alike on average.
Hold a confounder (a cause of both treatment choice and outcome) fixed by splitting on it; do not split on a result of the treatment. The numbers alone cannot decide.
Selecting on a common effect (e.g. "has trait H or trait E") makes independent traits negatively associated in the selected group.
Conditioning on a common cause can remove a dependence (lesson 4's coin); conditioning on a common effect can create one (Berkson).
$P(BB \mid \text{at least one boy}) = \tfrac13$; $P(BB \mid \text{older is a boy}) = \tfrac12$; $P(BB \mid \text{a randomly met child is a boy}) = \tfrac12$; with a Tuesday boy, $\tfrac{13}{27}$.
Boxes GG, SS, GS; a random coin from a random box is gold. $P(\text{other is gold}) = \tfrac23$, because GG was twice as likely as GS to produce a gold coin.
$G_X(s) = E(s^X) = \sum_k P(X = k)s^k$, for $X$ with values $0, 1, 2, \ldots$; it exists for $|s| \le 1$.
Bernoulli $q + ps$; binomial $(q + ps)^n$; Poisson $e^{\lambda(s-1)}$; geometric (trials) $ps/(1 - qs)$.

cards.front: PGF of a sum vs. a random sum
cards.back: Independent $X + Y$: $G_XG_Y$ (product). Random sum $X_1 + \cdots + X_N$: $G_N(G_X(s))$ (composition).
Keep each of a Poisson$(\lambda)$ number of events with probability $p$: the kept count is Poisson$(\lambda p)$, since $e^{\lambda(q + ps - 1)} = e^{\lambda p(s - 1)}$.
$G_{Z_n} = f \circ f \circ \cdots \circ f$ ($n$ times), where $f$ is the offspring PGF; $E(Z_n) = m^n$ with $m = f'(1)$.
$q$ is the smallest root of $f(s) = s$ in $[0, 1]$, and $P(Z_n = 0) = f_n(0)$ increases to $q$.
If $p_1 \ne 1$: $q = 1$ when $m \le 1$ (subcritical or critical); $q < 1$ when $m > 1$ (supercritical).
If $p_2 > p_0$, then $q = p_0/p_2$ (the other root of $p_2s^2 + (p_1 - 1)s + p_0 = 0$ besides 1).
$E(Z_n) = 1$ for every $n$, yet extinction is certain (unless $p_1 = 1$); the few surviving lines grow large.
Galton posed the surname question (1873); Watson's answer missed the smaller root; Bienaymé stated the criterion (1845); Steffensen gave a full solution (1930).
$d_{TV}(X, Y) = \max_A |P(X \in A) - P(Y \in A)| = \tfrac12\sum_k |P(X = k) - P(Y = k)|$; an absolute, not relative, error.
Independent indicators with probabilities $p_i$: $d_{TV}\big(\sum I_i, \text{Poisson}(\sum p_i)\big) \le \sum p_i^2$. Binomial: $\le np^2 = \lambda p$.
If $S$ and $T$ are built on one sample space, $d_{TV}(S, T) \le P(S \ne T)$.
A sharper version of Le Cam: $d_{TV} \le \dfrac{1 - e^{-\lambda}}{\lambda}\sum p_i^2$, much smaller when $\lambda$ is large.
Many rare, weakly dependent events $A_i$: the count is roughly Poisson$(\lambda)$ with $\lambda = \sum P(A_i)$, so $P(\text{none}) \approx e^{-\lambda}$. A heuristic.

cards.front: Pair check for a Poisson count
cards.back: $E[X(X-1)] = \sum_{i \ne j} P(A_i \cap A_j)$ (ordered pairs). Poisson needs about $\lambda^2$; much more means clustering and variance above the mean.
The number of letters in the right envelope has mean 1 and variance 1 for every $n \ge 2$, and is close to Poisson(1).

cards.front: Birthday problem by the Poisson paradigm
cards.back: $\lambda = \binom{n}{2}/365$; $P(\text{no shared birthday}) \approx e^{-\lambda}$. At $n = 23$, $\lambda \approx 0.693$ and $e^{-\lambda} \approx 0.500$ (exact 0.4927).
Bortkiewicz (1898): counts of rare events, such as horse-kick deaths in Prussian army corps (mean 0.61 per corps-year), fit the Poisson distribution.

cards.front: Hazard in terms of the survival function
cards.back: $h(x) = \dfrac{f(x)}{S(x)} = -\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln S(x)$; $h(x)\,\Delta x \approx P(\text{fail in the next } \Delta x \mid \text{alive at } x)$.

cards.front: When is a function a valid hazard?
cards.back: $h \ge 0$ and $\int_0^\infty h(t)\,dt = \infty$, so that $S(x) \to 0$.
$S(x) = e^{-(x/s)^k}$, $h(x) = \dfrac{k}{s}\left(\dfrac{x}{s}\right)^{k-1}$: decreasing for $k < 1$, constant for $k = 1$, increasing for $k > 1$.
$E(X) = s\,\Gamma(1 + 1/k)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X) = s^2[\Gamma(1 + 2/k) - \Gamma(1 + 1/k)^2]$.
Survival functions multiply and hazards add: $h_T = \sum h_i$. $n$ iid Weibull$(k, s)$ give Weibull$(k, s\,n^{-1/k})$.
Falling hazard (early failures), flat hazard (random failures), rising hazard (wear-out). An idealization; burn-in targets the first phase.
$m(t) = E(X - t \mid X > t) = \dfrac{1}{S(t)}\int_t^\infty S(x)\,dx$; constant $1/\lambda$ for the exponential, $(L - t)/2$ for U$(0, L)$.
$h(x) = a\,e^{bx}$: the hazard doubles every $\ln 2/b$ time units; a classic model of adult mortality.
Nondecreasing, right-continuous, $F(-\infty) = 0$, $F(\infty) = 1$; a jump at $a$ has size $P(X = a) = F(a) - F(a^-)$.

cards.front: Mean of a mixed random variable
cards.back: $E(X) = \sum_{\text{atoms}} a\,P(X = a) + \int x\,F'(x)\,dx$; for $X \ge 0$ simply $\int_0^\infty P(X > x)\,dx$.
Point mass $S(c)$ at $c$; $E[\min(X, c)] = \int_0^c S(x)\,dx$ (limited expected value).
$(X - d)^+$ has a point mass $F(d)$ at 0 and $E[(X - d)^+] = \int_d^\infty S(x)\,dx$; $E[\min(X, d)] + E[(X - d)^+] = E(X)$.
An item still running at the end time $c$ is recorded as "longer than $c$"; averaging $\min(X, c)$ as if it were the lifetime underestimates the mean.
$F^{-1}(u) = \min\{x : F(x) \ge u\}$; then $F^{-1}(U)$ has cdf $F$ for every distribution, but $F(X)$ is uniform only when $F$ is continuous.
For losses exponential with mean $\theta$: $E[(X - d)^+] = \theta e^{-d/\theta}$, and given a payment the excess is again exponential with mean $\theta$ (memoryless).

cards.front: Simulating from a cdf with a jump
cards.back: Draw $U$; if $U$ falls within the jump at $a$ (between $F(a^-)$ and $F(a)$), return $a$; otherwise solve $F(x) = U$ on the continuous part.
$\Sigma = E[(\mathbf{X} - \boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{X} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top]$, $\Sigma_{ij} = \operatorname{Cov}(X_i, X_j)$; symmetric, variances on the diagonal
$E = A\boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{b}$, $\operatorname{Cov} = A\Sigma A^\top$

cards.front: Variance of a linear combination (matrix form)
cards.back: $\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{a}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{a} = \sum_i\sum_j a_ia_j\Sigma_{ij}$
$\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{a}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{c}$
Exactly the symmetric positive semidefinite ones: $\mathbf{a}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{a} \ge 0$ for all $\mathbf{a}$, since it is a variance
$\rho \ge -1/(n-1)$, from $\operatorname{Var}(\sum Z_i) = n + n(n-1)\rho \ge 0$
$\mathbf{X} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + A\mathbf{Z}$, $\mathbf{Z}$ iid $N(0, 1)$, $AA^\top = \Sigma$ (e.g. the Cholesky factor $L$)
$(2\pi)^{-n/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\big(-\tfrac12(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\big)$, for invertible $\Sigma$

$\mathbf{X}_1 \mid \mathbf{X}_2 = \mathbf{x}_2$ is normal with mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 + \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2)$ and covariance $\Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}$

cards.front: Distribution of the squared Mahalanobis distance
cards.back: $(\mathbf{X} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{X} - \boldsymbol{\mu}) \sim \chi^2_n$; in two dimensions $P(Q \le c) = 1 - e^{-c/2}$

cards.front: Uncorrelated components of a multivariate normal
cards.back: Are independent (the density factors when $\Sigma$ is diagonal); not true without joint normality

cards.front: Joint density of all order statistics
cards.back: $n!\,f(y_1)\cdots f(y_n)$ for $y_1 < \cdots < y_n$

cards.front: Joint density of the min and max
cards.back: $n(n-1)f(u)f(v)[F(v) - F(u)]^{n-2}$ for $u < v$; also $P(\min > u, \max \le v) = [F(v) - F(u)]^n$
For iid exponentials with rate $\lambda$, the spacings $D_k = X_{(k)} - X_{(k-1)}$ are independent, $D_k \sim$ exponential with rate $(n - k + 1)\lambda$

cards.front: Mean and variance of the $k$th exponential order statistic
cards.back: $E[X_{(k)}] = \frac1\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac1{n-i+1}$, $\operatorname{Var}(X_{(k)}) = \frac1{\lambda^2}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac1{(n-i+1)^2}$
Distributed as the maximum of $n - 1$ of them: $P(R \le r) = (1 - e^{-\lambda r})^{n-1}$
At failure number $n - k + 1$, i.e. at $X_{(n-k+1)}$

cards.front: Which tool for a tail probability?
cards.back: Full distribution: compute exactly. Average of many iid values: CLT (approximate) or, with $\sigma^2$ or a bound on it, Chebyshev (guaranteed). Variance known: Chebyshev. Only the mean of $X \ge 0$: Markov.

cards.front: Why the continuity correction uses $k + 0.5$ for $P(X \le k)$
cards.back: The bar for $X = k$ runs from $k - 0.5$ to $k + 0.5$; the normal area must reach $k + 0.5$ to include it.
$P(X \ge a) \le \min_{t > 0} e^{-ta}M_X(t)$ (Markov applied to $e^{tX}$).
$P(X \ge \mu + z\sigma) \le e^{-z^2/2}$ (optimal $t = z/\sigma$).
$P(S \ge na) \le e^{-nD(a\|p)}$, $D(a\|p) = a\ln\frac{a}{p} + (1-a)\ln\frac{1-a}{1-p}$.

cards.front: Why Chernoff bounds decay exponentially in $n$
cards.back: For an independent sum the MGF is a product, so the bound is a single-term quantity raised to the power $n$.
$a \le X \le b \Rightarrow E[e^{s(X - E[X])}] \le e^{s^2(b-a)^2/8}$.
Independent $X_i \in [a_i, b_i]$: $P(S_n - E[S_n] \ge u) \le \exp\big(-2u^2/\sum(b_i - a_i)^2\big)$.

cards.front: Hoeffding for a mean of values in $[0, 1]$
cards.back: One side: $e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$. Two sides: $P(|\bar X - \mu| \ge \varepsilon) \le 2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$.
$n \ge \dfrac{(b-a)^2\ln(2/\delta)}{2\varepsilon^2}$ guarantees $P(|\bar X - \mu| \ge \varepsilon) \le \delta$; grows like $\ln(1/\delta)$, not $1/\delta$.
Chebyshev 1,000; Hoeffding 600; CLT approximation 271.

cards.front: Chernoff vs Hoeffding for Bernoulli terms
cards.back: Chernoff (exact MGF) is never weaker, since $D(a\|p) \ge 2(a - p)^2$.
$\frac1n\ln P(\bar X_n \ge a) \to -I(a)$, $I(a) = \sup_t[ta - \ln M(t)]$: the Chernoff exponent is the true rate.
$P(\lim Y_n = Y) = 1$: almost every whole sequence converges.
$E[(Y_n - c)^2] \to 0$; implies convergence in probability by Markov.
a.s. ⇒ in probability ⇒ in distribution; mean square ⇒ in probability; in distribution to a constant ⇒ in probability.
$\sum P(A_n) < \infty$ ⇒ finitely many occur (a.s.). Independent with $\sum P(A_n) = \infty$ ⇒ infinitely many occur (a.s.).

cards.front: In probability but not almost surely
cards.back: Independent $Y_n \sim$ Bernoulli$(1/n)$: $P(Y_n = 1) \to 0$, but $\sum 1/n = \infty$, so $Y_n = 1$ infinitely often.

cards.front: In probability but not in mean
cards.back: $Y_n = n$ with probability $1/n$, else 0: $Y_n \xrightarrow{P} 0$ but $E[Y_n] = 1$, $E[Y_n^2] = n$.

cards.front: In distribution but not in probability
cards.back: $Y_n = -Z$ with $Z \sim N(0,1)$: same distribution as $Z$, but $|Y_n - Z| = 2|Z|$.
$Y_n \xrightarrow{P} c$, $g$ continuous at $c$ ⇒ $g(Y_n) \xrightarrow{P} g(c)$; same for convergence in distribution.
$X_n \xrightarrow{d} X$, $Y_n \xrightarrow{P} c$ ⇒ $X_n + Y_n \to X + c$, $X_nY_n \to cX$, $X_n/Y_n \to X/c$ ($c \ne 0$), in distribution.
$(\bar X - \mu)/(S/\sqrt n) \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1)$ for any finite-variance population: CLT, $S \xrightarrow{P} \sigma$, Slutsky.
$\sqrt n(g(\bar X) - g(\mu)) = g'(\xi_n)\sqrt n(\bar X - \mu) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, g'(\mu)^2\sigma^2)$.

cards.front: Two facts about the score at the true $\theta$
cards.back: $E[U(\theta)] = 0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(U(\theta)) = nI(\theta)$, so $U(\theta)/\sqrt n \approx N(0, I(\theta))$ by the CLT.

cards.front: Why the MLE is approximately normal (sketch)
cards.back: $0 = U(\hat\theta) \approx U(\theta) + U'(\theta)(\hat\theta - \theta)$; CLT for $U(\theta)/\sqrt n$, LLN for $-U'(\theta)/n \to I(\theta)$; so $\hat\theta \approx N(\theta, 1/(nI(\theta)))$.
$\theta_{k+1} = \theta_k - \ell'(\theta_k)/\ell''(\theta_k)$. Fast near the answer; can overshoot or find a minimum from a poor start.
$\theta_{k+1} = \theta_k + \ell'(\theta_k)/(nI(\theta_k))$: Newton with expected information; always steps uphill.
$\text{SE} = 1/\sqrt{J(\hat\theta)}$ with $J(\hat\theta) = -\ell''(\hat\theta)$; Wald interval $\hat\theta \pm z_{\alpha/2}\text{SE}$.
$\hat\lambda = n/\sum x_i$, $J(\hat\lambda) = n/\hat\lambda^2$, $\text{SE} = \hat\lambda/\sqrt n$.
$\bar x = \lambda/(1 - e^{-\lambda})$; no closed form, solve numerically (fault data: $\bar x = 1.5$ gives $\hat\lambda \approx 0.874$).
Covariance $\approx (nI)^{-1}$; SE of $\hat\eta_j$ = square root of the $j$th diagonal entry of the inverse, not $1/\sqrt{nI_{jj}}$.
$\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & d\end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{ad - b^2}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -b & a\end{pmatrix}$; SEs $\sqrt{d/(ad - b^2)}$ and $\sqrt{a/(ad - b^2)}$.
Per observation $\operatorname{diag}(1/\sigma^2,\; 1/(2\sigma^4))$: $\hat\mu$ and $\hat\sigma^2$ asymptotically uncorrelated, $\text{SE}(\hat\sigma^2) \approx \sigma^2\sqrt{2/n}$.
Wald: symmetric, uses curvature at the peak. Likelihood: $2[\ell(\hat\theta) - \ell(\theta)] \le 3.84$, follows the shape of $\ell$; better for small $n$.
$R(\theta, \delta) = E_\theta[L(\theta, \delta(X))]$; under squared-error loss it is the MSE.
Squared error: posterior mean. Absolute error: posterior median. Zero–one (small tolerance): posterior mode.
$r(\pi, \delta) = \int R(\theta, \delta)\pi(\theta)\,d\theta$; the Bayes estimator minimizes it.
Minimizes $\max_\theta R(\theta, \delta)$. A Bayes estimator with constant risk is minimax.
$\dfrac{X + \sqrt n/2}{n + \sqrt n}$ (Bayes for Beta$(\sqrt n/2, \sqrt n/2)$), constant risk $\dfrac{1}{4(1 + \sqrt n)^2}$.
$\delta'$ dominates $\delta$ if its risk is never larger and sometimes smaller; a dominated estimator is inadmissible. Example: $S^2$ for normal $\sigma^2$ (divide by $n + 1$ instead).

cards.front: Why a unique Bayes estimator is admissible
cards.back: A dominating estimator would have Bayes risk no larger, so it would also be Bayes; uniqueness makes it the same estimator.
$c^2v + (1 - c)^2(\theta - \mu_0)^2$ with $v = \sigma^2/n$; beats $\bar X$ when $(\theta - \mu_0)^2 < \frac{1+c}{1-c}v$.

cards.front: Normal prior: Bayes estimator and Bayes risk
cards.back: Prior $N(\mu_0, \tau^2)$: $c = \tau^2/(\tau^2 + v)$, Bayes risk $cv$ (the posterior variance). $\bar X$ is minimax.
$C(p) = \sum_{x=0}^n \mathbf 1\{p \in \text{interval}(x)\}\binom nx p^x(1-p)^{n-x}$, a jagged function of $p$.

cards.front: Why the Wald interval for $p$ fails
cards.back: Plug-in SE is too small when $\hat p$ is near 0 or 1 (zero width at $x = 0$); symmetric although the binomial is skewed; coverage erratic in $n$.
Solve $|\hat p - p| \le z\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ for $p$: center $\dfrac{\hat p + z^2/2n}{1 + z^2/n}$, half-width $\dfrac{z}{1 + z^2/n}\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n} + \dfrac{z^2}{4n^2}}$.
$\tilde p = (x + 2)/(n + 4)$, then $\tilde p \pm 1.96\sqrt{\tilde p(1 - \tilde p)/(n + 4)}$.
Invert exact one-sided tests: $P(X \ge x; p_L) = \alpha/2$, $P(X \le x; p_U) = \alpha/2$. Coverage always at least $1 - \alpha$; wide.
Equal-tailed quantiles of Beta$(x + \tfrac12,\; n - x + \tfrac12)$ (Jeffreys prior Beta$(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$); coverage close to nominal.
Exact one-sided upper bound $1 - \alpha^{1/n}$; for 95%, about $3/n$ (rule of three).
Small $n$ (up to about 40): Wilson or Jeffreys. Larger $n$: Agresti–Coull is fine. Guaranteed coverage: Clopper–Pearson. Avoid plain Wald.

cards.front: Score function and its null distribution
cards.back: $U(\theta) = \ell'(\theta)$. At the true $\theta$: mean 0, variance $nI(\theta)$, so $U(\theta_0) \approx N(0, nI(\theta_0))$ under $H_0$.

cards.back: $J(\theta) = -\ell''(\theta)$, the curvature of the log-likelihood; $J(\theta)/n \to I(\theta)$.
cards.topic: Wald, score and likelihood ratio tests

cards.back: $W = (\hat\theta - \theta_0)^2\,nI(\hat\theta)$: variance at the MLE; needs only the unrestricted fit; approximately $\chi^2_1$.
cards.topic: Wald, score and likelihood ratio tests

cards.back: $S = U(\theta_0)^2/nI(\theta_0)$: everything evaluated at $\theta_0$; needs only the null fit; approximately $\chi^2_1$.
cards.topic: Wald, score and likelihood ratio tests

cards.back: $\text{LR} = 2[\ell(\hat\theta) - \ell(\theta_0)] = -2\ln\Lambda$: needs both fits; approximately $\chi^2_1$.
cards.topic: Wald, score and likelihood ratio tests

cards.back: On the graph of $\ell$: Wald uses the horizontal gap $\hat\theta - \theta_0$, score the slope at $\theta_0$, LR the vertical drop from the peak.
cards.topic: Wald, score and likelihood ratio tests

cards.front: When the three tests coincide exactly
cards.back: When the log-likelihood is exactly quadratic, e.g. a normal mean with $\sigma$ known: all equal $n(\bar x - \mu_0)^2/\sigma^2$.
cards.topic: Wald, score and likelihood ratio tests

cards.back: Score: $\dfrac{(\hat p - p_0)^2}{p_0(1-p_0)/n}$ (the one-proportion $z$ test, squared). Wald: $\dfrac{(\hat p - p_0)^2}{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$.
cards.topic: Wald, score and likelihood ratio tests

cards.back: Wald $\dfrac{(\bar x - \lambda_0)^2}{\bar x/n}$; score $\dfrac{(\bar x - \lambda_0)^2}{\lambda_0/n}$; LR $2n[\bar x\ln(\bar x/\lambda_0) - (\bar x - \lambda_0)]$.
cards.topic: Wald, score and likelihood ratio tests

cards.back: LR and score tests give the same result for $p$ or $\ln\frac{p}{1-p}$; the Wald test does not.
cards.topic: Wald, score and likelihood ratio tests

cards.back: Pearson $X^2 = \sum(O-E)^2/E$: score. $G^2$: likelihood ratio. Neyman $\sum(O-E)^2/O$: Wald.
cards.topic: Wald, score and likelihood ratio tests

cards.back: Wald: $\hat p \pm z\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$ (can leave $[0,1]$, poor coverage). Score: Wilson interval. LR: $\{p: 2[\ell(\hat p) - \ell(p)] \le \chi^2_{\alpha,1}\}$.
cards.topic: Wald, score and likelihood ratio tests

cards.back: $S_n = \sum_{i=1}^n \ln\dfrac{f(X_i;\theta_1)}{f(X_i;\theta_0)}$; large values favor $H_1$ (reciprocal of the Neyman–Pearson ratio).
Reject when $S_n \ge b = \ln\frac{1-\beta}{\alpha}$; accept $H_0$ when $S_n \le a = \ln\frac{\beta}{1-\alpha}$; otherwise continue.

cards.front: True error rates of an SPRT
cards.back: Because of overshoot they differ from $\alpha, \beta$, but $\alpha' \le \alpha/(1-\beta)$, $\beta' \le \beta/(1-\alpha)$ and $\alpha' + \beta' \le \alpha + \beta$.

cards.front: SPRT for a Bernoulli defect rate
cards.back: Defective adds $\ln(p_1/p_0)$, good item adds $\ln\frac{1-p_1}{1-p_0}$. In the (items $n$, defectives $d$) plane the boundaries are parallel lines $d = h_1 + sn$ and $d = -h_0 + sn$.

cards.front: SPRT increment for a normal mean ($\sigma$ known)
cards.back: $Z_i = \dfrac{\mu_1 - \mu_0}{\sigma^2}\left(X_i - \dfrac{\mu_0 + \mu_1}{2}\right)$.
$E(S_N) = E(N)\,E(Z)$ for an i.i.d. sum stopped at a time that depends only on the past (with $E(N)$ finite).

cards.front: Average sample number of an SPRT
cards.back: $E_0(N) \approx \dfrac{(1-\alpha)a + \alpha b}{E_0(Z)}$, $E_1(N) \approx \dfrac{\beta a + (1-\beta)b}{E_1(Z)}$ (overshoot ignored).

cards.front: Optimality of the SPRT (Wald and Wolfowitz, 1948)
cards.back: No test with error probabilities at most the SPRT's has a smaller expected sample size under $H_0$ or under $H_1$.

cards.front: Why not just peek at a fixed-sample test?
cards.back: Testing at 5% after every observation and stopping at the first rejection inflates the Type I error (about 0.37 with 100 looks). Sequential and group sequential designs use boundaries built for repeated looks.

$\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon$, $\boldsymbol\varepsilon \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2\mathbf{I})$; $\mathbf{X}$ is $n \times p$ with a column of ones and $p = k + 1$.
$\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}$, so $\mathbf{b} = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}$; equivalently $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$.

$\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top$; $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}$, $\mathbf{e} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}$; symmetric, idempotent, trace $p$.
$\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the column space of $\mathbf{X}$; the residual vector is perpendicular to every column.

cards.front: Covariance of the least squares coefficients
cards.back: $\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{b}) = \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}$, so $\operatorname{Var}(b_j) = \sigma^2c_{jj}$.
$t = b_j/(s\sqrt{c_{jj}})$ on $n - p$ df, with $s^2 = \text{SSE}/(n - p)$.
$R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - \dfrac{\text{SSE}/(n - p)}{\text{SST}/(n - 1)}$; plain $R^2$ never falls when a predictor is added.

cards.front: Overall F test in multiple regression
cards.back: $F = \dfrac{\text{SSR}/(p - 1)}{\text{SSE}/(n - p)} \sim F_{p-1,\,n-p}$ under $H_0: \beta_1 = \cdots = \beta_k = 0$.
$\text{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2)$; with two predictors $\operatorname{Var}(b_1) = \sigma^2/[S_{11}(1 - r_{12}^2)]$.
$h_{ii}$ = diagonal of $\mathbf{H}$; $\sum h_{ii} = p$; $\operatorname{Var}(e_i) = \sigma^2(1 - h_{ii})$; flag $h_{ii} > 2p/n$. Simple regression: $h_{ii} = 1/n + (x_i - \bar x)^2/S_{xx}$.

cards.front: Meaning of a multiple regression coefficient
cards.back: The change in mean response per unit of $x_j$ with the other predictors held fixed; it can differ from the simple-regression slope when predictors are correlated.

Another linear unbiased estimator is $(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{D})\mathbf{Y}$ with $\mathbf{D}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{0}$; its covariance is $\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1} + \sigma^2\mathbf{D}\mathbf{D}^\top$.
SST = SSTr + SSB + SSE with df $kb - 1 = (k - 1) + (b - 1) + (k - 1)(b - 1)$; $\text{SSTr} = b\sum(\bar y_{i\cdot} - \bar y)^2$, $\text{SSB} = k\sum(\bar y_{\cdot j} - \bar y)^2$.
$F = \text{MSTr}/\text{MSE} \sim F_{k-1,\,(k-1)(b-1)}$ under $H_0$: all treatment effects zero.
Block-to-block variation moves out of the error into SSB, so MSE shrinks; the cost is fewer error df ($(k - 1)(b - 1)$ instead of $kb - k$).
It is the paired $t$ test: the block-design $F$ equals $t^2$.
$Y_{ijl} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijl}$, $l = 1, \dots, r$; effects sum to zero over each index.
$\text{SS}_{AB} = r\sum_i\sum_j(\bar y_{ij\cdot} - \bar y_{i\cdot\cdot} - \bar y_{\cdot j\cdot} + \bar y)^2$.
Test the interaction first. If it is significant, describe each factor's effect at each level of the other (interaction plot); if not, interpret the main effects.
With one observation per cell there is no within-cell error, so interaction cannot be separated from error; the block design assumes additivity instead.

glossary.definition: The set $S$ of all possible outcomes of a random experiment.
A single element of the sample space: one complete result of the experiment.
A subset of the sample space. The event $A$ occurs when the actual outcome belongs to $A$.
$A \cup B$, the event that $A$ occurs, $B$ occurs, or both.
$A \cap B$, the event that both $A$ and $B$ occur.
$A^c$, the event that $A$ does not occur; $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$.
Events that cannot occur together: $A \cap B = \varnothing$, so $P(A \cap B) = 0$.
A collection of pairwise disjoint events whose union is the whole sample space, so exactly one of them occurs.
$(A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c$ and $(A \cap B)^c = A^c \cup B^c$: "not (A or B)" is "neither", and "not both" is "at least one fails".
A rule assigning a number $P(A)$ to each event so that the three axioms of probability hold.
(1) $P(A) \ge 0$; (2) $P(S) = 1$; (3) for pairwise disjoint events, $P(\bigcup A_i) = \sum P(A_i)$. Every other rule of probability is derived from these.
The third axiom: the probability of a union of countably many pairwise disjoint events is the sum of their probabilities.
$P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$, because $A$ and $A^c$ are disjoint with union $S$.
$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$; the overlap is subtracted because the sum counts it twice.
The probability of a union equals the sum of single probabilities, minus the sum over pairs of intersections, plus the sum over triples, and so on with alternating signs.
$P(\bigcup A_i) \le \sum P(A_i)$ for any events; it needs no information about overlaps.
$P(A \cap B) \ge P(A) + P(B) - 1$, a lower bound for an intersection that holds however the events are related.
A finite sample space in which every outcome has probability $1/|S|$, so $P(A) = |A|/|S|$.
If a procedure has stages with $n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k$ choices (the count at each stage not depending on earlier choices), it can be done in $n_1 n_2 \cdots n_k$ ways.
An ordered arrangement. There are $n!$ orderings of $n$ distinct objects and $n!/(n-r)!$ ordered selections of $r$ of them.
An unordered selection. The number of $r$-element subsets of an $n$-element set is $\binom{n}{r}$.
$\binom{n}{r} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}$, the number of ways to choose $r$ objects from $n$ when order does not matter.
$(x + y)^n = \sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{n}{r}x^r y^{n-r}$.
$\dfrac{n!}{n_1!\,n_2!\cdots n_k!}$, the number of ways to divide $n$ objects into labeled groups of sizes $n_1, \ldots, n_k$ (or to arrange $n$ objects with identical copies).
The chance that at least two of $n$ people share a birthday, $1 - \prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(1 - i/365)$; it passes 50% at $n = 23$.
The chance that a random permutation of $n$ items fixes at least one item, $\sum_{k=1}^{n}(-1)^{k+1}/k!$, which tends to $1 - 1/e \approx 0.632$.
$P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B)$ for $P(B) > 0$: the probability of $A$ once we know $B$ occurred.
$P(A \cap B) = P(B)\,P(A \mid B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$.
$P(A_1 \cap \cdots \cap A_n) = P(A_1)P(A_2 \mid A_1)\cdots P(A_n \mid A_1 \cap \cdots \cap A_{n-1})$.
For a partition $B_1, \ldots, B_k$: $P(A) = \sum_i P(B_i)\,P(A \mid B_i)$.
$P(B_j \mid A) = \dfrac{P(B_j)P(A \mid B_j)}{\sum_i P(B_i)P(A \mid B_i)}$: it reverses a conditional probability.
The probability of a hypothesis or scenario before the evidence is taken into account.
The probability of a hypothesis or scenario after updating on the evidence with Bayes' theorem.
In Bayes' theorem, the probability $P(A \mid B_i)$ of the observed evidence under each scenario.
The ratio $P(B)/P(B^c)$. Odds of $o$ correspond to the probability $o/(1 + o)$.
$P(A \mid B)/P(A \mid B^c)$, the factor by which evidence $A$ multiplies the odds on $B$: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio.
The prior probability of a condition in the population; ignoring it is the most common error in Bayes problems.
For a test, $P(\text{positive} \mid \text{condition present})$.
For a test, $P(\text{negative} \mid \text{condition absent})$; one minus it is the false-positive rate.
Events with $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$; when $P(B) > 0$ this means $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$.
Events such that every subcollection of two or more satisfies the product rule for its intersection.
Events in which every pair is independent. This is weaker than mutual independence.
Repetitions of an experiment in which events determined by different trials are mutually independent.
$A$ and $B$ are conditionally independent given $C$ if $P(A \cap B \mid C) = P(A \mid C)\,P(B \mid C)$.
The probability that a component or system works.
A system that works only if every component works; with independent components its reliability is $\prod p_i$.
A system that works if at least one component works; with independent components its reliability is $1 - \prod(1 - p_i)$.
The mistaken belief that a run of failures in independent trials makes a success more likely next time.
A function $X : S \to \mathbb{R}$ that assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment.
A random variable whose possible values form a finite or countably infinite list.
$I_A = 1$ if $A$ occurs and 0 otherwise; $E(I_A) = P(A)$. Counts are sums of indicators.
For a discrete random variable, $p(x) = P(X = x)$; it is nonnegative and sums to 1.
$F(x) = P(X \le x)$. It is nondecreasing, right-continuous, and rises from 0 to 1.
A function that is constant between jumps; the cdf of a discrete random variable jumps by $p(x_i)$ at each value $x_i$.
The probability-weighted average $E(X) = \sum x\,p(x)$ (discrete) or $\int x f(x)\,dx$ (continuous), when it converges absolutely.
$E[g(X)] = \sum g(x)p(x)$ or $\int g(x)f(x)\,dx$: the mean of a function of $X$ without finding its distribution.
$\operatorname{Var}(X) = E[(X - \mu)^2] = E(X^2) - \mu^2$, the mean squared distance from the mean.
The square root of the variance, measured in the units of $X$.
The variance shortcut $\operatorname{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2$.
The $k$-th moment of $X$ is $E(X^k)$; the mean is the first moment.
An experiment with two outcomes, success (with probability $p$) and failure.
The distribution of a 0–1 variable with $P(X = 1) = p$; mean $p$, variance $p(1-p)$.
The number of successes in $n$ independent trials with success probability $p$: $P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$; mean $np$, variance $np(1-p)$.
$E[X(X-1)]$ (and higher analogues), often easier to compute for discrete distributions; $\operatorname{Var}(X) = E[X(X-1)] + E(X) - [E(X)]^2$.

The most likely value of a discrete distribution (or the peak of a density). For $\text{Bin}(n, p)$ it is $\lfloor (n+1)p \rfloor$; when $(n+1)p$ is a whole number between 1 and $n$, both $(n+1)p - 1$ and $(n+1)p$ are modes.
The number of successes in a sample of $n$ drawn without replacement from $N$ items containing $K$ successes: $\binom{K}{k}\binom{N-K}{n-k}/\binom{N}{n}$; mean $nK/N$.
The factor $(N - n)/(N - 1)$ that shrinks the variance when sampling without replacement from a finite population.
The number of independent trials up to and including the first success: $P(X = k) = (1-p)^{k-1}p$; mean $1/p$, variance $(1-p)/p^2$.
For a variable with values in $\{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$, $E(X) = \sum_{k \ge 0}P(X > k)$; for a nonnegative continuous variable, $E(X) = \int_0^\infty P(X > x)\,dx$.

$P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)$: having waited $s$ does not change the distribution of the remaining wait. The geometric (discrete) and exponential (continuous) distributions are the only ones with it.
The number of independent trials needed for the $r$-th success: $P(X = k) = \binom{k-1}{r-1}p^r(1-p)^{k-r}$; mean $r/p$, variance $r(1-p)/p^2$.
Collecting all $n$ equally likely types takes on average $n(1 + \tfrac12 + \cdots + \tfrac1n)$ draws, a sum of geometric waiting times.
The count of rare events in a fixed interval: $P(X = k) = e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$; mean and variance both $\lambda$.
Events in time with independent, stationary increments and no simultaneous events; the count in time $t$ is Poisson$(\lambda t)$ and the gaps are exponential.
In a Poisson process or exponential distribution, the parameter $\lambda$: the expected number of events per unit time.
Count data whose variance is clearly larger than its mean, a sign that a Poisson model is inadequate (events cluster or the rate varies).
$M_X(t) = E(e^{tX})$. Its derivatives at 0 are the moments, it determines the distribution, and $M_{X+Y} = M_X M_Y$ for independent $X, Y$.
If two MGFs exist and agree on an open interval around 0, the two distributions are identical.
A random variable with a density $f$ such that $P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$; every single value has probability 0.
A function $f \ge 0$ with total integral 1 whose areas give probabilities; $f(x)$ is probability per unit length, not a probability.
The quantile of order $p$ is the value $x_p$ with $F(x_p) = p$.
The $100p$-th percentile is the quantile of order $p$.
The value $m$ with $F(m) = \tfrac12$, which splits the probability in half.
A heavy-tailed distribution with $P(X > x) = (\theta/x)^{\alpha}$ for $x \ge \theta$; its mean is finite only for $\alpha > 1$ and its variance only for $\alpha > 2$.
The density $1/[\pi(1 + x^2)]$, symmetric about 0 but with no mean, because $\int |x| f(x)\,dx$ diverges.
$\text{U}(a, b)$ has constant density $1/(b - a)$ on $[a, b]$; mean $(a+b)/2$, variance $(b-a)^2/12$.
The uniform distribution on $(0, 1)$, from which computers simulate other distributions.
Density $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x \ge 0$, with $P(X > x) = e^{-\lambda x}$; mean $1/\lambda$, variance $1/\lambda^2$; memoryless.
$P(X > x) = 1 - F(x)$, the probability of lasting beyond $x$.
$h(x) = f(x)/P(X > x)$, the instantaneous failure rate among items that have survived to $x$; constant for the exponential.
$\text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ has density $\dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}$, a bell curve with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$.
The normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 1; its cdf is written $\Phi$ and its density $\phi$.
$z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$, the number of standard deviations from the mean; it turns any normal variable into a standard normal one.
Widening each integer value of a discrete variable to the interval $[k - 0.5, k + 0.5]$ when approximating it by a continuous (usually normal) distribution.
$\Gamma(\alpha) = \int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x}\,dx$; $\Gamma(\alpha + 1) = \alpha\Gamma(\alpha)$, $\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!$, $\Gamma(\tfrac12) = \sqrt\pi$.
Density $x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x/\theta}/[\Gamma(\alpha)\theta^\alpha]$ for $x > 0$; mean $\alpha\theta$, variance $\alpha\theta^2$, MGF $(1 - \theta t)^{-\alpha}$.
A parameter that changes the form of a density (for the gamma distribution, $\alpha$), not just its location or spread.
A parameter that stretches a distribution along the axis (for the gamma distribution, $\theta$; the rate is $1/\theta$).
A gamma distribution with integer shape $k$: the time of the $k$-th event in a Poisson process.

$\chi^2(
u) = 	ext{Gamma}(
u/2, 2)$, the distribution of a sum of $
u$ independent squared standard normals; mean $
u$, variance $2
u$.
The parameter $\nu$ of a chi-square distribution (and later of $t$ and $F$ distributions).
$B(a, b) = \int_0^1 x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}\,dx = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a + b)$.
Density $x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}/B(a, b)$ on $(0, 1)$; mean $a/(a + b)$, variance $ab/[(a+b)^2(a+b+1)]$. Used for proportions and as a prior for $p$.
Finding the distribution of $Y = g(X)$ by writing $F_Y(y) = P(g(X) \le y)$ as a probability about $X$ and differentiating.
For strictly monotone $g$: $f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y))\,\left|\dfrac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\right|$.
The derivative factor $|dx/dy|$ (in higher dimensions, the absolute determinant of the derivative matrix) that rescales a density under a change of variables.
The distribution of $e^X$ when $X$ is normal; its median is $e^\mu$ and its mean is $e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$.
If $X$ is continuous with cdf $F$, then $F(X)$ is uniform on $(0, 1)$.
Simulating $X$ with cdf $F$ as $F^{-1}(U)$, where $U$ is a standard uniform random number.
A lifetime distribution with $P(X > x) = e^{-(x/s)^k}$; $k = 1$ is the exponential, and $k > 1$ gives an increasing hazard rate (wear-out).
The probability distribution of two or more random variables considered together, describing the probabilities of events that involve all of them at once.
For discrete $X$ and $Y$, the function $p(x, y) = P(X = x,\ Y = y)$; it is nonnegative and sums to 1 over all pairs.
A function $f(x, y) \ge 0$ with total integral 1 such that $P((X, Y) \in A) = \iint_A f\,dA$ for regions $A$ of the plane.
The function $F(x, y) = P(X \le x,\ Y \le y)$; for continuous pairs $f = \partial^2F/\partial x\,\partial y$.
The distribution of one variable taken from a joint distribution by summing or integrating out the others, e.g. $f_X(x) = \int f(x, y)\,dy$.
The set of values (or points of the plane) where a pmf or density is positive. Limits of integration come from intersecting the support with the event.
A pair $(X, Y)$ whose joint density is the constant $1/\text{area}(R)$ on a region $R$; probabilities are then ratios of areas.
For discrete variables, $p_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) = p(x, y)/p_X(x)$: the distribution of $Y$ once $X = x$ is known.
For continuous variables, $f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) = f(x, y)/f_X(x)$ where $f_X(x) > 0$; a density in $y$ for each fixed $x$.
A joint model built in stages: a distribution for $X$, then a conditional distribution for $Y$ given $X$, combined by $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x)$.
Random variables whose joint pmf or density equals the product of their marginals for all values; then conditional distributions equal marginal ones.
If a joint density can be written $g(x)h(y)$ for all $(x, y)$, with the support a rectangle (product set), then $X$ and $Y$ are independent.
Describes random variables that are mutually independent and all have the same distribution; the standard model for a random sample.
Observations $X_1, \dots, X_n$ modeled as iid from a population distribution, so their joint density is $\prod f(x_i)$.
$\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = E[(X - \mu_X)(Y - \mu_Y)] = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]$; positive when large values of one tend to go with large values of the other.
$\rho = \operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y)$, a unit-free measure of linear association with $-1 \le \rho \le 1$; $|\rho| = 1$ exactly when $Y$ is a linear function of $X$.
Having covariance 0. Independent variables are uncorrelated, but uncorrelated variables can be dependent (e.g. $Y = X^2$ with $X$ symmetric about 0).
The distribution of a sum of independent variables: $P(Z = z) = \sum_k p_X(k)p_Y(z - k)$ or $f_Z(z) = \int f_X(x)f_Y(z - x)\,dx$.
Finding the distribution of a sum of independent variables by multiplying their moment generating functions and recognizing the product.
$E[Y \mid X = x]$, the mean of the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X = x$; $E[Y \mid X]$ is the random variable obtained by plugging in $X$.
The function $x \mapsto E[Y \mid X = x]$; it is the best predictor of $Y$ from $X$ in mean squared error.
$\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X = x) = E[Y^2 \mid X = x] - (E[Y \mid X = x])^2$, the variance of the conditional distribution.
$E[Y] = E\big[E[Y \mid X]\big]$: average the conditional means, weighted by how likely each condition is.
$\operatorname{Var}(Y) = E[\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X)] + \operatorname{Var}(E[Y \mid X])$: average within-group variance plus variance between group means.
A total $T = X_1 + \cdots + X_N$ with a random number of terms $N$; if $N$ is independent of the iid $X_i$, $E[T] = \mu E[N]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(T) = \sigma^2E[N] + \mu^2\operatorname{Var}(N)$.
The distribution of a value drawn by first choosing a group at random and then drawing from that group's distribution; its variance comes from the law of total variance.
A joint distribution of $(X, Y)$ with normal marginals, normal conditionals and a linear regression function, determined by $\mu_X, \mu_Y, \sigma_X, \sigma_Y$ and $\rho$.
For a bivariate normal pair, the line $E[Y \mid X = x] = \mu_Y + \rho\frac{\sigma_Y}{\sigma_X}(x - \mu_X)$.
When $|\rho| < 1$, a value $k$ SDs from average in $X$ predicts a value only $\rho k$ SDs from average in $Y$, closer to the mean.
The sample values sorted into increasing order, $X_{(1)} \le \cdots \le X_{(n)}$; $X_{(1)}$ is the minimum and $X_{(n)}$ the maximum.
For $X \ge 0$ and $a > 0$, $P(X \ge a) \le E[X]/a$.
For $X$ with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2$, $P(|X - \mu| \ge k\sigma) \le 1/k^2$ for every $k > 0$.
$Y_n$ converges in probability to $c$ if $P(|Y_n - c| \ge \varepsilon) \to 0$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$; written $Y_n \xrightarrow{P} c$.
For iid variables with mean $\mu$ (and finite variance in the simple proof), $\bar X_n$ converges in probability to $\mu$.
For iid variables with finite mean $\mu$, $\bar X_n \to \mu$ with probability 1, a stronger statement than the weak law.
Estimating $\int_0^1 g(u)\,du = E[g(U)]$ by averaging $g$ at many random uniform points; it works by the law of large numbers.
For iid variables with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2$, $(\bar X_n - \mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)$ converges in distribution to $N(0, 1)$.
$Y_n$ converges in distribution to $Y$ if the cdfs satisfy $F_n(y) \to F(y)$ at every continuity point of $F$.
A quantity computed from the sample alone (no unknown parameters), such as $\bar X$ or $S^2$; it is a random variable.
The probability distribution of a statistic over repeated random samples of the same size.
$S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum(X_i - \bar X)^2$, an unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2$.

The distribution of $Z/\sqrt{V/\nu}$ with $Z \sim N(0, 1)$ and independent $V \sim \chi^2_\nu$; symmetric with heavier tails than the normal. For a normal sample, $(\bar X - \mu)/(S/\sqrt n) \sim t_{n-1}$.
The distribution of $(U/\nu_1)/(V/\nu_2)$ for independent chi-squares $U, V$; used for ratios of sample variances.
A fixed numerical characteristic of a population or model, such as $\mu$, $\sigma^2$, $p$ or $\lambda$, usually unknown and estimated from data.
A statistic $\hat\theta = h(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ used to guess a parameter $\theta$; as a function of random data it has a sampling distribution.
The number an estimator produces from one particular observed sample.
$\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta) = E[\hat\theta] - \theta$, the systematic error of an estimator.
An estimator is unbiased if $E[\hat\theta] = \theta$ for every value of $\theta$.
The standard deviation of an estimator's sampling distribution (or an estimate of it), e.g. $\sigma/\sqrt n$ for $\bar X$.
$\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta) = E[(\hat\theta - \theta)^2] = \operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) + \operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta)^2$.
An estimator $\hat\theta_n$ is consistent if it converges in probability to $\theta$; MSE tending to 0 is sufficient.
For unbiased estimators, $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_2)/\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_1)$: how many times more data $\hat\theta_2$ needs to match $\hat\theta_1$.
$I(\theta) = E[(\partial_\theta \ln f(X; \theta))^2] = -E[\partial_\theta^2 \ln f(X; \theta)]$, the information about $\theta$ in one observation.
Under regularity conditions, every unbiased estimator from an iid sample of size $n$ has $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) \ge 1/(nI(\theta))$.
An unbiased estimator whose variance attains the Cramér–Rao lower bound.
Smoothness assumptions needed for the Cramér–Rao bound and MLE asymptotics; chiefly, the support of $f(x; \theta)$ must not depend on $\theta$.
The $k$th sample moment $m_k = \frac1n\sum x_i^k$, the data analogue of $E[X^k]$.
Estimation by setting population moments $E[X^k]$ equal to sample moments $m_k$, $k = 1, \dots, p$, and solving for the $p$ parameters.
$L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i; \theta)$: the joint density or pmf of the observed data, viewed as a function of the parameter.
The parameter value $\hat\theta$ that maximizes the likelihood $L(\theta)$, i.e. makes the observed data most probable.
$\ell(\theta) = \ln L(\theta) = \sum \ln f(x_i; \theta)$; it has the same maximizer as $L$ and is easier to differentiate.
If $\hat\theta$ is the MLE of $\theta$, then $g(\hat\theta)$ is the MLE of $g(\theta)$.
If $\hat\theta \approx N(\theta, v)$ and $g$ is differentiable with $g'(\theta) \ne 0$, then $g(\hat\theta) \approx N(g(\theta), [g'(\theta)]^2 v)$, from a first-order Taylor expansion.
A statistic $T$ such that the conditional distribution of the sample given $T$ does not depend on $\theta$; once $T$ is known, the rest of the data carries no more information about $\theta$.
$T = u(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ is sufficient for $\theta$ if and only if the joint pmf or pdf factors as $\phi(u(x_1, \dots, x_n); \theta)\,h(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ with $h$ free of $\theta$.
A function of the data and the parameter whose distribution is completely known (free of unknown parameters), used to build confidence intervals.
A random interval $[L, U]$ computed from the data with $P(L \le \theta \le U) = 1 - \alpha$ before sampling; it covers $\theta$ in that fraction of repeated samples.
The long-run proportion $1 - \alpha$ of intervals from a procedure that contain the true parameter.
The half-width of a symmetric confidence interval, such as $z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n$.
A confidence interval for a proportion found by solving $|\hat p - p| \le z\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ for $p$; it has better coverage than $\hat p \pm z\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$ in small samples.
Inference that describes uncertainty about parameters with probability distributions, updating a prior to a posterior with Bayes' theorem.
The distribution $\pi(\theta)$ expressing beliefs about a parameter before the data are seen.
The distribution $\pi(\theta \mid x) \propto f(x \mid \theta)\pi(\theta)$ of the parameter after updating the prior with the data.
A prior family is conjugate to a model when the posterior is in the same family, e.g. beta priors for binomial data.
The mean of the posterior distribution; it minimizes posterior expected squared error and is a weighted average of prior information and data.
An interval with a stated posterior probability, e.g. $P(\theta \in [a, b] \mid \text{data}) = 0.95$.
The reciprocal of a variance. In the normal–normal model, posterior precision = prior precision + $n/\sigma^2$.
The maximum a posteriori estimate: the value of $\theta$ that maximizes the posterior density (likelihood × prior).
A rule that uses the data to decide whether to reject a stated null hypothesis about a parameter in favor of an alternative.
The hypothesis $H_0: \theta \in \Omega_0$ that a test controls errors against, usually the "no effect" or status-quo claim.
The hypothesis $H_1: \theta \in \Omega_1$ (also written $H_a$) that the investigator seeks evidence for; it may be one-sided ($\mu > \mu_0$) or two-sided ($\mu \ne \mu_0$).
A hypothesis that specifies the distribution of the data completely, such as $\mu = 50$ for a normal sample with known $\sigma$.
A hypothesis that allows more than one distribution, such as $\mu > 50$, or $\mu = 50$ with $\sigma$ unknown.
A function $T$ of the data whose value decides the test; its distribution under $H_0$ (the null distribution) sets the rejection region and p-values.
The set $C$ of values of the test statistic (or of the data) for which $H_0$ is rejected.
A boundary point of the rejection region, such as $c$ in "reject when $T \ge c$".
Rejecting $H_0$ when it is true. Its probability is at most the significance level $\alpha$.
Failing to reject $H_0$ when $H_1$ is true. Its probability at a parameter value $\theta \in \Omega_1$ is $\beta(\theta) = 1 - \pi(\theta)$.
The function $\pi(\theta) = P_\theta(\text{reject } H_0)$ over the whole parameter space; it gives Type I error probabilities on $\Omega_0$ and powers on $\Omega_1$.
The largest Type I error probability of a test, $\alpha = \sup_{\theta \in \Omega_0}\pi(\theta)$.
The bound $\alpha$ chosen in advance for the Type I error probability; a level-$\alpha$ test has size at most $\alpha$.
The probability $\pi(\theta)$ that a test rejects $H_0$ when the parameter is a particular alternative value $\theta$; equal to $1 - \beta(\theta)$.

The probability, computed under $H_0$, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed; equivalently the smallest $\alpha$ at which the data would reject. Under a simple $H_0$ with a continuous statistic it is Uniform(0, 1).
The test of $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ for a normal sample with unknown $\sigma$, based on $T = (\bar X - \mu_0)/(S/\sqrt n) \sim t_{n-1}$ under $H_0$.
A test whose statistic is approximately or exactly standard normal under $H_0$, such as $(\bar X - \mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)$ with $\sigma$ known.
The combined estimate $S_p^2 = [(m-1)S_1^2 + (n-1)S_2^2]/(m + n - 2)$ of a variance shared by two populations; used in the pooled two-sample $t$ test with $m + n - 2$ df.

The two-sample test of $\mu_1 = \mu_2$ that does not assume equal variances: $T = (\bar X - \bar Y)/\sqrt{S_1^2/m + S_2^2/n}$, referred to a $t$ distribution with the Satterthwaite approximate degrees of freedom.
For matched pairs, the one-sample $t$ test applied to the differences $D_i = X_i - Y_i$, with $n - 1$ df.
The test of $\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$ for independent normal samples using $F = S_1^2/S_2^2 \sim F_{m-1,\,n-1}$ under $H_0$; sensitive to non-normality.
The test of $\sigma^2 = \sigma_0^2$ for a normal sample using $(n-1)S^2/\sigma_0^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}$ under $H_0$; not robust to non-normality.
For a simple null versus a simple alternative, a level-$\alpha$ test whose power is at least that of every other test of size at most $\alpha$.

For simple $H_0: \theta_0$ versus simple $H_1: \theta_1$, the test that rejects when $L(\theta_0)/L(\theta_1) \le k$, with $k$ set to give size $\alpha$, is most powerful among tests of size at most $\alpha$.

A level-$\alpha$ test that is most powerful against every alternative in a composite $H_1$ at once; it exists for one-sided alternatives in families with a monotone likelihood ratio, but generally not for two-sided ones.

A family has a monotone likelihood ratio in a statistic $T$ if $L(\theta_1)/L(\theta_0)$ is an increasing function of $T$ whenever $\theta_1 > \theta_0$; a one-parameter exponential family has it in its natural statistic $T$ when the natural parameter is increasing in $\theta$ (in $-T$ when it is decreasing).
The test that rejects $H_0$ when $\Lambda = \sup_{\Omega_0}L(\theta)/\sup_{\Omega}L(\theta) = L(\hat\theta_0)/L(\hat\theta)$ is small.
Under regularity conditions and $H_0$, $-2\ln\Lambda$ is approximately $\chi^2_r$ for large samples, where $r = \dim\Omega - \dim\Omega_0$ is the number of parameters fixed by $H_0$.
The large-sample test of $p = p_0$ using $Z = (\hat p - p_0)/\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}$, approximately $N(0,1)$ under $H_0$.
The large-sample test of $p_1 = p_2$ using $(\hat p_1 - \hat p_2)/\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)(1/n_1 + 1/n_2)}$ with the pooled proportion $\hat p$.
The estimate $\hat p = (X_1 + X_2)/(n_1 + n_2)$ of the common success probability under $H_0: p_1 = p_2$.
The count a cell would have on average if $H_0$ were true: $np_{i0}$ in a goodness-of-fit test, $R_iC_j/n$ in a two-way table.
The statistic $X^2 = \sum (O - E)^2/E$ over all cells, approximately chi-square under $H_0$ when expected counts are not too small.

The joint distribution of the counts in $k$ categories from $n$ independent trials with category probabilities $p_1, \dots, p_k$: $P(o_1, \dots, o_k) = \frac{n!}{o_1!\cdots o_k!}p_1^{o_1}\cdots p_k^{o_k}$; each count is $\text{Bin}(n, p_i)$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(O_i, O_j) = -np_ip_j$.
A test of whether multinomial counts in $k$ categories follow specified probabilities; $X^2$ has approximately $k - 1 - m$ df, where $m$ parameters are estimated from the data.
A table of counts classifying each item by two categorical variables, with $r$ rows and $c$ columns.
A test of whether two categorical variables are independent, using $X^2$ with $E_{ij} = R_iC_j/n$ and $(r-1)(c-1)$ df.
A chi-square test of whether several separately sampled populations share the same distribution over categories; computed exactly like the test of independence.
The likelihood ratio statistic $G^2 = 2\sum O\ln(O/E)$ for counts; it equals $-2\ln\Lambda$ and is close to Pearson's $X^2$.
The model $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + \varepsilon_i$ with fixed $x_i$ and independent errors $\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$.
Choosing $b_0, b_1$ to minimize $\sum(y_i - b_0 - b_1x_i)^2$; gives $b_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ and $b_0 = \bar y - b_1\bar x$.
The equations obtained by setting the partial derivatives of the sum of squared errors to zero; for a line they say $\sum e_i = 0$ and $\sum x_ie_i = 0$.
The difference $e_i = y_i - \hat y_i$ between an observed response and its fitted value.
Shorthand sums in regression: $S_{xx} = \sum(x_i - \bar x)^2$, $S_{xy} = \sum(x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)$, $S_{yy} = \sum(y_i - \bar y)^2$.
The unexplained variation: $\sum e_i^2$ in regression (on $n - 2$ df) or $\sum\sum(Y_{ij} - \bar Y_{i\cdot})^2$ in ANOVA (on $N - k$ df).
The total variation of the responses about their overall mean, $\sum(y - \bar y)^2$; it splits into an explained part and SSE.
The variation explained by the fitted line, $\text{SSR} = \sum(\hat y_i - \bar y)^2 = b_1^2S_{xx}$; $\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}$.
The fraction of variation in $y$ explained by the regression, $r^2 = \text{SSR}/\text{SST} = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}$; for a line it is the squared correlation.

glossary.term: confidence interval for the mean response
aliases: confidence interval for a mean response
glossary.definition: An interval for $\beta_0 + \beta_1x_0$: $\hat y_0 \pm t_{\alpha/2,n-2}\,s\sqrt{1/n + (x_0 - \bar x)^2/S_{xx}}$.
An interval for a single new response at $x_0$: $\hat y_0 \pm t_{\alpha/2,n-2}\,s\sqrt{1 + 1/n + (x_0 - \bar x)^2/S_{xx}}$; wider than the mean-response interval because it includes the new error.

In a linear model with uncorrelated, equal-variance errors, the least squares estimators have the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators (they are BLUE: best linear unbiased estimators).
A method that tests equality of several means by comparing variation between group means with variation within groups, using $F = \text{MSTr}/\text{MSE}$.
The between-group variation $\text{SSTr} = \sum n_i(\bar Y_{i\cdot} - \bar Y_{\cdot\cdot})^2$, on $k - 1$ df.
A sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom, such as $\text{MSTr} = \text{SSTr}/(k-1)$ and the error mean square $\text{SSE}/(N-k)$, which estimates $\sigma^2$.
A table listing, for each source of variation (treatments, error, total), its df, sum of squares, mean square, and the $F$ statistic with its p-value.
The probability of making at least one Type I error among a whole family of tests or comparisons.
Running each of $m$ comparisons at level $\alpha/m$; by the union bound the familywise error rate is at most $\alpha$.

A multiple comparison procedure for all pairwise differences of means, based on the distribution of the largest standardized difference; it controls the familywise error rate exactly for equal group sizes.
Follow-up comparisons among group means after ANOVA, done with a method (Bonferroni, Tukey) that controls the familywise error rate.
A test whose null distribution does not depend on the population's distribution (beyond continuity or symmetry), typically because it uses only signs or ranks.
A test of a median (or median difference) using the number of positive observations, which is $\text{Bin}(n, 1/2)$ under $H_0$; zeros are dropped.

A one-sample or paired test that ranks $\lvert D_i\rvert$ and sums the ranks of positive differences, $W^+$; under $H_0$ (symmetry about 0) $E(W^+) = n(n+1)/4$ and $\operatorname{Var}(W^+) = n(n+1)(2n+1)/24$.
A two-sample test using $W$, the sum of the first sample's ranks in the combined sample; under $H_0$ $E(W) = m(N+1)/2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(W) = mn(N+1)/12$.
The statistic $U = W - m(m+1)/2$, the number of pairs with $X_i > Y_j$; equivalent to the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, and $U/(mn)$ estimates $P(X > Y)$.
The rank-based alternative to one-way ANOVA: rank all observations together and compare group average ranks; approximately $\chi^2_{k-1}$ under $H_0$.

A test that computes a statistic for every relabeling of the data (or a random sample of relabelings) that is equally likely under $H_0$, and reports the fraction at least as extreme as the observed value.
The limiting ratio of sample sizes two tests need for equal power; Wilcoxon versus $t$ is $3/\pi \approx 0.955$ for normal data, and the sign test versus $t$ is $2/\pi \approx 0.64$.
An unbiased estimator of $\tau(\theta)$ whose variance is no larger than that of any other unbiased estimator, for every value of $\theta$.

If $W$ is unbiased for $\tau(\theta)$ and $T$ is sufficient, then $\phi(T) = E[W \mid T]$ is an estimator, is unbiased for $\tau(\theta)$, and has $\operatorname{Var}(\phi(T)) \le \operatorname{Var}(W)$ for every $\theta$.
Replacing an unbiased estimator $W$ by its conditional expectation $E[W \mid T]$ given a sufficient statistic $T$, which keeps it unbiased and never increases its variance.
A statistic $T$ such that $E_\theta[g(T)] = 0$ for every $\theta$ forces $g(T) = 0$ with probability 1; then an unbiased estimator that is a function of $T$ is unique.
If $T$ is a complete sufficient statistic and $\phi(T)$ is unbiased for $\tau(\theta)$, then $\phi(T)$ is the unique minimum-variance unbiased estimator of $\tau(\theta)$.

A family of densities or pmfs of the form $h(x)\,c(\theta)\exp(w(\theta)\,t(x))$ with support free of $\theta$; $w(\theta)$ is the natural parameter, and $\sum t(X_i)$ is complete sufficient when $w(\theta)$ ranges over an interval.
A method that estimates the sampling distribution of a statistic by recomputing it on many samples drawn with replacement from the observed data.
The distribution $\hat F_n$ that puts probability $1/n$ on each observed value $x_1, \dots, x_n$; it converges to the population distribution as $n$ grows.
Estimate a feature of the unknown distribution $F$ by the same feature of the empirical distribution $\hat F_n$; the bootstrap applies it to whole sampling distributions.
A sample of size $n$ drawn with replacement from the $n$ observed values; on average it contains about 63% of the distinct original values.
The value $\hat\theta^*$ of a statistic computed on one bootstrap sample.
The standard deviation of $B$ bootstrap replicates, used as an estimate of the standard error of $\hat\theta$; for the mean it tends to $\hat\sigma/\sqrt n$ as $B \to \infty$.
A bootstrap confidence interval whose endpoints are the $\alpha/2$ and $1 - \alpha/2$ quantiles of the bootstrap replicates.
A bootstrap that fits a model to the data and draws new samples from the fitted model, rather than from the data themselves.
An estimator that deliberately pulls raw estimates toward a target (such as 0 or the grand mean), accepting some bias in exchange for lower variance.
Bayesian estimation in which the parameters of the prior are estimated from the data themselves, which is possible when many related quantities are observed at once.

For $p \ge 3$ independent $X_i \sim N(\theta_i, \sigma^2)$, the estimator $\big(1 - (p - 2)\sigma^2/\|\mathbf X\|^2\big)\mathbf X$; its total squared-error risk is below $p\sigma^2$ for every $\boldsymbol\theta$.
The multiplier, such as $1 - (p - 2)\sigma^2/\|\mathbf X\|^2$ in James–Stein, that scales the distance of each estimate from the shrinkage target.
