CLT: $P(|\bar X - \mu| \ge {eps}) \approx 2P\Big(Z \ge \dfrac{{eps}\sqrt n}{{sig}}\Big)$. Setting $\dfrac{{eps}\sqrt n}{{sig}} = z = {zz:num4}$ gives
$n = \left(\dfrac{{zz:num4} \times {sig}}{{eps}}\right)^2$, rounded up: **{nclt:int}** (rounding $z$ differently can shift this by 1,
which is accepted). The guarantee costs many more observations than the approximation.

drills.title: CLT for a total of uniform amounts
drills.prompt:
A machine cuts {nn} lengths of cable, each independently uniform between {aa} and {bb:int} metres. Use the
Central Limit Theorem to approximate the probability that the total length exceeds {cut:int} metres. Give 4
decimals.
drills.solution:
Each length has mean $\dfrac{{aa} + {bb:int}}{2} = {mu:num2}$ and variance $\dfrac{({bb:int} - {aa})^2}{12} = {var1:num4}$.
The total of {nn} has mean ${nn} \times {mu:num2} = {mt:num2}$ and SD $\sqrt{{nn} \times {var1:num4}} = {sdt:num4}$, and is approximately normal.
$z = \dfrac{{cut:int} - {mt:num2}}{{sdt:num4}} = {zz:num2}$, so $P \approx$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Normal approximation to the binomial

calc.exact: if(side == 0, binomcdf(nn, pp, kc), 1 - binomcdf(nn, pp, kc - 1))

drills.prompt:
Each of {nn} passengers independently buys a reserved seat with probability {pp}. Use the normal
approximation with a continuity correction to estimate the probability that **{side} {kc:int}** buy one.
Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
$X \sim \text{Bin}({nn}, {pp})$ has mean $np = {mu:num2}$ and SD $\sqrt{np(1-p)} = {sd:num4}$.
The continuity correction treats {kc:int} as the interval from {kc:int} − 0.5 to {kc:int} + 0.5, so for "{side} {kc:int}" the
cutoff is ${edge:num1}$. $z = \dfrac{{edge:num1} - {mu:num2}}{{sd:num4}} = {zz:num2}$, giving **{pr:num4}**. (The exact binomial value is {exact:num4}.)

drills.title: CLT for a mean of Poisson counts
drills.prompt:
The number of faults per kilometre of track is Poisson with mean {lam}. Inspectors survey {nn} randomly chosen
kilometres. Approximate the probability that the average number of faults per kilometre exceeds {cut}.
Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
A Poisson count has mean and variance both equal to {lam}, so $\bar X$ has mean {lam} and SD
$\sqrt{{lam}/{nn}} = {se:num4}$. By the CLT, $\bar X$ is approximately normal:
$z = \dfrac{{cut} - {lam}}{{se:num4}} = {zz:num2}$, so $P(\bar X > {cut}) \approx$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Probabilities for the sample variance
drills.prompt:
A random sample of {nn} measurements is taken from a normal population with variance $\sigma^2 = {vv}$.
Find the probability that the sample variance $S^2$ is {side} {cut}. Give 4 decimals.

drills.title: A probability from the t distribution
drills.prompt:
A random sample of size {nn} is taken from a normal population with unknown mean and variance. Find
the probability that the sample mean exceeds the population mean by more than {kk} sample
standard deviations: $P(\bar X - \mu > {kk}S)$. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
Divide both sides by $S/\sqrt n$: $\bar X - \mu > {kk}S \iff T = \dfrac{\bar X - \mu}{S/\sqrt{{nn}}} > {kk}\sqrt{{nn}} = {tt:num4}$.
For a normal sample $T \sim t_{{df}}$, so the probability is $P(t_{{df}} > {tt:num4}) =$ **{pr:num4}**.
(If $\sigma$ were known, the normal tail would give {pz:num4}; the $t$ tail is heavier.)

drills.title: Ratio of two sample variances
drills.prompt:
Independent random samples of sizes {n1} and {n2} are drawn from two normal populations with equal
variances. Find the probability that the first sample variance is more than {cc} times the
second: $P(S_1^2/S_2^2 > {cc})$. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
$\dfrac{S_1^2/\sigma_1^2}{S_2^2/\sigma_2^2} \sim F_{n_1 - 1,\, n_2 - 1}$, and with $\sigma_1 = \sigma_2$ the ratio $S_1^2/S_2^2$ itself is
$F_{{d1},\,{d2}}$ (numerator df first). So $P(F_{{d1},{d2}} > {cc}) =$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Bias, variance and MSE of a shrinkage estimator
drills.prompt:
To estimate a mean $\mu$, an engineer combines the sample mean of $n = {nn}$ observations (population
SD $\sigma = {sig}$) with a prior guess of {m0}: $T = {ww}\bar X + {w1:num2}({m0})$. If the true mean is
$\mu = {mu}$, find the bias of $T$, its mean squared error, and the MSE of $\bar X$ for comparison.
Give 2 decimals.
drills.solution:
$E[T] = {ww}\mu + {w1:num2}({m0})$, so the bias is $E[T] - \mu = {w1:num2}({m0} - \mu) = {w1:num2}({m0} - {mu}) =$ **{bias:num2}**.
$\operatorname{Var}(T) = {ww}^2\,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n} = {ww}^2 \times \dfrac{{sig}^2}{{nn}} = {var:num4}$.
$\operatorname{MSE}(T) = \operatorname{Var} + \operatorname{Bias}^2 = {var:num4} + ({bias:num2})^2 =$ **{mse:num2}**.

$\bar X$ is unbiased, so $\operatorname{MSE}(\bar X) = \sigma^2/n = {sig}^2/{nn} =$ **{msex:num2}**. Shrinking helps when the guess is close to
$\mu$ and hurts when it is far off.

drills.title: Comparing estimators of a uniform limit
drills.prompt:
A sample of $n = {nn}$ comes from Uniform$(0, \theta)$ with $\theta = {th}$. Two unbiased estimators are
$\hat\theta_1 = 2\bar X$ and $\hat\theta_2 = \tfrac{n+1}{n}X_{(n)}$. Find both variances and the efficiency of $\hat\theta_2$
relative to $\hat\theta_1$. Give 4 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$\operatorname{Var}(X) = \theta^2/12$, so $\operatorname{Var}(2\bar X) = 4 \cdot \dfrac{\theta^2}{12n} = \dfrac{\theta^2}{3n} = \dfrac{{th}^2}{3 \times {nn}} =$ **{v1:sig4}**.

From the density $nx^{n-1}/\theta^n$ of the maximum, $\operatorname{Var}(X_{(n)}) = \dfrac{n\theta^2}{(n+1)^2(n+2)}$, so
$\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_2) = \dfrac{(n+1)^2}{n^2}\operatorname{Var}(X_{(n)}) = \dfrac{\theta^2}{n(n+2)} = \dfrac{{th}^2}{{nn}({nn} + 2)} =$ **{v2:sig4}**.

Relative efficiency $= \dfrac{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_1)}{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_2)} = \dfrac{n + 2}{3} =$ **{eff:sig4}**.

drills.title: Fisher information and the Cramér–Rao bound
drills.prompt:
An iid sample of size {nn} comes from a **{fam}** distribution whose parameter (the success probability
for Bernoulli, the mean for Poisson) equals {par}. Find the Fisher information in one observation and
the Cramér–Rao lower bound for the variance of an unbiased estimator of the parameter. Give 4
significant figures.
drills.solution:
Use $I(\theta) = -E\big[\partial^2 \ln f(X; \theta)/\partial\theta^2\big]$.

- Bernoulli: $\ln f = x\ln p + (1 - x)\ln(1 - p)$, second derivative $-x/p^2 - (1-x)/(1-p)^2$, so $I(p) = \dfrac{1}{p(1-p)}$.
- Poisson: $\ln f = x\ln\lambda - \lambda - \ln x!$, second derivative $-x/\lambda^2$, so $I(\lambda) = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$.

For this {fam} sample with parameter {par}: $I =$ **{info:sig4}**, and
$\text{CRLB} = \dfrac{1}{nI} = \dfrac{1}{{nn} \times {info:sig4}} =$ **{crlb:sig4}**. The sample mean attains it in both families.

drills.title: Exponential MLE and invariance
drills.prompt:
Six component lifetimes (hours) are {x1}, {x2}, {x3}, {x4}, {x5}, {x6}. Model them as iid exponential with
rate $\lambda$. Find the maximum likelihood estimate $\hat\lambda$ (4 significant figures) and the MLE of the
reliability $P(X > {tt})$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\ell(\lambda) = n\ln\lambda - \lambda\sum x_i$, and $\ell'(\lambda) = n/\lambda - \sum x_i = 0$ gives $\hat\lambda = n/\sum x_i = 1/\bar x$
($\ell''(\lambda) = -n/\lambda^2 < 0$, so it is a maximum). Here $\sum x_i = {tot:int}$, $\bar x = {xbar:num2}$, so
$\hat\lambda = 6/{tot:int} =$ **{lam:sig4}** per hour.

By invariance, the MLE of $P(X > {tt}) = e^{-{tt}\lambda}$ is $e^{-{tt}\hat\lambda} = e^{-{tt}/{xbar:num2}} =$ **{rel:num4}**.

drills.title: Normal MLEs from data

calc.mhat: mean(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5, x6)
calc.vhat: pvariance(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5, x6)
calc.s2: variance(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5, x6)

drills.prompt:
Gauge readings {x1:num1}, {x2:num1}, {x3:num1}, {x4:num1}, {x5:num1}, {x6:num1} are modeled as iid $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ with both
parameters unknown. Find the maximum likelihood estimates $\hat\mu$ and $\hat\sigma$. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
Setting the partial derivatives of $\ell(\mu, \sigma^2)$ to zero gives $\hat\mu = \bar x$ and $\hat\sigma^2 = \tfrac1n\sum(x_i - \bar x)^2$ (divide by $n$).

$\hat\mu = \bar x =$ **{mhat:num4}**. The squared deviations from $\bar x$ sum to ${ss6:num4}$, so
$\hat\sigma^2 = {vhat:num4}$ and, by invariance, $\hat\sigma = \sqrt{{vhat:num4}} =$ **{shat:num4}**.
(The unbiased $s^2 = {s2:num4}$ divides by $n - 1 = 5$ instead.)

drills.title: Method of moments versus MLE for a uniform limit
drills.prompt:
Five readings {x1:num1}, {x2:num1}, {x3:num1}, {x4:num1}, {x5:num1} are modeled as iid Uniform$(0, \theta)$. Find the
method-of-moments estimate and the maximum likelihood estimate of $\theta$. Give 2 decimals.
drills.solution:
Method of moments: $E[X] = \theta/2$; set it equal to $\bar x = {xbar:num4}$, so $\tilde\theta = 2\bar x =$ **{mom:num2}**.

Maximum likelihood: $L(\theta) = \theta^{-5}$ when $\theta \ge \max x_i$ and 0 otherwise. It decreases for $\theta \ge \max x_i$, so
$\hat\theta = \max x_i =$ **{mle:num2}**. (If the MoM value is below the maximum it is impossible as a value of $\theta$; the
bias-corrected $\tfrac{6}{5}\max x_i = {unb:num2}$ is the unbiased estimator based on the maximum, which has a much smaller variance than $2\bar x$.)

drills.title: Delta-method standard error
drills.prompt:
Faults on {nn} days are modeled as iid Poisson($\lambda$), and the total count is {tot}. Find the MLE of
the probability of a fault-free day, $e^{-\lambda}$, and use the delta method to estimate its standard
error. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
$\hat\lambda = \bar x = {tot}/{nn} = {xbar:num4}$, so by invariance the MLE of $e^{-\lambda}$ is $e^{-{xbar:num4}} =$ **{est:num4}**.

$\hat\lambda$ has variance $\lambda/n$ (Fisher information $1/\lambda$), estimated SE $\sqrt{{xbar:num4}/{nn}} = {sel:num4}$. For
$g(\lambda) = e^{-\lambda}$, $|g'(\lambda)| = e^{-\lambda}$, so the delta method gives
$\operatorname{SE} \approx e^{-\hat\lambda}\sqrt{\hat\lambda/n} = {est:num4} \times {sel:num4} =$ **{se:num4}**.

drills.title: MVUEs for Bernoulli trials
drills.prompt:
In {nn} independent Bernoulli($p$) trials there are $T = {tt}$ successes. Find the minimum-variance unbiased
estimates of $p^2$ and of $p(1 - p)$. Give exact fractions or 4 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$T$ is complete sufficient, so an unbiased function of $T$ is the MVUE (Lehmann–Scheffé). Rao–Blackwellizing
$X_1X_2$ gives $P(X_1 = X_2 = 1 \mid T) = \dfrac{T(T-1)}{n(n-1)}$, and Rao–Blackwellizing $X_1(1 - X_2)$ gives $\dfrac{T(n-T)}{n(n-1)}$.

- $p^2$: $\dfrac{{tt} \times {tm}}{{nm}} = {p2:texfrac} \approx$ **{p2:sig4}**.
- $p(1-p)$: $\dfrac{{tt} \times {nt}}{{nm}} = {pq:texfrac} \approx$ **{pq:sig4}**.

Compare the biased plug-in $\hat p^2 = ({ph:sig4})^2 = {plug:sig4}$.

drills.title: MVUEs for Poisson probabilities
drills.prompt:
Daily fault counts on six days are {c1}, {c2}, {c3}, {c4}, {c5}, {c6}, modeled as iid Poisson($\lambda$). Find the
minimum-variance unbiased estimates of $P(X = 0) = e^{-\lambda}$ and of $P(X = 1) = \lambda e^{-\lambda}$. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
$T = \sum X_i = {tt}$ is complete sufficient. Given $T = t$, $X_1 \sim$ Binomial$(t, 1/6)$, so Rao–Blackwellizing the
indicators of $X_1 = 0$ and $X_1 = 1$ gives

- $P(X_1 = 0 \mid T) = (5/6)^T = (5/6)^{{tt}} =$ **{u0:num4}**;
- $P(X_1 = 1 \mid T) = T\cdot\tfrac16\,(5/6)^{T-1} = {tt} \times \tfrac16 \times (5/6)^{{tm}} =$ **{u1:num4}**.

These are unbiased functions of $T$, hence the MVUEs. (The MLE of $P(X = 0)$ is $e^{-\bar x} = e^{-{xb:num4}} = {mle0:num4}$, which is biased.)

drills.title: MLE versus MVUE of an exponential rate
drills.prompt:
Five component lifetimes (hours) are {x1}, {x2}, {x3}, {x4}, {x5}, modeled as iid exponential with rate
$\lambda$. Find the MLE of $\lambda$ and the minimum-variance unbiased estimate of $\lambda$. Give 4 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$T = \sum X_i = {tot:dp0}$ is complete sufficient (exponential family). The MLE is $n/T = 5/{tot:dp0} =$ **{mle:sig4}** per hour.

$T \sim$ Gamma(shape $n$, scale $1/\lambda$), and $E[1/T] = \dfrac{\lambda}{n - 1}$, so $E[n/T] = \dfrac{n}{n-1}\lambda$: the MLE is biased upward.
$(n-1)/T$ is unbiased and a function of $T$, so it is the MVUE: $4/{tot:dp0} =$ **{mvue:sig4}** per hour.

drills.title: t confidence interval for a mean
drills.prompt:
A random sample of {nn} brake-pad tests from a normal population gives $\bar x = {xbar:num1}$ mm and
$s = {ss:num1}$ mm. Construct a {lev} confidence interval for the mean wear $\mu$. Give the endpoints to 2
decimals.
drills.solution:
The pivot $\dfrac{\bar X - \mu}{S/\sqrt n} \sim t_{{df}}$ gives $\bar x \pm t^*\,s/\sqrt n$ with $t^* = {tc:num4}$ ({lev}, {df} df).
$SE = {ss:num1}/\sqrt{{nn}} = {se:num4}$, margin $= {tc:num4} \times {se:num4} = {me:num4}$.
Interval: from **{lo:num2}** to **{hi:num2}**.

drills.title: Chi-square confidence interval for a variance
drills.prompt:
A sample of {nn} rail-gauge measurements from a normal population has standard deviation $s = {ss:num1}$ mm.
Construct a {lev} confidence interval for the population variance $\sigma^2$. Give the endpoints to 2 decimals.
drills.solution:
Pivot: $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{{df}}$. For {lev} confidence, the lower and upper quantiles are
$\chi^2_L = {qlo:num4}$ and $\chi^2_U = {qhi:num4}$. With $(n-1)s^2 = {df} \times {s2:num4} = {num:num4}$:
$$\frac{{num:num4}}{{qhi:num4}} \le \sigma^2 \le \frac{{num:num4}}{{qlo:num4}},$$
so the interval is from **{lo:num2}** to **{hi:num2}** mm². (For $\sigma$: {slo:num2} to {shi:num2} mm.)

drills.title: Pooled two-sample t interval
drills.prompt:
Brake pads from supplier A ($n_1 = {n1}$) last on average {m1:num1} thousand km with SD {s1:num1}; pads from
supplier B ($n_2 = {n2}$) average {m2:num1} with SD {s2:num1}. Assuming normal populations with equal
variances, construct a 95% confidence interval for $\mu_A - \mu_B$. Give the endpoints to 2 decimals.
drills.solution:
Pooled variance: $s_p^2 = \dfrac{({n1} - 1)({s1:num1})^2 + ({n2} - 1)({s2:num1})^2}{{df}} = {sp2:num4}$, so $s_p = {sp:num4}$.
$SE = s_p\sqrt{1/{n1} + 1/{n2}} = {se:num4}$, and $t_{0.025,\,{df}} = {tc:num4}$.
Interval: $({m1:num1} - {m2:num1}) \pm {tc:num4} \times {se:num4}$, from **{lo:num2}** to **{hi:num2}**.

drills.title: Ideal bootstrap standard error of a mean
drills.prompt:
For the data {x1}, {x2}, {x3}, {x4}, {x5}, find the ideal bootstrap standard error of the sample mean
(the limit as the number of resamples $B \to \infty$) and, for comparison, the usual $s/\sqrt n$. Give 3 decimals.
drills.solution:
$\bar x = {xb:num4}$, and the squared deviations sum to {ss:sig6}. Under the empirical distribution one draw has
variance $\hat\sigma^2 = {ss:sig6}/5 = {pv:sig6}$ (divide by $n$), and a bootstrap mean averages 5 independent draws, so

$$\operatorname{SE}_{\text{boot}} = \sqrt{\hat\sigma^2/n} = \sqrt{{pv:sig6}/5} = \textbf{{bse:dp3}}.$$

The usual estimate divides by $n - 1 = 4$ inside $s$: $s/\sqrt 5 = \sqrt{{ss:sig6}/4/5} =$ **{usual:dp3}**, larger by the factor $\sqrt{5/4}$.

drills.title: Exact bootstrap distribution of a median of three
drills.prompt:
A sample of three is {hi}, {lo}, {mid}, and the statistic is the sample median. Using all 27 equally likely
bootstrap samples, find the mean of the bootstrap medians, the bootstrap estimate of the median's bias,
and the bootstrap standard error. Give 3 decimals.
drills.solution:
Sorted, the data are {lo}, {mid}, {hi}, and the sample median is {mid}. A bootstrap median equals {lo} when at least
two of the three draws are {lo}: $3 \cdot 2 + 1 = 7$ of the 27 samples. Likewise it is {hi} in 7 samples, and {mid} in the other 13.

Mean: $\dfrac{7({lo}) + 13({mid}) + 7({hi})}{27} = \dfrac{{s7:dp0}}{27} =$ **{mb:dp3}**. Bias estimate: ${mb:dp3} - {mid} =$ **{bias:dp3}**.

$E[(\text{median}^*)^2] = \dfrac{{q7:dp0}}{27} = {m2:dp4}$, so the bootstrap SE is $\sqrt{{m2:dp4} - {mb:dp4}^2} =$ **{se:dp3}**.

drills.title: Exact permutation p-value for two small groups
drills.prompt:
Group A: {x1}, {x2}, {x3}. Group B: {y1}, {y2}, {y3}. Test whether A tends to be larger with a permutation
test based on the difference in means, using all $\binom63 = 20$ ways to choose which three values are labeled A.
Find the one-sided p-value (exact, as a decimal or fraction).
drills.solution:
The six values total {tot}, so the difference in means is $\tfrac{2}{3}(\text{A sum}) - \tfrac{{tot}}{3}$: a larger
difference is the same as a larger A sum. The observed A sum is {obs} (means {ma:num2} and {mb:num2}).

Listing the 20 possible A groups, {cnt} of them (the observed one included) have a sum of at least {obs}. Under $H_0$ every
labeling is equally likely, so $p = {cnt}/20 =$ **{pv:num2}**.

drills.title: Beta–binomial updating
drills.prompt:
A new coupling passes a stress test with unknown probability $\theta$, which is given a Beta({aa}, {bb}) prior.
In {nn} independent tests, {xx:int} couplings pass. Find the parameters of the posterior beta distribution
and the posterior mean (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior $= \theta^{{xx:int}}(1-\theta)^{{fail:int}} \cdot \theta^{{aa} - 1}(1-\theta)^{{bb} - 1}$, which is Beta$({aa} + {xx:int},\ {bb} + {fail:int})$:
$a =$ **{a2:int}**, $b =$ **{b2:int}**.

Posterior mean $= \dfrac{a}{a + b} = \dfrac{{a2:int}}{{a2:int} + {b2:int}} =$ **{pm:num4}**, a weighted average of the prior mean {pmean:num4}
and the sample proportion {ph:num4} with data weight $\dfrac{{nn}}{{aa} + {bb} + {nn}} = {wt:num4}$.

drills.title: Normal–normal posterior and credible interval
drills.prompt:
A sensor offset $\theta$ has prior $N({m0}, {t0}^2)$. Readings are $N(\theta, {sig}^2)$ with known SD {sig}, and $n = {nn}$
readings average $\bar x = {xbar:num1}$. Find the posterior mean, the posterior SD and a 95% credible
interval (use 1.96). Give 2 decimals.
drills.solution:
Precisions add: prior $1/{t0}^2 = {p0:num4}$, data $n/\sigma^2 = {nn}/{sig}^2 = {pd:num4}$, total ${pt:num4}$. So the posterior
variance is $1/{pt:num4} = {vn:num4}$ and the posterior SD is **{sdn:num2}**.

Posterior mean $= \dfrac{{p0:num4}({m0}) + {pd:num4}({xbar:num1})}{{pt:num4}} =$ **{mn:num2}**.

95% credible interval: ${mn:num2} \pm 1.96 \times {sdn:num2}$, from **{lo:num2}** to **{hi:num2}**.

drills.title: Gamma–Poisson updating
drills.prompt:
A fault rate $\lambda$ (faults per day) has a gamma prior with shape {al} and rate {be} (scale $1/{be}$). Daily fault counts,
modeled as iid Poisson($\lambda$), are {c1}, {c2}, {c3}, {c4}, {c5}. Find the posterior shape and rate, and the
posterior mean (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Likelihood ∝ $\lambda^{\sum x_i}e^{-n\lambda} = \lambda^{{tot:int}}e^{-5\lambda}$; prior ∝ $\lambda^{{al} - 1}e^{-{be}\lambda}$. The product is
$\lambda^{{al} + {tot:int} - 1}e^{-({be} + 5)\lambda}$, a gamma with shape **{a2:int}** and rate **{b2:int}**.

Posterior mean $= {a2:int}/{b2:int} =$ **{pm:num4}** (posterior SD $\sqrt{{a2:int}}/{b2:int} = {psd:num4}$), between the prior mean
${al}/{be}$ and the sample mean {xbar:num2}.

drills.title: Size and power of a binomial test
drills.prompt:
$X \sim \text{Bin}({nn}, p)$. To test $H_0: p \le {p0}$ against $H_1: p > {p0}$, you reject $H_0$
when $X \ge {cc}$. Find the size of the test and its power at $p = {p1}$ (4 decimals each).
drills.solution:
The power function $\pi(p) = P_p(X \ge {cc})$ increases in $p$, so the size is its value at the
boundary $p = {p0}$: $1 - P(X \le {cm1} \mid p = {p0}) =$ **{size:num4}**.

At $p = {p1}$: $\pi({p1}) = 1 - P(X \le {cm1} \mid p = {p1}) =$ **{pw:num4}** (so $\beta = {beta:num4}$).

drills.title: Power of a two-sided z test
drills.prompt:
$X_1, \dots, X_{{nn}}$ are $N(\mu, {sig}^2)$. A two-sided test of $H_0: \mu = {mu0}$ at
$\alpha = {al}$ rejects when $\bar X$ falls outside an interval $(c_1, c_2)$ centered at {mu0}.
Find $c_1$ and $c_2$ (2 decimals) and the power when $\mu = {mua:num1}$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\sigma/\sqrt n = {sig}/\sqrt{{nn}} = {se:num4}$ and $z_{\alpha/2} = {zs:dp3}$, so
$c_1 = {mu0} - {zs:dp3}({se:num4}) =$ **{lo:num2}** and $c_2 =$ **{hi:num2}**.

If $\mu = {mua:num1}$, then $\bar X \sim N({mua:num1}, {se:num4}^2)$ and the power is
$P(\bar X \le c_1) + P(\bar X \ge c_2) = \Phi({zlo:num2}) + 1 - \Phi({zhi:num2}) \approx$ **{pw:num4}**.

drills.title: Sample size for a one-sided z test
drills.prompt:
Measurements are normal with $\sigma = {sig}$. You will test $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ against
$H_1: \mu > \mu_0$ at $\alpha = {al}$ and want power {pwr} when $\mu = \mu_0 + {delta}$.
What is the smallest sample size $n$ that achieves this?
drills.solution:
Power $1 - \beta$ at $\mu_0 + \delta$ needs $n \ge \left(\dfrac{(z_\alpha + z_\beta)\sigma}{\delta}\right)^2$ with
$z_\alpha = {za:dp3}$ and $z_\beta = {zb:dp3}$:
$\left(\dfrac{({za:dp3} + {zb:dp3})({sig})}{{delta}}\right)^2 = {nraw:num2}$. Round up: $n =$ **{nreq}**.

drills.title: Paired t test from data

calc.dbar: mean(d1, d2, d3, d4, d5, d6)
calc.sd: stdev(d1, d2, d3, d4, d5, d6)

drills.prompt:
Six units are each measured under treatment A and treatment B.

$$\begin{array}{c|cccccc} \text{unit} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline A & {a1:num1} & {a2:num1} & {a3:num1} & {a4:num1} & {a5:num1} & {a6:num1} \\ B & {b1:num1} & {b2:num1} & {b3:num1} & {b4:num1} & {b5:num1} & {b6:num1} \end{array}$$

Test $H_0: \mu_D = 0$ against $H_1: \mu_D > 0$, where $D = A - B$. Find $\bar d$ (4 decimals),
the $t$ statistic (3 decimals) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Differences $A - B$: {d1:num1}, {d2:num1}, {d3:num1}, {d4:num1}, {d5:num1}, {d6:num1}.
Their mean is $\bar d =$ **{dbar:num4}** and their s.d. is $s_d = {sd:num4}$.

$t = \dfrac{\bar d}{s_d/\sqrt 6} = \dfrac{{dbar:num4}}{{sd:num4}/\sqrt 6} =$ **{tt:dp3}** on 5 df, and the
p-value is $P(t_5 \ge {tt:dp3}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Welch two-sample t test
drills.prompt:
Two independent normal samples give $\bar x_1 = {m1:num1}$, $s_1 = {s1:num1}$, $n_1 = {n1}$ and
$\bar x_2 = {m2:num1}$, $s_2 = {s2:num1}$, $n_2 = {n2}$. Using Welch's test of $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$
against $H_1: \mu_1 \ne \mu_2$, find $t$ (3 decimals), the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
(2 decimals) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$s_1^2/n_1 = {v1:num4}$ and $s_2^2/n_2 = {v2:num4}$, so the standard error is
$\sqrt{{v1:num4} + {v2:num4}} = {se:num4}$ and $t = ({m1:num1} - {m2:num1})/{se:num4} =$ **{tt:dp3}**.

$\nu = \dfrac{({v1:num4} + {v2:num4})^2}{{v1:num4}^2/({n1} - 1) + {v2:num4}^2/({n2} - 1)} =$ **{nu:num2}**,
and the two-sided p-value is $2P(t_\nu \ge |t|) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Chi-square test for a variance
drills.prompt:
A normal sample of $n = {nn}$ has $s = {ss:num2}$. Test $H_0: \sigma = {sig0}$ against
$H_1: \sigma {side} {sig0}$. Find the test statistic (3 decimals) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\chi^2 = \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2} = \dfrac{{dfree}({ss:num2})^2}{{sig0}^2} =$ **{chi:dp3}**, which has a
$\chi^2_{{dfree}}$ distribution under $H_0$. The alternative points to the tail where
$\sigma {side} {sig0}$, so the p-value is that tail area of $\chi^2_{{dfree}}$ beyond {chi:dp3}: **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Most powerful test for an exponential rate
drills.prompt:
$X_1, \dots, X_{{nn}}$ are exponential with rate $\lambda$ (density $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$). The most
powerful level-{al} test of $H_0: \lambda = {l0}$ against $H_1: \lambda = {l1}$ rejects when
$\sum X_i \ge c$. Using $2\lambda\sum X_i \sim \chi^2_{2n}$, find $c$ (3 decimals) and the power of the
test (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
The ratio $L({l0})/L({l1}) = ({l0}/{l1})^{{nn}}e^{-({l0} - {l1})\sum x_i}$ decreases in $\sum x_i$, so reject for large $\sum x_i$.
Under $H_0$, $2({l0})\sum X_i \sim \chi^2_{{df2}}$, whose upper-{al} point is {q:dp3}. So
$c = {q:dp3}/(2 \cdot {l0}) =$ **{cc:dp3}**.

Under $H_1$, $2({l1})\sum X_i \sim \chi^2_{{df2}}$, so power $= P(\chi^2_{{df2}} \ge 2({l1})({cc:dp3})) = P(\chi^2_{{df2}} \ge {arg:dp3}) \approx$ **{pw:num4}**.

drills.title: Likelihood ratio test for a Poisson mean
drills.prompt:
Counts $X_1, \dots, X_{{nn}}$ are Poisson($\lambda$) with total $\sum x_i = {tot}$. Compute
$-2\ln\Lambda$ for the likelihood ratio test of $H_0: \lambda = {lam0}$ against $H_1: \lambda \ne {lam0}$
(3 decimals), and its approximate p-value from Wilks' theorem (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
The MLE is $\hat\lambda = \bar x = {tot}/{nn} = {xbar:num4}$, and
$-2\ln\Lambda = 2\left[\sum x_i\ln\dfrac{\bar x}{\lambda_0} - n(\bar x - \lambda_0)\right] = 2\left[{tot}\ln\dfrac{{xbar:num4}}{{lam0}} - ({tot} - {nn} \cdot {lam0})\right] =$ **{g2:dp3}**.

$H_0$ fixes one parameter, so compare with $\chi^2_1$: p-value $= P(\chi^2_1 \ge {g2:dp3}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Likelihood ratio test for a proportion
drills.prompt:
In {nn} independent trials there are {xx} successes. Compute $-2\ln\Lambda$ for the likelihood ratio
test of $H_0: p = {p0}$ against $H_1: p \ne {p0}$ (3 decimals) and its approximate p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\hat p = {phat:num4}$. With observed counts {xx} and {nmx} and null expected counts {e1:num2} and {e2:num2},
$-2\ln\Lambda = 2\left[{xx}\ln\dfrac{{xx}}{{e1:num2}} + {nmx}\ln\dfrac{{nmx}}{{e2:num2}}\right] =$ **{g2:dp3}**.

With 1 df: p-value $= P(\chi^2_1 \ge {g2:dp3}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Two-proportion z test
drills.prompt:
Sample 1 has {x1} successes in {n1} trials; sample 2 has {x2} in {n2}. Test $H_0: p_1 = p_2$
against $H_1: p_1 \ne p_2$ with the pooled $z$ test. Find $z$ (3 decimals) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\hat p_1 = {ph1:num4}$, $\hat p_2 = {ph2:num4}$, pooled $\hat p = ({x1} + {x2})/({n1} + {n2}) = {pp:num4}$.
Standard error $\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)(1/{n1} + 1/{n2})} = {se:num4}$, so $z =$ **{zz:dp3}** and the
two-sided p-value is $2P(Z \ge |z|) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Chi-square goodness of fit
drills.prompt:
{nn} items fall into four categories with counts {o1}, {o2}, {o3}, {o4}. Test whether the category
probabilities are {q1}, {q2}, {q3}, {q4}. Find Pearson's $X^2$ (3 decimals) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Expected counts: {ex1:num2}, {ex2:num2}, {ex3:num2}, {ex4:num2}. Contributions $(O - E)^2/E$:
{c1:num4}, {c2:num4}, {c3:num4}, {c4:num4}. Total $X^2 =$ **{x2:dp3}** on $4 - 1 = 3$ df, so the
p-value is $P(\chi^2_3 \ge {x2:dp3}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Chi-square test of independence
drills.prompt:
Test whether the row and column variables are independent in this table of counts:

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & \text{C1} & \text{C2} & \text{C3} \\ \hline \text{R1} & {a1} & {a2} & {a3} \\ \text{R2} & {b1} & {b2} & {b3} \end{array}$$

Find the expected count for row R1, column C1 (2 decimals), $X^2$ (3 decimals) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Row totals {ra} and {rb}, column totals {k1}, {k2}, {k3}, grand total {nt}.
$E_{11} = {ra} \cdot {k1}/{nt} =$ **{ea1:num2}**; the other expected counts are {ea2:num2}, {ea3:num2} (row R1)
and {eb1:num2}, {eb2:num2}, {eb3:num2} (row R2).

Summing $(O - E)^2/E$ over the six cells gives $X^2 =$ **{x2:dp3}** on $(2-1)(3-1) = 2$ df, so the
p-value is $P(\chi^2_2 \ge {x2:dp3}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Multinomial probabilities and covariances
drills.prompt:
Each of {nn} independent inspections rates a sleeper as good, fair or poor with probabilities {p1}, {p2} and {p3:num4}.
Find the probability of exactly {o1} good, {o2} fair and {o3} poor ratings (4 significant figures), and the covariance
of the good and fair counts (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
The counts are multinomial: $P = \dfrac{n!}{o_1!\,o_2!\,o_3!}\,p_1^{o_1}p_2^{o_2}p_3^{o_3}$. The coefficient is
$\dfrac{{nn}!}{{o1}!\,{o2}!\,{o3}!} = {coef:dp0}$, so
$$P = {coef:dp0} \times {p1}^{{o1}} \times {p2}^{{o2}} \times {p3:num4}^{{o3}} = \textbf{{pr:sig4}}.$$

Two counts compete for the same trials: $\operatorname{Cov}(O_1, O_2) = -np_1p_2 = -{nn} \times {p1} \times {p2} =$ **{cv:dp3}**.

drills.title: Fit a least squares line
drills.prompt:
Fit the least squares line $\hat y = b_0 + b_1x$ to these five points, and find $r^2$
(4 decimals each).

$$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & {x1} & {x2} & {x3} & {x4} & {x5} \\ \hline y & {y1:num1} & {y2:num1} & {y3:num1} & {y4:num1} & {y5:num1} \end{array}$$
drills.solution:
$\bar x = {xb:num4}$, $\bar y = {yb:num4}$, $S_{xx} = {sxx:num4}$, $S_{xy} = {sxy:num4}$, $S_{yy} = {syy:num4}$.

$b_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx} =$ **{b1:num4}**, $b_0 = \bar y - b_1\bar x =$ **{b0:num4}**, and
$r^2 = S_{xy}^2/(S_{xx}S_{yy}) =$ **{rsq:num4}**.

drills.title: t test for the slope from summary statistics
drills.prompt:
A regression on $n = {nn}$ points has $S_{xx} = {sxx}$, $S_{xy} = {sxy:num1}$ and $S_{yy} = {syy:num1}$.
Test $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ against $H_1: \beta_1 \ne 0$. Find $b_1$ (4 decimals), the $t$ statistic
(3 decimals) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$b_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx} =$ **{b1:num4}**. $\text{SSE} = S_{yy} - b_1S_{xy} = {sse:num4}$, so
$s = \sqrt{\text{SSE}/(n-2)} = \sqrt{{sse:num4}/{dfree}} = {s:num4}$ and $\text{SE}(b_1) = s/\sqrt{S_{xx}} = {se:num4}$.

$t = b_1/\text{SE}(b_1) =$ **{tt:dp3}** on {dfree} df; two-sided p-value $\approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Confidence and prediction intervals at x0
drills.prompt:
A regression on $n = {nn}$ points gives $\hat y = {b0v:num2} {b1v:signedcoef}x$, with $s = {sres:num2}$,
$\bar x = {xbar:num1}$ and $S_{xx} = {sxx}$. At $x_0 = {x0:num1}$, find $\hat y_0$, the half-width of the
95% confidence interval for the mean response, and the half-width of the 95% prediction interval
for a new observation (3 decimals each).
drills.solution:
$\hat y_0 = {b0v:num2} {b1v:signed}({x0:num1}) =$ **{yh:dp3}**. With {dfree} df, $t_{0.025} = {ts:dp3}$, and
$\dfrac1n + \dfrac{(x_0 - \bar x)^2}{S_{xx}} = {kk:num4}$.

Mean response: ${ts:dp3}({sres:num2})\sqrt{{kk:num4}} =$ **{hci:dp3}**.
New observation: ${ts:dp3}({sres:num2})\sqrt{1 + {kk:num4}} =$ **{hpi:dp3}**.

drills.title: One-way ANOVA from raw data

calc.sse: 3*(variance(g11, g12, g13, g14) + variance(g21, g22, g23, g24) + variance(g31, g32, g33, g34))

drills.prompt:
Three treatments are each applied to four units:

$$\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{A} & {g11} & {g12} & {g13} & {g14} \\ \text{B} & {h1} & {h2} & {h3} & {h4} \\ \text{C} & {g31} & {g32} & {g33} & {g34} \end{array}$$

Find SSTr, SSE and the $F$ statistic (3 decimals each) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Group means {m1:num4}, {m2:num4}, {m3:num4}; grand mean {gm:num4}.
$\text{SSTr} = 4\sum(\bar y_i - \bar y)^2 =$ **{sstr:dp3}**; $\text{SSE} = \sum\sum(y_{ij} - \bar y_i)^2 =$ **{sse:dp3}**.

$\text{MSTr} = {sstr:dp3}/2 = {mstr:dp3}$, $\text{MSE} = {sse:dp3}/9 = {mse:dp3}$, so $F =$ **{ff:dp3}** on (2, 9) df,
and the p-value is $P(F_{2,9} \ge {ff:dp3}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: One-way ANOVA from summary statistics
drills.prompt:
Three independent groups give:

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & \text{group 1} & \text{group 2} & \text{group 3} \\ \hline n_i & {n1} & {n2} & {n3} \\ \bar y_i & {m1:num1} & {m2:num1} & {m3:num1} \\ s_i & {s1:num1} & {s2:num1} & {s3:num1} \end{array}$$

Find the ANOVA $F$ statistic (3 decimals) and its p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$N = {bign}$; weighted grand mean $= \sum n_i\bar y_i/N = {gm:num4}$.
$\text{SSTr} = \sum n_i(\bar y_i - \bar y)^2 = {sstr:dp3}$ and $\text{SSE} = \sum(n_i - 1)s_i^2 = {sse:dp3}$.

$\text{MSTr} = {sstr:dp3}/2 = {mstr:dp3}$, $\text{MSE} = {sse:dp3}/{dfe} = {mse:dp3}$, so $F =$ **{ff:dp3}** on (2, {dfe}) df,
with p-value $\approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Complete an ANOVA table
drills.prompt:
A one-way ANOVA compares {kk} groups of {ng} observations each. The treatment sum of squares is
$\text{SSTr} = {sstr:num1}$ and the total sum of squares is $\text{SST} = {sst:num1}$. Find MSE and $F$
(3 decimals each) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$N = {bign}$. Degrees of freedom: treatments $k - 1 = {df1}$, error $N - k = {df2}$, total {dft}.
$\text{SSE} = \text{SST} - \text{SSTr} = {sse2:num1}$, so $\text{MSE} = {sse2:num1}/{df2} =$ **{mse:dp3}**.

$\text{MSTr} = {sstr:num1}/{df1} = {mstr:dp3}$, $F = {mstr:dp3}/{mse:dp3} =$ **{ff:dp3}**, and
the p-value is $P(F_{{df1},{df2}} \ge {ff:dp3}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Sign test p-value
drills.prompt:
In a paired study of {nn} units, {kk} differences are positive, {neg} are negative and {zz} are exactly
zero. Use the sign test of $H_0$: median difference $= 0$ against $H_1$: median difference $> 0$.
Find the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Drop the {zz} zero differences, leaving $n = {nz}$. Under $H_0$ the number of positive signs is
$B \sim \text{Bin}({nz}, 1/2)$, so the p-value is $P(B \ge {kk}) = 1 - P(B \le {km1}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
drills.prompt:
Eight paired differences are
$${d1:num1},\ {d2:num1},\ {d3:num1},\ {d4:num1},\ {d5:num1},\ {d6:num1},\ {d7:num1},\ {d8:num1}$$
Find the Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic $W^+$, its normal-approximation $z$ (no continuity correction,
3 decimals) and the one-sided p-value for $H_1$: median $> 0$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Rank the absolute values from 1 to 8. The ranks of the differences, in the order given, are
{r1}, {r2}, {r3}, {r4}, {r5}, {r6}, {r7}, {r8}. Adding the ranks of the positive differences gives
$W^+ =$ **{wp}** (and $W^- = {wm}$; the two add to 36).

Under $H_0$, $E(W^+) = 8 \cdot 9/4 = 18$ and $\operatorname{Var}(W^+) = 8 \cdot 9 \cdot 17/24 = 51$, so
$z = ({wp} - 18)/\sqrt{51} =$ **{zz:dp3}** and the p-value is $P(Z \ge {zz:dp3}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
drills.prompt:
Sample A: {a1}, {a2}, {a3}, {a4}, {a5}. Sample B: {b1}, {b2}, {b3}, {b4}, {b5}.
Rank all ten values together (1 = smallest). Find the rank sum $W$ of sample A, the Mann–Whitney
$U = W - 15$, and the one-sided normal-approximation p-value for $H_1$: A is shifted upward (no continuity
correction, 4 decimals).
drills.solution:
The ranks of A's values are {ra1}, {ra2}, {ra3}, {ra4}, {ra5}, so $W =$ **{ww}** and $U = {ww} - 15 =$ **{uu}**.

Under $H_0$, $E(W) = 5 \cdot 11/2 = 27.5$ and $\operatorname{Var}(W) = 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 11/12 = 22.917$, so
$z = ({ww} - 27.5)/\sqrt{22.917} = {zz:dp3}$ and the p-value is $P(Z \ge {zz:dp3}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: James–Stein estimate toward zero
drills.prompt:
Five independent observations $X_i \sim N(\theta_i, \sigma^2)$ with $\sigma = {sg}$ are
$$({x1:num1},\; {x2:num1},\; {x3:num1},\; {x4:num1},\; {x5:num1}).$$
Find the James–Stein shrinkage factor toward 0 (4 decimals) and the James–Stein estimate of $\theta_1$ (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\|\mathbf X\|^2 = {ss:num4}$ and $(p - 2)\sigma^2 = 3({sg2}) = {k3}$.

Factor: $1 - {k3}/{ss:num4} =$ **{fac:num4}**.

$\hat\theta_1 = {fac:num4} \times ({x1:num1}) =$ **{est:dp3}**.

drills.title: Shrink toward the grand mean

calc.xb: mean(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5, x6)

drills.prompt:
Six track sections have mean scores $X_i \sim N(\theta_i, \sigma^2)$, independent, with $\sigma^2 = {s2}$:
$$({x1:num1},\; {x2:num1},\; {x3:num1},\; {x4:num1},\; {x5:num1},\; {x6:num1}).$$
Shrinking toward the grand mean, find the shrinkage factor (4 decimals) and the estimate of $\theta_1$ (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\bar X = {xb:num4}$ and $S = \sum(X_i - \bar X)^2 = {ss:num4}$. With $p = 6$, $(p - 3)\sigma^2 = 3({s2}) = {k3}$.

Factor: $1 - {k3}/{ss:num4} =$ **{fac:num4}**.

$\hat\theta_1 = {xb:num4} + {fac:num4}({x1:num1} - {xb:num4}) =$ **{est:dp3}**.

drills.title: Ridge slope for one predictor
drills.prompt:
A centered predictor has $S_{xx} = {sxx}$ and $S_{xy} = {sxy:num1}$. Find the ridge estimate of the slope,
minimizing $\sum(y_i - \bar y - b x_i)^2 + \lambda b^2$ with $\lambda = {lam}$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Setting the derivative $-2S_{xy} + 2bS_{xx} + 2\lambda b$ to zero gives $b = S_{xy}/(S_{xx} + \lambda)$:

$b = {sxy:num1}/({sxx} + {lam}) = {sxy:num1}/{den} =$ **{b:num4}**.

(Least squares would give ${bls:num4}$; the penalty shrinks it toward 0.)

drills.title: Lasso slope by soft thresholding
drills.prompt:
A centered predictor has $S_{xx} = {sxx}$ and $S_{xy} = {sxy:num1}$. Find the lasso estimate of the slope,
minimizing $\sum(y_i - \bar y - b x_i)^2 + \lambda|b|$ with $\lambda = {lam}$ (4 decimals; enter 0 if the slope is zero).
drills.solution:
Soft thresholding: $b = \operatorname{sign}(S_{xy})\max(|S_{xy}| - \lambda/2,\, 0)/S_{xx}$.

$|S_{xy}| - \lambda/2 = {ab:num1} - {half:num1} = {cut:num1}$. If this is not positive the slope is 0; otherwise divide by $S_{xx} = {sxx}$ and keep the sign of $S_{xy}$.

$b =$ **{b:num4}** (least squares: ${bls:num4}$).

drills.title: Bias, variance and MSE of a ridge slope
drills.prompt:
One centered predictor has $S_{xx} = {sxx}$; the true slope is $\beta = {beta}$ and the error variance is $\sigma^2 = {s2}$.
For the ridge slope $b = S_{xy}/(S_{xx} + \lambda)$ with $\lambda = {lam}$, find its variance and its MSE (3 significant figures each).
drills.solution:
$\operatorname{Var}(b) = \sigma^2S_{xx}/(S_{xx} + \lambda)^2 = {s2}({sxx})/{den}^2 =$ **{vr:sig3}**.

Bias $= -\lambda\beta/(S_{xx} + \lambda) = {bias:sig3}$, so $\operatorname{MSE} = \operatorname{Var} + \text{Bias}^2 =$ **{mse:sig3}**.

For comparison, least squares has MSE $\sigma^2/S_{xx} = {mls:sig3}$, and the best penalty is $\lambda^* = \sigma^2/\beta^2 = {lstar:sig3}$.

drills.title: Chance of a false rejection among many tests
drills.prompt:
$m = {m}$ independent tests are each run at level $\alpha = {al}$, and every null hypothesis is true.
Find the probability of at least one false rejection (4 decimals) and the expected number of false rejections.
drills.solution:
$P(\text{no false rejection}) = (1 - {al})^{{m}} = {none:num4}$, so $P(V \ge 1) = 1 - {none:num4} =$ **{fw:num4}**.

Each test rejects with probability ${al}$, so $E(V) = m\alpha = {m}({al}) =$ **{ev}**.

drills.title: Count Benjamini–Hochberg rejections
drills.prompt:
Six sorted p-values are
$${p1:dp3},\; {p2:dp3},\; {p3:dp3},\; {p4:dp3},\; {p5:dp3},\; {p6:dp3}.$$
How many hypotheses does the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure reject at $q = {q}$?
drills.solution:
Compare each $p_{(k)}$ with its line $kq/m$:
$${t1:dp4},\; {t2:dp4},\; {t3:dp4},\; {t4:dp4},\; {t5:dp4},\; {t6:dp4}.$$
Find the *largest* $k$ with $p_{(k)}$ on or below its line (BH is step-up: earlier p-values above their lines don't matter)
and reject the $k$ smallest. Answer: **{k}**.

drills.title: Count Holm rejections
drills.prompt:
Six sorted p-values are
$${p1:dp3},\; {p2:dp3},\; {p3:dp3},\; {p4:dp3},\; {p5:dp3},\; {p6:dp3}.$$
How many hypotheses does Holm's procedure reject at $\alpha = {al}$?
drills.solution:
Holm compares $p_{(k)}$ with $\alpha/(m - k + 1)$:
$${t1:dp4},\; {t2:dp4},\; {t3:dp4},\; {t4:dp4},\; {t5:dp4},\; {t6:dp4}.$$
Start at the smallest p-value and reject while each is on or below its threshold; stop at the first one above.
Answer: **{k}**.

drills.title: Expected share of false discoveries in a screen
drills.prompt:
A screen runs {m:dp0} tests, each at level $\alpha = {al}$. Suppose {pct}% of the null hypotheses are true and each real effect is
detected with power {pw}. Find the expected number of false discoveries and, using expected counts, the fraction of discoveries that are false (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
True nulls: $m_0 = {m0:dp0}$; real effects: ${m1:dp0}$.

Expected false discoveries $= m_0\alpha = {m0:dp0}({al}) =$ **{ev:num4}**; expected true discoveries $= {m1:dp0}({pw}) = {es:num4}$.

Fraction false $\approx {ev:num4}/({ev:num4} + {es:num4}) =$ **{fr:dp3}**.

drills.title: Metropolis acceptance probability
drills.prompt:
A random-walk Metropolis sampler (symmetric normal proposal) targets $N({mu}, {sd}^2)$, so $f(x) = e^{-(x - {mu})^2/(2 \cdot {sd}^2)}$
up to a constant. The current state is $x = {x:num1}$ and the proposal is $y = {y:num1}$. Find the acceptance probability (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
With a symmetric proposal, $\alpha = \min\big(1, f(y)/f(x)\big)$ and
$$\ln\frac{f(y)}{f(x)} = -\frac{({y:num1} - {mu})^2 - ({x:num1} - {mu})^2}{2({sd})^2} = {lr:num4}.$$
So $f(y)/f(x) = {rt:num4}$ and $\alpha = \min(1, {rt:num4}) =$ **{al:num4}**.

drills.title: Effective sample size and Monte Carlo error
drills.prompt:
An MCMC run of $N = {n:dp0}$ draws has autocorrelations close to $\rho^k$ with $\rho = {rho}$, and the draws have
standard deviation $s = {s:num1}$. Estimate the effective sample size (nearest whole number) and the Monte Carlo
standard error of the posterior mean estimate (3 significant figures, using the unrounded ESS).
drills.solution:
$\text{ESS} \approx N\dfrac{1 - \rho}{1 + \rho} = {n:dp0} \cdot \dfrac{1 - {rho}}{1 + {rho}} =$ **{ess:dp1}**.

Monte Carlo standard error $\approx s/\sqrt{\text{ESS}} = {s:num1}/\sqrt{{ess:dp1}} =$ **{mcse:sig3}**
(independent draws would give $s/\sqrt N = {iid:sig3}$).

drills.title: Alternating race by first-step analysis
drills.solution:
Condition on the first round. Ann wins at once with probability {pa:num2}; both miss with
probability $(1 - {pa:num2})(1 - {pb:num2}) = {both:num4}$, and then the game starts over. So
$a = {pa:num2} + {both:num4}\,a$, which gives
$a = \dfrac{{pa:num2}}{1 - {both:num4}} =$ **{win:num4}**.

drills.title: Gambler's ruin probability
drills.prompt:
A gambler bets \$1 at a time, winning each bet with probability {pw:num2}, independently. She
starts with \${st} and stops when she reaches \${nn} or \$0. Find the probability that she
reaches \${nn}, and the probability that she is ruined (4 decimal places).
drills.solution:
Here $\rho = q/p = {qq:num2}/{pw:num2} \approx {rho:num4}$, so
$P_{{st}} = \dfrac{1 - \rho^{{st}}}{1 - \rho^{{nn}}} \approx \dfrac{1 - {rho:num4}^{{st}}}{1 - {rho:num4}^{{nn}}} =$
**{ans:num4}**, and the probability of ruin is $1 - {ans:num4} =$ **{ruin:num4}**.

drills.title: The problem of points
drills.prompt:
Player A wins each round with probability {pw:num2}, independently. A match is interrupted when
A needs {na} more wins and B needs {nb}. What is A's fair share of the stake, that is, her
probability of winning the match had it continued (4 decimal places)?
drills.solution:
The match is surely decided within ${na} + {nb} - 1 = {rounds}$ more rounds, and playing all
{rounds} does not change who wins. A wins the match exactly when she wins at least {na} of
those {rounds} rounds. With $X \sim \text{Bin}({rounds}, {pw:num2})$,
$P(X \ge {na}) = 1 - P(X \le {na} - 1) =$ **{win:num4}**.

drills.title: Combined rates and Simpson's paradox
drills.prompt:
Method A succeeds on {sa1:int} of {na1} easy jobs ({ra1}%) and {sa2:int} of {na2} hard jobs
({ra2}%). Method B succeeds on {sb1:int} of {nb1} easy jobs ({rb1}%) and {sb2:int} of {nb2} hard
jobs ({rb2}%). Find each method's overall success rate as a percent, to 1 decimal place.
drills.solution:
Combine the counts, not the percents. A: $\dfrac{{sa1:int} + {sa2:int}}{{na1} + {na2}} =$
**{tota:num1}%**. B: $\dfrac{{sb1:int} + {sb2:int}}{{nb1} + {nb2}} =$ **{totb:num1}%**.
A is better on easy jobs and on hard jobs, yet B is better overall, because hard jobs make up a
larger share of A's jobs ({hda:num1}%) than of B's ({hdb:num1}%): Simpson's paradox.

drills.title: Selection creates dependence (Berkson)
drills.prompt:
A prize goes to every applicant with a high score ($H$) or a strong essay ($E$). Among all
applicants $P(H) = {ph:num2}$ and $P(E) = {pe:num2}$, independently. Find $P(\text{winner})$,
$P(H \mid \text{winner})$, and $P(H \mid \text{winner with a strong essay})$ (4 decimal places).
drills.solution:
$P(\text{winner}) = P(H \cup E) = {ph:num2} + {pe:num2} - {ph:num2} \times {pe:num2} =$ **{pw:num4}**.
Every high scorer wins, so $P(H \mid \text{winner}) = {ph:num2}/{pw:num4} =$ **{hw:num4}**.
Every strong essay wins, so "winner with a strong essay" is just $E$, and by independence
$P(H \mid E) = P(H) =$ **{ph:num4}**. Among winners, a strong essay makes a high score less
likely: selection has created a negative association.

drills.title: PGF of a sum of independent counts
drills.prompt:
$X \sim \text{Bin}({n}, {pp})$ and $Y \sim \text{Poisson}({lam})$ are independent, and $T = X + Y$.
Use the PGF of $T$ to find $P(T = 0)$ and $P(T = 1)$ (4 decimals), and $E(T)$ and
$\operatorname{Var}(T)$.
drills.solution:
Independent sums multiply PGFs:
$$G_T(s) = ({qq} + {pp}s)^{{n}}\,e^{{lam}(s - 1)}.$$
$P(T = 0) = G_T(0) = {qq}^{{n}}e^{-{lam}} \approx$ **{p0:num4}**.

$P(T = 1)$ is the coefficient of $s$: either $X = 1, Y = 0$ or $X = 0, Y = 1$, so
$P(T = 1) = \left[{n}({pp})({qq})^{{n} - 1} + ({qq})^{{n}}({lam})\right]e^{-{lam}} \approx$ **{p1:num4}**.

$G_T'(1)$ gives $E(T) = {n}({pp}) + {lam} =$ **{mu}**, and the variance adds over independent terms:
$\operatorname{Var}(T) = {n}({pp})({qq}) + {lam} =$ **{var}**.

drills.title: Thinning a Poisson count
drills.prompt:
Requests reach a server as Poisson({lam}) per minute, and each one is flagged for review with
probability {pp}, independently. Let $S$ be the number flagged in a minute. Find $E(S)$ and
$P(S = {k})$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$S$ is a random sum of Poisson({lam})-many Bernoulli({pp}) indicators, so
$$G_S(s) = G_N({qq} + {pp}s) = e^{{lam}({qq} + {pp}s - 1)} = e^{{mu}(s - 1)}.$$
That is the Poisson PGF with mean $\lambda p = {lam}({pp}) =$ **{mu}**, so by uniqueness
$S \sim \text{Poisson}({mu})$ and
$P(S = {k}) = e^{-{mu}}\dfrac{{mu}^{{k}}}{{k}!} \approx$ **{prob:num4}**.

drills.title: Extinction probability of a branching process
drills.prompt:
In a branching process each individual has 0, 1 or 2 children with probabilities {p0}, {p1} and
{p2}. Starting from one individual, find the mean offspring number $m$, the probability
$P(Z_2 = 0)$ that the line is extinct by generation 2, and the extinction probability $q$
(4 decimals).
drills.solution:
The offspring PGF is $f(s) = {p0} + {p1}s + {p2}s^2$, so $m = f'(1) = {p1} + 2({p2}) =$ **{m}**.
Since $m > 1$, survival is possible.

$P(Z_1 = 0) = f(0) = {p0}$, and $P(Z_2 = 0) = f(f(0)) = f({p0}) = {p0} + {p1}({p0}) + {p2}({p0})^2 \approx$ **{z2:num4}**.

The extinction probability is the smallest root of $f(s) = s$, that is of
${p2}s^2 + ({p1} - 1)s + {p0} = 0$. One root is $s = 1$ and the product of the roots is
${p0}/{p2}$, so the other root is $q = {p0}/{p2} \approx$ **{q:num4}**.

drills.title: Poisson approximation with Le Cam's bound
drills.prompt:
$X \sim \text{Bin}({nn:dp0}, {pp:sig3})$. Using the Poisson approximation, find $\lambda$ and
$P(X = {k})$ (4 decimals), and give the bound that Le Cam's inequality puts on the total variation
error.
drills.solution:
$\lambda = np = {nn:dp0}({pp:sig3}) =$ **{lam}**, and
$P(X = {k}) \approx e^{-\lambda}\dfrac{\lambda^{{k}}}{{k}!} \approx$ **{approx:num4}**.

Le Cam: every $p_i = {pp:sig3}$, so $d_{TV} \le \sum p_i^2 = np^2 = {nn:dp0}({pp:sig3})^2 =$ **{bound:sig3}**.
(The exact binomial value is {exact:num4}, well within the bound.)

drills.title: Unequal probabilities and the Poisson approximation
drills.prompt:
Four independent components fail this year with probabilities {a}, {b}, {c} and {d}. Let $S$ be
the number that fail. Find $\lambda = E(S)$, Le Cam's bound $\sum p_i^2$, the exact $P(S = 0)$ and
its Poisson approximation (4 decimals each).
drills.solution:
$\lambda = {a} + {b} + {c} + {d} =$ **{lam}** and
$\sum p_i^2 = {a}^2 + {b}^2 + {c}^2 + {d}^2 =$ **{ssq:dp4}**.

Exactly, all four must survive: $P(S = 0) = (1 - {a})(1 - {b})(1 - {c})(1 - {d}) \approx$ **{exact:dp4}**.

Poisson: $P(S = 0) \approx e^{-\lambda} = e^{-{lam}} \approx$ **{approx:dp4}**. The two differ by
less than the bound {ssq:dp4}, as Le Cam's inequality guarantees.

drills.title: Weibull survival, hazard and B10 life
drills.prompt:
A component's life in hours is Weibull with shape $k = {kk}$ and scale $s = {sc:dp0}$, so
$S(x) = e^{-(x/{sc:dp0})^{{kk}}}$. Find $P(X > {t0:dp0})$ (4 decimals), the hazard rate $h({t0:dp0})$ per hour
(3 significant figures) and the B10 life in hours (3 significant figures).
drills.solution:
$\dfrac{x}{s} = \dfrac{{t0:dp0}}{{sc:dp0}} = {fr}$, so $H({t0:dp0}) = ({fr})^{{kk}} \approx {hh:num4}$ and
$P(X > {t0:dp0}) = e^{-{hh:num4}} \approx$ **{surv:num4}**.

$h(x) = \dfrac{k}{s}\left(\dfrac{x}{s}\right)^{k - 1}$, so $h({t0:dp0}) = \dfrac{{kk}}{{sc:dp0}}({fr})^{{kk} - 1} \approx$ **{haz:sig3}** per hour.

B10: solve $1 - e^{-(x/{sc:dp0})^{{kk}}} = 0.10$, so $(x/{sc:dp0})^{{kk}} = -\ln 0.9 \approx 0.10536$ and
$x = {sc:dp0}\,(0.10536)^{1/{kk}} \approx$ **{b10:sig3}** hours.

drills.title: Weibull mean and median
drills.prompt:
A lifetime is Weibull with shape $k = {kk}$ and scale $s = {sc:dp0}$. Find its mean and its median
(3 significant figures each).
drills.solution:
Mean: $E(X) = s\,\Gamma\!\left(1 + \tfrac1k\right) = {sc:dp0}\,\Gamma(1 + {ik:num4}) \approx {sc:dp0} \times {g1:num4} \approx$ **{mu:sig3}**.

Median: $e^{-(m/{sc:dp0})^{{kk}}} = \tfrac12$ gives $(m/{sc:dp0})^{{kk}} = \ln 2$, so $m = {sc:dp0}\,(\ln 2)^{1/{kk}} \approx$ **{med:sig3}**.

drills.title: Weibull components in series
drills.prompt:
A unit works only while all {nn} of its parts work. The parts fail independently, and each part's
life in hours is Weibull with shape {kk} and scale {sc:dp0}. Find the scale of the unit's (Weibull)
lifetime (3 significant figures) and the probability that the unit lasts more than {t0:dp0} hours
(4 decimals).
drills.solution:
In series the cumulative hazards add: $H_T(x) = {nn}\,(x/{sc:dp0})^{{kk}} = (x/s')^{{kk}}$ with
$s' = {sc:dp0} \cdot {nn}^{-1/{kk}} \approx$ **{sys:sig3}** hours (same shape {kk}).

$P(T > {t0:dp0}) = e^{-{nn}({fr})^{{kk}}} \approx$ **{psys:num4}**, compared with {one:num4} for a single part.

drills.title: Waiting at a traffic light
drills.prompt:
A light is red for {red} seconds and green for {grn} seconds (ignore amber), and you arrive at a time
uniform over the {cyc}-second cycle. If it is red, you wait for the rest of the red phase. Find
$P(W = 0)$ and $P(W > {w0})$ (4 decimals) and the expected wait $E(W)$ in seconds (2 decimals).
drills.solution:
The wait is 0 when you arrive on green: $P(W = 0) = \dfrac{{grn}}{{cyc}} \approx$ **{p0:num4}** (a point mass).
On red (probability $\tfrac{{red}}{{cyc}}$) the remaining red time is uniform on $(0, {red})$.

$P(W > {w0}) = \dfrac{{red}}{{cyc}} \cdot \dfrac{{red} - {w0}}{{red}} \approx$ **{pw:num4}**.

$E(W) = \dfrac{{grn}}{{cyc}} \cdot 0 + \dfrac{{red}}{{cyc}} \cdot {halfr} \approx$ **{ew:num2}** seconds.

drills.title: Expected payment with a deductible
drills.prompt:
Losses are exponential with mean {th:dp0} dollars, and a policy pays the loss minus a deductible of
{ded:dp0} dollars (nothing if the loss is below the deductible). Find the probability that a loss pays
nothing (4 decimals) and the expected payment per loss in dollars (2 decimals).
drills.solution:
No payment when $X \le {ded:dp0}$: $1 - e^{-{ded:dp0}/{th:dp0}} = 1 - e^{-{fr}} \approx$ **{p0:num4}**.

$E[(X - {ded:dp0})^+] = \displaystyle\int_{{ded:dp0}}^\infty e^{-x/{th:dp0}}\,dx = {th:dp0}\,e^{-{fr}} \approx$ **{epay:num2}** dollars.
(The policyholder's share is $E[\min(X, {ded:dp0})] = {th:dp0}(1 - e^{-{fr}}) \approx$ {elim:num2} dollars, and the two add to {th:dp0}.)

drills.title: A censored exponential life test
drills.solution:
Censored means $X > {cc:dp0}$: $e^{-{cc:dp0}/{mm:dp0}} = e^{-{fr}} \approx$ **{pc:num4}**.

$E(T) = \displaystyle\int_0^{{cc:dp0}} P(X > x)\,dx = \int_0^{{cc:dp0}} e^{-x/{mm:dp0}}\,dx = {mm:dp0}(1 - e^{-{fr}}) \approx$ **{et:num1}** hours,
well below the true mean {mm:dp0}.

drills.title: Variance of a linear combination from a covariance matrix
drills.prompt:
The random vector $(X_1, X_2, X_3)$ has covariance matrix
$$\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} {v1} & {c12} & {c13} \\ {c12} & {v2} & {c23} \\ {c13} & {c23} & {v3} \end{pmatrix}.$$
Find $\operatorname{Var}({a1:coef}X_1 {a2:signedcoef}X_2 {a3:signedcoef}X_3)$.
drills.solution:
With $\mathbf{a} = ({a1}, {a2}, {a3})^\top$, $\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{a}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{a} = \sum_i a_i^2\Sigma_{ii} + 2\sum_{i<j}a_ia_j\Sigma_{ij}$.

Diagonal part: $({a1})^2({v1}) + ({a2})^2({v2}) + ({a3})^2({v3}) = {dg:int}$.

Off-diagonal part: $2\big[({a1})({a2})({c12}) + ({a1})({a3})({c13}) + ({a2})({a3})({c23})\big] = {od:int}$.

Total: ${dg:int} + ({od:int}) =$ **{vq:int}**.

drills.title: Cholesky factor of a 2 by 2 covariance matrix
drills.prompt:
Find the lower-triangular matrix $L = \begin{pmatrix} \ell_{11} & 0 \\ \ell_{21} & \ell_{22} \end{pmatrix}$ with $\ell_{11}, \ell_{22} > 0$ and
$LL^\top = \begin{pmatrix} {s11} & {s12} \\ {s12} & {s22} \end{pmatrix}$.
drills.solution:
Multiplying out, $LL^\top = \begin{pmatrix} \ell_{11}^2 & \ell_{11}\ell_{21} \\ \ell_{11}\ell_{21} & \ell_{21}^2 + \ell_{22}^2 \end{pmatrix}$.

- $\ell_{11} = \sqrt{{s11}} =$ **{l11}**.
- $\ell_{21} = {s12}/{l11} =$ **{l21}**.
- $\ell_{22} = \sqrt{{s22} - {l21sq}} =$ **{l22}**.

So $X_1 = \mu_1 + {l11:coef}Z_1$ and $X_2 = \mu_2 {l21:signedcoef}Z_1 {l22:signedcoef}Z_2$ has this covariance matrix.

drills.title: Mahalanobis distance in a bivariate normal
drills.prompt:
$(X, Y)$ is bivariate normal with $\mu_X = {mx}$, $\sigma_X = {sx}$, $\mu_Y = {my}$, $\sigma_Y = {sy}$ and $\rho = {rho}$.
For the point $(x, y) = ({xx:num1}, {yy:num1})$, find the squared Mahalanobis distance $Q$ (2 decimals) and the
probability $P(Q(X, Y) \ge Q)$ that a random point lies at least this far out (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Standardize: $z_x = ({xx:num1} - {mx})/{sx} = {zx:num1}$ and $z_y = ({yy:num1} - {my})/{sy} = {zy:num1}$.

$Q = \dfrac{z_x^2 - 2\rho z_xz_y + z_y^2}{1 - \rho^2} = \dfrac{{nm:num4}}{{den:num4}} =$ **{qq:num2}**.

In two dimensions $Q(X, Y) \sim \chi^2_2$, the exponential distribution with mean 2, so
$P(Q(X, Y) \ge {qq:num2}) = e^{-{qq:num2}/2} =$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: The range of a uniform sample
drills.prompt:
{nn} values are drawn independently from the Uniform$(0, {th})$ distribution. Find the probability that their
range $R = X_{(n)} - X_{(1)}$ is at most {rr} (4 decimals), and the expected range (2 decimals).
drills.solution:
Rescale to $(0, 1)$: $r/\theta = {rr}/{th} = {fr:num2}$. For $n$ uniforms, $P(R \le r) = n\,(r/\theta)^{n-1} - (n-1)(r/\theta)^n$:

$P(R \le {rr}) = {nn}({fr:num2})^{{n1:int}} - {n1:int}({fr:num2})^{{nn:int}} =$ **{pr:num4}**.

$E[R] = \theta\,\dfrac{n-1}{n+1} = {th}\cdot\dfrac{{n1:int}}{{nn:int} + 1} =$ **{er:num2}**.

drills.title: Mean and SD of an exponential order statistic
drills.prompt:
{nn} components are switched on together; their lifetimes are iid exponential with mean {th} hours. Find the
mean and the SD of the time of failure number {kk} (both to 1 decimal place).
drills.solution:
By the Rényi representation the gaps between failures are independent exponentials. While $m$ components
are still working, the next gap has mean $\theta/m$ and variance $\theta^2/m^2$. Failure number {kk} comes after the
gaps with $m = {nn}, \dots, {lo:int}$:

$E = {th:dp0}\displaystyle\sum_{m={lo:int}}^{{nn:int}}\frac1m = {th:dp0}({s1:dp4}) =$ **{ek:num1}** hours.

$\operatorname{Var} = {th:dp0}^2\displaystyle\sum_{m={lo:int}}^{{nn:int}}\frac1{m^2} = {th:dp0}^2({s2:dp4})$, so the SD is **{sk:num1}** hours.

drills.title: How close together are exponential failures?
drills.prompt:
{nn} components have iid exponential lifetimes with mean {th} hours. Find the probability that every failure
happens within {rr:dp0} hours of the first failure, that is $P(X_{(n)} - X_{(1)} \le {rr:dp0})$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
After the first failure, the remaining gaps are independent exponentials with rates $(n-1)\lambda, \dots, \lambda$:
exactly the gaps of the maximum of $n - 1 = {n1:int}$ iid exponentials. So the range is distributed as that maximum, and

$P(R \le {rr:dp0}) = \big(1 - e^{-{rr:dp0}/{th}}\big)^{{n1:int}} = (1 - e^{-{fr:num2}})^{{n1:int}} =$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Sample size from Hoeffding's inequality
drills.prompt:
Each observation is known to lie between 0 and {rg}; nothing else is known about its distribution.
Using Hoeffding's inequality, find the smallest $n$ that guarantees
$P(|\bar X_n - \mu| \ge {eps}) \le {dl}$.
drills.solution:
Two-sided Hoeffding for values in an interval of length {rg}:
$P(|\bar X_n - \mu| \ge {eps}) \le 2\exp\!\Big(-\dfrac{2n({eps})^2}{{rg}^2}\Big)$.
Setting this $\le {dl}$ and taking logs: $n \ge \dfrac{{rg}^2\ln(2/{dl})}{2({eps})^2} = {raw:num2}$.
Round up: $n =$ **{nh:int}**.

drills.title: Chernoff and Hoeffding bounds for a binomial tail
drills.prompt:
$S \sim \text{Bin}({nn}, {pp})$. Find (a) the Chernoff bound $e^{-nD(a\,\|\,p)}$ and (b) the Hoeffding bound
$e^{-2n(a - p)^2}$ for $P(S \ge {kk:int})$. Give each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
The cutoff as a proportion is $a = {kk:int}/{nn} = {aa:num2}$, above $p = {pp}$ (the mean is {mu:num1}).

(a) $D(a\,\|\,p) = {aa:num2}\ln\dfrac{{aa:num2}}{{pp}} + {qa:num2}\ln\dfrac{{qa:num2}}{{qp:num2}}$. Computing,
$D = {kl:dp3}$ (to 3 places; keep full precision), so the bound is $e^{-{nn}D} =$ **{ch:sig3}**.

(b) $e^{-2({nn})({aa:num2} - {pp})^2} =$ **{hf:sig3}**. It is never smaller than the Chernoff bound, because $D(a\,\|\,p) \ge 2(a - p)^2$.

drills.title: Large-sample interval for a mean using S
drills.prompt:
A random sample of {nn} observations from a population of unknown shape has $\bar x = {xb:num1}$ and $s = {sd:num1}$.
Using the CLT with Slutsky's theorem, give an approximate {cf} confidence interval for $\mu$. Give 2 decimals.
drills.solution:
By the CLT and Slutsky, $(\bar X - \mu)/(S/\sqrt n)$ is approximately $N(0, 1)$ for large $n$, so we use $z = {zz:num4}$.
Standard error: ${sd:num1}/\sqrt{{nn}} = {se:num4}$. Margin: ${zz:num4} \times {se:num4} = {me:num4}$.
Interval: ${xb:num1} \pm {me:num4}$, from **{lo:num2}** to **{hi:num2}**.

drills.title: Wald interval for a proportion
drills.prompt:
In a random sample of {nn} people, {xx:int} have a certain trait. Give the approximate {cf} Wald interval
$\hat p \pm z\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)/n}$ for the population proportion. Give 3 decimals.
drills.solution:
$\hat p = {xx:int}/{nn} = {ph:num4}$. Slutsky lets us use $\hat p$ inside the standard error:
$\sqrt{{ph:num4}(1 - {ph:num4})/{nn}} = {se:sig3}$. With $z = {zz:num4}$ the margin is {me:num4},
so the interval runs from **{lo:dp3}** to **{hi:dp3}**.

drills.title: One Newton step for a truncated Poisson MLE
drills.prompt:
A log records daily fault counts only on days with at least one fault, modeled as zero-truncated
Poisson$(\lambda)$. There are $n = {nn}$ logged days with $\sum x_i = {sx}$, so
$$\ell'(\lambda) = \frac{{sx}}{\lambda} - \frac{{nn}}{1 - e^{-\lambda}}, \qquad \ell''(\lambda) = -\frac{{sx}}{\lambda^2} + \frac{{nn}\,e^{-\lambda}}{(1 - e^{-\lambda})^2}.$$
Starting from $\lambda_0 = {l0}$, find $\ell'(\lambda_0)$, $\ell''(\lambda_0)$ and the next Newton iterate $\lambda_1$ (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
With $e^{-{l0}} = {e0:num4}$:
$\ell'({l0}) = {sx}/{l0} - {nn}/(1 - {e0:num4}) = {s1:dp3}$ and
$\ell''({l0}) = -{sx}/{l0}^2 + {nn}({e0:num4})/(1 - {e0:num4})^2 = {s2:dp3}$.
Newton: $\lambda_1 = \lambda_0 - \ell'(\lambda_0)/\ell''(\lambda_0) = {l0} - ({s1:dp3})/({s2:dp3}) =$ **{l1:dp3}**.
(Repeating the step converges to the MLE, which solves $\bar x = \lambda/(1 - e^{-\lambda})$ with $\bar x = {xbar:num2}$.)

drills.title: Standard error and Wald interval for an exponential rate
drills.prompt:
$n = {nn}$ component lifetimes, modeled as exponential with rate $\lambda$, total $\sum x_i = {sx:num1}$ hours.
Find the MLE $\hat\lambda$, its standard error $1/\sqrt{J(\hat\lambda)}$ from the observed information, and the
{lev} Wald interval for $\lambda$. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
$\ell(\lambda) = n\ln\lambda - \lambda\sum x_i$, so $\hat\lambda = n/\sum x_i = {nn}/{sx:num1} =$ **{lam:num4}** per hour.
$\ell''(\lambda) = -n/\lambda^2$, so $J(\hat\lambda) = {nn}/{lam:num4}^2 = {jj:num1}$ and SE $= 1/\sqrt{J} = \hat\lambda/\sqrt n =$ **{se:num4}**.
With $z = {zc:num4}$ ({lev}): ${lam:num4} \pm {zc:num4} \times {se:num4}$, from **{lo:num4}** to **{hi:num4}**.

drills.title: Standard errors from a two-parameter information matrix
drills.prompt:
The information matrix of a whole sample for two parameters $(\eta_1, \eta_2)$, evaluated at the MLE, is
$$\begin{pmatrix} {aa} & {bb} \\ {bb} & {dd} \end{pmatrix}.$$
Find the approximate standard errors of $\hat\eta_1$ and $\hat\eta_2$ and the correlation between them (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
The covariance matrix is the inverse. Determinant: ${aa} \times {dd} - ({bb})^2 = {det}$, so
$\operatorname{Var}(\hat\eta_1) \approx {dd}/{det} = {v1:num4}$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\eta_2) \approx {aa}/{det} = {v2:num4}$; the covariance is $-({bb})/{det}$.
SEs: **{se1:num4}** and **{se2:num4}**. Correlation: $\dfrac{-({bb})/{det}}{\text{SE}_1\,\text{SE}_2} = -({bb})/\sqrt{{aa} \times {dd}} =$ **{rho:num4}**.
(The naive $1/\sqrt{{aa}} = {nv1:num4}$ would ignore the second parameter.)

drills.title: Minimax versus maximum likelihood for a proportion
drills.prompt:
$X \sim$ Binomial$({nn}, p)$, squared-error loss. The minimax estimator has the form $\dfrac{X + a}{{nn} + 2a}$.
Find $a$, the (constant) risk of the minimax estimator, and the risk of the MLE $X/{nn}$ when $p = {pp}$.
Give the risks to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
The risk of $(X + a)/(n + 2a)$ is constant when $a = \sqrt n/2 = \sqrt{{nn}}/2 =$ **{ka}**, giving $\dfrac{X + {ka}}{{den}}$ with risk
$\dfrac{1}{4(1 + \sqrt n)^2} = \dfrac{1}{4(1 + {rt})^2} =$ **{rmm:sig3}**.
The MLE is unbiased, so its risk is its variance $p(1-p)/n = {pp}(1 - {pp})/{nn} =$ **{rml:sig3}**.
The MLE is better at this $p$ exactly when its risk is the smaller of the two.

drills.title: Risk of shrinking a normal mean toward a prior guess
drills.prompt:
$\bar X$ is the mean of {nn} readings with $\sigma = {sig}$, so $\bar X \sim N(\theta, v)$ with $v = \sigma^2/n$. The prior is
$\theta \sim N({m0}, {tau}^2)$. Find the weight $c$ in the Bayes estimator $c\bar X + (1 - c)({m0})$, its risk (MSE) when the true
$\theta = {tt}$, and its Bayes risk. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
$v = {sig}^2/{nn} = {vv:num4}$ and $\tau^2 = {tau}^2$, so $c = \dfrac{\tau^2}{\tau^2 + v} =$ **{cc:num4}**.
Risk $= c^2v + (1 - c)^2(\theta - \mu_0)^2 = {cc:num4}^2({vv:num4}) + (1 - {cc:num4})^2({dd})^2 =$ **{rk:num4}**
(compare $v = {vv:num4}$ for $\bar X$). Bayes risk $= cv =$ **{br:num4}**, the posterior variance.

drills.title: Wilson interval for a proportion
drills.prompt: In {nn} trials there are {xx} successes. Find the {lev} Wilson interval for $p$. Give the endpoints to 3 decimals.
drills.solution:
$\hat p = {xx}/{nn} = {ph:num4}$, $z = {zc:num4}$, $z^2/n = {z2n:num4}$.
Center: $\dfrac{\hat p + z^2/(2n)}{1 + z^2/n} = {cen:num4}$. Half-width: $\dfrac{z}{1 + z^2/n}\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n} + \dfrac{z^2}{4n^2}} = {hw:num4}$.
Interval: from **{lo:dp3}** to **{hi:dp3}**. (The Wald interval would be ${wl:dp3}$ to ${wh:dp3}$.)

drills.title: Upper bound after zero events
drills.prompt:
A part passes all {nn} tests, with no failures. Find the exact one-sided {lev} upper confidence bound for its
failure probability, $1 - \alpha^{1/n}$, and its approximation $-\ln(\alpha)/n$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
The bound is the $p$ at which zero failures has probability $\alpha = {al:num2}$: $(1 - p)^{{nn}} = {al:num2}$, so
$p = 1 - {al:num2}^{1/{nn}} =$ **{up:num4}**. Since $\ln(1 - p) \approx -p$, $p \approx -\ln({al:num2})/{nn} = {lal:num4}/{nn} =$ **{apx:num4}**.
(For 95%, $-\ln 0.05 \approx 3$: the rule of three.)

drills.title: Exact coverage of a Wald interval
drills.prompt:
With $n = 5$ trials, the {lv}% Wald interval is $\hat p \pm {zc}\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)/5}$. If the true $p = {pp}$, what
is the exact probability that the interval contains $p$? Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
The half-widths are 0 for $x = 0$ and 5, ${h1:num4}$ for $x = 1$ and 4, and ${h2:num4}$ for $x = 2$ and 3. For each $x$, the
contribution is $P(X = x)$ if $|x/5 - {pp}|$ is at most the half-width, and 0 otherwise:
$x = 0$: {c0:num4}; $x = 1$: {c1:num4}; $x = 2$: {c2:num4}; $x = 3$: {c3:num4}; $x = 4$: {c4:num4}; $x = 5$: {c5:num4}.
Coverage $=$ **{cvg:num4}**, compared with the nominal {lv}%.

drills.title: Score and Wald statistics for a proportion
drills.topic: Wald, score and likelihood ratio tests
drills.prompt:
In {nn} independent trials there are {xx} successes. For $H_0: p = {p0}$ against $H_1: p \ne {p0}$,
compute the score statistic $S$ and the Wald statistic $W$ (both on the chi-square scale, 3 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\hat p = {xx}/{nn} = {phat:num4}$. The score statistic uses the null variance
$p_0(1 - p_0)/n = {nv:sig4}$:
$S = \dfrac{(\hat p - p_0)^2}{p_0(1-p_0)/n} =$ **{sc:dp3}** (the square of the one-proportion $z$).

The Wald statistic uses the variance at the MLE, $\hat p(1 - \hat p)/n = {av:sig4}$:
$W = \dfrac{(\hat p - p_0)^2}{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n} =$ **{wd:dp3}**.

Each is compared with $\chi^2_1$ (3.841 at the 5% level).

drills.title: Wald, score and likelihood ratio statistics for a Poisson mean
drills.topic: Wald, score and likelihood ratio tests
drills.prompt:
Counts $X_1, \dots, X_{{nn}}$ are Poisson($\lambda$) with total $\sum x_i = {tot}$. For $H_0: \lambda = {lam0}$,
compute the Wald, score and likelihood ratio statistics (3 decimals each).
drills.solution:
$\hat\lambda = \bar x = {tot}/{nn} = {xbar:num4}$ and $I(\lambda) = 1/\lambda$.

Wald (variance at the MLE): $W = \dfrac{(\bar x - \lambda_0)^2}{\bar x/n} =$ **{wd:dp3}**.

Score (variance at $\lambda_0$): $S = \dfrac{(\bar x - \lambda_0)^2}{\lambda_0/n} =$ **{sc:dp3}**.

Likelihood ratio: $2\left[\sum x_i\ln\dfrac{\bar x}{\lambda_0} - n(\bar x - \lambda_0)\right] =$ **{lr:dp3}**.

All three are compared with $\chi^2_1$; they differ because they measure the distance from $\lambda_0$ in different ways.

drills.title: Wald's SPRT boundaries
drills.prompt:
A sequential probability ratio test is to have Type I error probability $\alpha = {al}$ and Type II
error probability $\beta = {be}$. Find Wald's lower and upper boundaries for the log likelihood ratio
sum $S_n$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Lower (accept $H_0$): $\ln\dfrac{\beta}{1 - \alpha} = \ln\dfrac{{be}}{{qa:sig4}} =$ **{lowb:num4}**.

Upper (reject $H_0$): $\ln\dfrac{1 - \beta}{\alpha} = \ln\dfrac{{qb:sig4}}{{al}} =$ **{upb:num4}**.

drills.title: SPRT acceptance and rejection lines for a defect rate
drills.prompt:
Items are defective independently with probability $p$. An SPRT of $H_0: p = {p0}$ against
$H_1: p = {p1}$ uses $\alpha = {al}$ and $\beta = {be}$. After $n$ items with $d$ defectives it rejects when
$d \ge h_1 + sn$ and accepts $H_0$ when $d \le -h_0 + sn$. Find $s$, $h_1$ and $h_0$ (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
A defective adds $\ln({p1}/{p0}) = {du:num4}$ and a good item adds $\ln\dfrac{1 - {p1}}{1 - {p0}} = {dv:num4}$, so
$S_n = d({du:num4}) + (n - d)({dv:num4})$. Divide by ${du:num4} - ({dv:num4}) = {den:num4}$.

Boundaries: lower $\ln\frac{\beta}{1-\alpha} = {lowb:num4}$, upper $\ln\frac{1-\beta}{\alpha} = {upb:num4}$.

Solving $S_n \ge$ upper and $S_n \le$ lower for $d$:
slope $s = \dfrac{-({dv:num4})}{{den:num4}} =$ **{slope:dp3}**,
rejection intercept $h_1 = \dfrac{{upb:num4}}{{den:num4}} =$ **{hrej:dp3}**,
acceptance intercept $h_0 = \dfrac{-({lowb:num4})}{{den:num4}} =$ **{hacc:dp3}**.

drills.title: Average sample number of an SPRT
drills.prompt:
An SPRT of $H_0: p = {p0}$ against $H_1: p = {p1}$ for Bernoulli data uses $\alpha = {al}$ and $\beta = {be}$
with Wald's boundaries. Use Wald's approximation (ignore overshoot) to find the average sample number
under $H_0$ and under $H_1$ (3 significant figures).
drills.solution:
Increments: defective ${du:num4}$, good ${dv:num4}$. Boundaries: $a = {lowb:num4}$, $b = {upb:num4}$.

Mean increments: $E_0(Z) = {p0}({du:num4}) + (1 - {p0})({dv:num4}) = {ez0:sig4}$ and
$E_1(Z) = {p1}({du:num4}) + (1 - {p1})({dv:num4}) = {ez1:sig4}$.

By Wald's identity, $E_0(N) \approx \dfrac{(1-\alpha)a + \alpha b}{E_0(Z)} =$ **{asn0:sig3}** and
$E_1(N) \approx \dfrac{\beta a + (1-\beta) b}{E_1(Z)} =$ **{asn1:sig3}**.

drills.title: Fit a regression with two predictors
drills.prompt:
A regression of $y$ on two predictors has means $\bar x_1 = {x1b:num1}$, $\bar x_2 = {x2b:num1}$,
$\bar y = {ybv:num1}$ and centered sums of squares and products

$$S_{11} = {s11v}, \quad S_{22} = {s22v}, \quad S_{12} = {s12v}, \quad S_{1y} = {s1y:num1}, \quad S_{2y} = {s2y:num1}.$$

Find the least squares coefficients $b_1$, $b_2$ and $b_0$ (4 decimals each).
drills.solution:
Solve $\begin{bmatrix} {s11v} & {s12v} \\ {s12v} & {s22v} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} {s1y:num1} \\ {s2y:num1} \end{bmatrix}$.
The determinant is $S_{11}S_{22} - S_{12}^2 = {det:dp0}$.

$b_1 = \dfrac{S_{22}S_{1y} - S_{12}S_{2y}}{{det:dp0}} =$ **{b1:num4}**, $\quad b_2 = \dfrac{S_{11}S_{2y} - S_{12}S_{1y}}{{det:dp0}} =$ **{b2:num4}**.

$b_0 = \bar y - b_1\bar x_1 - b_2\bar x_2 =$ **{b0:num4}**.

drills.title: t test for one coefficient in a multiple regression
drills.prompt:
A regression on $n = {nn}$ observations has {kk} predictors plus an intercept and residual
standard deviation $s = {sres:num2}$. For one coefficient, $b_j = {bj:num2}$ and the matching
diagonal entry of $(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ is $c_{jj} = {cjj:num4}$. Find $\text{SE}(b_j)$
(4 decimals), the $t$ statistic for $H_0: \beta_j = 0$ (3 decimals) and the two-sided p-value
(4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\text{SE}(b_j) = s\sqrt{c_{jj}} = {sres:num2}\sqrt{{cjj:num4}} =$ **{se:num4}**.

$t = b_j/\text{SE}(b_j) =$ **{tt:dp3}** on $n - p = {nn} - {pp} = {dfree}$ df; two-sided p-value $\approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: R-squared, adjusted R-squared and the overall F test
drills.prompt:
A regression on $n = {nn}$ observations with {kk} predictors plus an intercept has
$\text{SST} = {sst:dp0}$ and $\text{SSE} = {sse:dp1}$. Find $R^2$ and adjusted $R^2$ (4 decimals each), the
overall $F$ statistic (2 decimals) and its p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$p = {pp}$ coefficients. $R^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST} = 1 - {sse:dp1}/{sst:dp0} =$ **{rsq:num4}**.

$R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - \dfrac{\text{SSE}/(n - p)}{\text{SST}/(n - 1)} = 1 - \dfrac{{sse:dp1}/{dfe}}{{sst:dp0}/({nn} - 1)} =$ **{radj:num4}**.

$\text{SSR} = {ssr:dp1}$, so $F = \dfrac{\text{SSR}/{kk}}{\text{SSE}/{dfe}} =$ **{ff:num2}** on ({kk}, {dfe}) df; p-value $\approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Randomized block ANOVA from raw data
drills.prompt:
Three treatments are compared in four blocks (one observation per treatment in each block):

$$\begin{array}{c|cccc} & \text{Block 1} & \text{Block 2} & \text{Block 3} & \text{Block 4} \\ \hline \text{T1} & {y11} & {y12} & {y13} & {y14} \\ \text{T2} & {y21} & {y22} & {y23} & {y24} \\ \text{T3} & {y31} & {y32} & {y33} & {y34} \end{array}$$

Find SSTr, SSB and SSE (2 decimals each) and the treatment $F$ statistic (2 decimals).
drills.solution:
Treatment means ${tm1:num2}, {tm2:num2}, {tm3:num2}$; block means ${bm1:num2}, {bm2:num2}, {bm3:num2}, {bm4:num2}$; grand mean ${gm:num4}$.

$\text{SSTr} = 4\sum(\bar y_{i\cdot} - \bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2 =$ **{sstr:num2}**, $\quad \text{SSB} = 3\sum(\bar y_{\cdot j} - \bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2 =$ **{ssb:num2}**.

$\text{SST} = {sst:dp2}$, so $\text{SSE} = \text{SST} - \text{SSTr} - \text{SSB} =$ **{sse:num2}** on $(2)(3) = 6$ df.

$F = \dfrac{\text{SSTr}/2}{\text{SSE}/6} = \dfrac{{mstr:num4}}{{mse:num4}} =$ **{ff:num2}** on (2, 6) df (p-value {pv:num4}).

drills.title: Sums of squares in a 2 by 2 factorial
drills.prompt:
A balanced $2 \times 2$ factorial has $r = {rr}$ observations per cell, cell means

$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & B_1 & B_2 \\ \hline A_1 & {m11} & {m12} \\ A_2 & {m21} & {m22} \end{array}$$

and $\text{MSE} = {mse:num1}$. Find $\text{SS}_A$, $\text{SS}_B$, $\text{SS}_{AB}$ (2 decimals each) and the $F$ statistic for
interaction (2 decimals).
drills.solution:
Row means ${ga:num2}$ and ${gb2:num2}$, column means ${ca:num2}$ and ${cb:num2}$, grand mean ${gm:num2}$.

$\text{SS}_A = br\sum(\bar y_{i\cdot\cdot} - \bar y)^2 = 2({rr})\big[({ga:num2} - {gm:num2})^2 + ({gb2:num2} - {gm:num2})^2\big] =$ **{ssa:num2}**, and likewise $\text{SS}_B =$ **{ssb:num2}**.

Here $\bar y_{11} - \bar y_{12} - \bar y_{21} + \bar y_{22} = {con}$, and in a $2 \times 2$ design each of the four interaction
estimates is plus or minus a quarter of it, so $\text{SS}_{AB} = 4r({con}/4)^2 =$ **{ssab:num2}**.

$F_{AB} = \text{SS}_{AB}/\text{MSE} =$ **{fab:num2}** on (1, {dfe}) df (p-value {pv:num4}).
